# Overview



This page is the entry point to the DyMoE-Pert documentation. It explains what the project does, how its main idea works at a glance, and how the repository is organized, so that a first-time reader can decide exactly where to go next. Everything on this page is verified directly against the source code and README; deeper implementation details are left to the dedicated Deep Dive pages.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L10)

## What Problem Does DyMoE-Pert Solve?

DyMoE-Pert predicts how a genetic perturbation — switching a gene off or knocking it down — changes single-cell gene expression. The central challenge it addresses is **generalization to unseen perturbations**: wet-lab screens can never measure every single-gene or combinatorial intervention, so the model must estimate the effect of perturbations it has never observed during training. The README states this motivation explicitly and notes that predictions can help prioritize which new experiments to run.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L10)

The core insight of the method is that a perturbed gene is described by **two complementary information sources**: biological knowledge-graph embeddings (which encode functional relationships between genes) and representations from the single-cell foundation model **scGPT** (which encode learned genomic context). Instead of fusing these two signals with one fixed rule for every perturbation, DyMoE-Pert *learns* how much to trust each source on a per-input basis — this is the "Dynamic" in its name, implemented as a residual mixture-of-experts fusion module.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L10), [models/model.py](models/model.py#L99-L297)

## How the Method Works at a Glance

The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow verified in the code: two pretrained embedding tables are projected into a shared hidden space, passed through three experts plus a residual base branch, weighted by a soft router, and finally decoded into predicted post-perturbation expression.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Inputs["Multimodal Gene Inputs"]
        KG["Knowledge-graph embedding<br/>(gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz)"]
        SC["scGPT embedding<br/>(gene_embeddings_&lt;dataset&gt;_512.npy)"]
        PERT["Perturbation embedding<br/>(gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz)"]
    end

    subgraph Fusion["ResidualMoEFusion (models/model.py)"]
        direction TB
        PROJ["Projectors: KG 128d → hidden, scGPT 512d → hidden"]
        BASE["Residual base branch<br/>(shared multimodal MLP)"]
        E1["KG expert"]
        E2["scGPT expert"]
        E3["Cross-modal interaction expert"]
        ROUTER["Soft router<br/>(dynamic or fixed_uniform)"]
        SUM["output_norm(base + Σ wᵢ · expertᵢ)"]
    end

    subgraph Model["scPert_Model backbone (models/model.py)"]
        GIL["Gene interaction layer"]
        DEC["Prediction decoder + loss"]
    end

    KG --> PROJ
    SC --> PROJ
    PERT --> Model
    PROJ --> BASE
    PROJ --> E1
    PROJ --> E2
    PROJ --> E3
    BASE --> SUM
    E1 --> ROUTER
    E2 --> ROUTER
    E3 --> ROUTER
    ROUTER --> SUM
    SUM --> GIL
    GIL --> DEC
```

A few verified facts worth anchoring before you read the code: the fusion module hard-requires **exactly 3 experts**, supports a `dynamic` router or a `fixed_uniform` control mode, and exposes four ablation modes (`full`, `base_only`, `no_interaction`, `experts_only`) that selectively freeze submodules during construction. An optional **balance loss** on router weights can be enabled with a configurable weight; it is automatically disabled when the router is fixed-uniform or in `base_only` mode.

> [!TIP]
> The router's final linear layer is initialized with near-zero weights (`std=1e-3`, zero bias), meaning training starts from an almost-uniform expert mixture and the routing specialization emerges gradually — a deliberate stabilizer you will see again in the router deep dive.

Sources: [models/model.py](models/model.py#L99-L297), [models/model.py](models/model.py#L299-L328), [models/model.py](models/model.py#L330-L400)

The published architecture figure provides a visual counterpart to the diagram above:

![DyMoE-Pert model architecture: multimodal feature embedding, dynamic residual mixture-of-experts fusion, and expression prediction](https://github.com/zhyzhy12512/DyMoE-Pert/blob/main/figures/dymoe_architecture.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L23-L27)

## Repository Tour

The repository is deliberately compact — a single `models/` package, two command-line scripts, and a directory of precomputed embedding files. It ships the **core runnable implementation only**: no expression datasets, no trained checkpoints, and no experiment logs are included. Expression data in GEARS format is downloaded automatically on first run.

```
DyMoE-Pert/
├── embeddings/          ← 7 precomputed gene embedding files (required at runtime)
├── figures/             ← architecture diagram shown above
├── models/              ← core library: model, data, training, inference
│   ├── model.py             ResidualMoEFusion + scPert_Model (nn.Module)
│   ├── scpert.py            scPert training/prediction wrapper class
│   ├── ProcePertdata.py     PertData: download, split, dataloaders
│   ├── data_utils.py        splitting logic, DE genes, dropout genes
│   ├── inference.py         evaluate, compute_metrics, deeper_analysis
│   └── utils.py             gene similarity networks, loss, helpers
├── scripts/
│   ├── train.py             CLI: train on one of 5 datasets
│   └── infer.py             CLI: predict one perturbation from a checkpoint
└── requirements.txt     ← validated with Python 3.8, PyTorch 2.3.0, PyG 2.6.1
```

| Component | File | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MoE fusion module | `models/model.py` | `ResidualMoEFusion`: 3 experts + residual base + soft router + ablation modes |
| Model backbone | `models/model.py` | `scPert_Model`: embedding loading, gene interaction layer, decoder |
| Training wrapper | `models/scpert.py` | `scPert` class: training loop, checkpointing, multi-GPU, `predict()` API (seed 0 fixed at import) |
| Data pipeline | `models/ProcePertdata.py` | `PertData`: auto-downloads GEARS-format ZIPs, builds perturbation splits and dataloaders |
| Train entry point | `scripts/train.py` | CLI with single-GPU and multi-GPU (PyG `DataParallel` + `DataListLoader`) paths |
| Inference entry point | `scripts/infer.py` | CLI that loads `config.pkl` + `model.pt` and predicts one perturbation |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L22), [README.md](README.md#L29-L42), [models/scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L1-L30), [models/ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L26-L60), [scripts/train.py](scripts/train.py#L55-L100), [scripts/infer.py](scripts/infer.py#L1-L15)

## Supported Datasets and Embeddings

Five perturbation datasets are supported, named via `--data-name`; each maps to an auto-downloaded processed GEARS-format ZIP (containing `perturb_processed.h5ad`) and a dataset-aligned scGPT embedding file resolved from a hardcoded dictionary in both scripts:

| `--data-name` | Processed data ZIP | Dataset-aligned scGPT embedding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `norman` | dataverse.harvard.edu 6154020 | `gene_embeddings_norman_512.npy` |
| `adamson` | dataverse.harvard.edu 6154417 | `gene_embeddings_adamson_512.npy` |
| `dixit` | dataverse.harvard.edu 6154416 | `gene_embeddings_dixit_512.npy` |
| `replogle_k562_essential` | dataverse.harvard.edu 7458695 | `gene_embeddings_replogle_k562_essential_512.npy` |
| `replogle_rpe1_essential` | dataverse.harvard.edu 7458694 | `gene_embeddings_replogle_rpe1_essential_512.npy` |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L44-L56), [scripts/train.py](scripts/train.py#L12-L18), [scripts/infer.py](scripts/infer.py#L17-L23)

The `embeddings/` directory holds **seven files in total**: two *common* tables shared across all datasets — the knowledge-graph embeddings (`gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz`, loaded inside `scPert_Model`) and the common perturbation embeddings (`gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz`) — plus the five dataset-aligned 512-dimensional scGPT arrays listed above. Genes missing from the scGPT vocabulary received deterministic random fallback vectors. Note the path sensitivity: the model reads the two common files via paths **relative to the working directory**, so all commands must run from the repository root.

> [!TIP]
> If training crashes with a file-not-found on an embedding `.npz`, the cause is almost always the working directory — the common embedding paths in `scPert_Model.__init__` are hardcoded to `./embeddings/` rather than resolved from `--embedding-dir` (which only controls the dataset-aligned file).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L29-L42), [README.md](README.md#L52-L56), [models/model.py](models/model.py#L330-L400)

## Minimal Usage Flow

Two commands cover the entire lifecycle. Training defaults mirror the main reported configuration (simulation split seed 77, 25 epochs, batch size 64, hidden size 64, dynamic routing, balance weight 0.0) and write `config.pkl` plus model weights into the save directory; prediction then loads that checkpoint, simulates a control-cell population, and writes `pred_dymoe_<perturbation>.npz` containing a mean vector plus 32 individual cell predictions:

| Step | Command | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Train | `python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --device cuda:0 --batch-size 4 --model-save-name norman_dymoe` | Checkpoint dir with `config.pkl`, `model.pt` |
| Train (4 GPUs) | `python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --multi-gpu --device-ids 0,1,2,3 --model-save-name norman_dymoe` | Same, distributed across GPUs |
| Predict | `python scripts/infer.py --data-name norman --checkpoint norman_dymoe --perturbation CEBPA+ctrl --device cuda:0` | `pred_dymoe_CEBPA_ctrl.npz` |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L58-L70), [README.md](README.md#L72-L79), [scripts/train.py](scripts/train.py#L20-L53), [scripts/infer.py](scripts/infer.py#L40-L52)

For `--perturbation`, single-gene interventions use the form `GENE+ctrl` and double-gene combinations use `GENE1+GENE2`; both gene names must exist in the selected dataset's perturbation vocabulary.

Sources: [scripts/infer.py](scripts/infer.py#L26-L30)

# Quick Start



This page walks you through running DyMoE-Pert end to end for the first time: installing the dependencies, letting the loader fetch a processed dataset automatically, training the model, and predicting the effect of a perturbation that the model never saw during training. Everything here uses the repository's default settings, so you can go from `git clone` to your first prediction in three commands.

## Before You Begin: What DyMoE-Pert Does

DyMoE-Pert predicts how genetic perturbations (knocking out or activating one or two genes) change single-cell gene expression — including for perturbations that were never measured during training. The model fuses two complementary views of each perturbed gene — **knowledge-graph (KG) embeddings** and **scGPT foundation-model embeddings** — through a **dynamic residual mixture-of-experts (MoE) fusion module** with three experts (KG expert, scGPT expert, cross-modal interaction expert) plus a residual base branch. A soft router assigns input-dependent weights to expert outputs.

![DyMoE-Pert architecture](https://github.com/zhyzhy12512/DyMoE-Pert/blob/main/figures/dymoe_architecture.png?raw=true)

You do not need to understand these internals to get started — the training and prediction scripts expose sane defaults. When you are ready to look under the hood, see [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L3-L13), [model.py](/models/model.py#L96-L114)

## System Requirements

The code was validated with **Python 3.8.20, PyTorch 2.3.0, and PyTorch Geometric 2.6.1 on Linux**. A CUDA-capable GPU is strongly recommended; CPU works but training and inference will be much slower.

| Component | Requirement | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OS | Linux (validated) | Other OSes untested |
| Python | 3.8.20 | |
| PyTorch | 2.3.0 | Install a build matching your CUDA driver first |
| PyTorch Geometric | 2.6.1 | Required for graph data loading |
| Other dependencies | see `requirements.txt` | anndata, scanpy, networkx, etc. |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L28-L32), [requirements.txt](/requirements.txt#L1-L12)

## Project Structure at a Glance

Everything you need is included except expression datasets and trained checkpoints — those are fetched or produced by the commands below.

```text
DyMoE-Pert/
├── models/                  # Core library: data loader, model, training logic
│   ├── ProcePertdata.py     # PertData: dataset download + GEARS-format loading
│   ├── scpert.py            # scPert wrapper: train / predict / save_model
│   ├── model.py             # ResidualMoEFusion and network components
│   ├── inference.py         # Prediction helpers
│   ├── data_utils.py        # DE genes, splitting, filtering
│   └── utils.py             # Download helpers, printing
├── scripts/
│   ├── train.py             # CLI entry point for training
│   └── infer.py             # CLI entry point for prediction
├── embeddings/              # Fixed gene-embedding files (shipped in repo)
│   ├── gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz   # Common KG embeddings
│   ├── gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz     # Common scGPT embeddings
│   └── gene_embeddings_<dataset>_512.npy    # Dataset-aligned scGPT embeddings
├── figures/                 # Architecture figure
└── requirements.txt
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L34-L50)

## Step 0: Clone and Install

Install a PyTorch 2.3.0 build suitable for your CUDA driver first (see the [official PyTorch installation guide](https://pytorch.org/get-started/previous-versions/)), then install the remaining pinned dependencies. **Run all commands from the repository root** — the model reads embedding files by paths relative to the working directory.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zhyzhy12512/DyMoE-Pert.git
cd DyMoE-Pert
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L21-L34)

## Step 1: Understand Your Data Sources

Two kinds of inputs are involved, and they behave differently:

1. **Expression data** — *not included in the repo*. On the first run, the `PertData` loader automatically downloads and extracts the processed GEARS-format data into `./data/<dataset-name>/` and builds a graph cache (`cell_graphs.pkl`). Later runs reuse the cache.
2. **Gene embeddings** — *already shipped in `embeddings/`*. The training script automatically picks the dataset-aligned 512-dimensional scGPT file for your `--data-name`; the two common embedding files must simply remain in `./embeddings/`.

The table below lists the five supported datasets. The Replogle entries are filtered essential-gene subsets.

| `--data-name` | Processed data source |
| --- | --- |
| `norman` | Harvard Dataverse file 6154020 |
| `adamson` | Harvard Dataverse file 6154417 |
| `dixit` | Harvard Dataverse file 6154416 |
| `replogle_k562_essential` | Harvard Dataverse file 7458695 |
| `replogle_rpe1_essential` | Harvard Dataverse file 7458694 |

The loader also retrieves the essential perturbation gene list and GO similarity graph when needed. For manual downloads and embedding provenance details, see [Dataset and Embedding Setup](3-dataset-and-embedding-setup).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L36-L50), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L150-L215), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L12-L18)

## Step 2: Train Your First Model

The defaults correspond to the main DyMoE-Pert configuration: simulation split seed 77, 25 epochs, batch size 64, hidden size 64, dynamic routing, dropout 0.1, and balance weight 0.0. For a memory-conscious **single-GPU run on Norman**:

```bash
python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --device cuda:0 --batch-size 4 --test-batch-size 4 --model-save-name norman_dymoe
```

To use **four GPUs**, as in the reported benchmark runs:

```bash
python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --multi-gpu --device-ids 0,1,2,3 --model-save-name norman_dymoe
```

Key training parameters:

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--data-name` | `norman` | Dataset key; selects the matching embedding file automatically |
| `--device` | `auto` | `auto`, `cpu`, `cuda`, or `cuda:N` |
| `--batch-size` / `--test-batch-size` | `64` / same as train | Reduce if you hit GPU memory limits |
| `--epochs` | `25` | Training epochs |
| `--hidden-size` | `64` | Model hidden dimension |
| `--lr` | `0.001` | Learning rate (AdamW + OneCycleLR) |
| `--seed` | `77` | Simulation split seed |
| `--model-save-name` | `<data>_model_FINAL` | Checkpoint directory name |
| `--multi-gpu` / `--device-ids` | off / `0,1,2,3` | PyG DataParallel across GPUs |

When training finishes, the script calls `save_model`, which writes two files into the checkpoint directory: **`config.pkl`** (the model configuration) and **`model.pt`** (the best model weights). Training also prints test metrics, including subgroup analysis for the simulation split.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L52-L66), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L21-L54), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L119-L153), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L420-L422)

## Step 3: Predict an Unseen Perturbation

Use a checkpoint produced by `train.py` to predict the expression response for a perturbation given as `GENE+GENE` (use `ctrl` for the unperturbed partner). Both gene names must occur in the selected dataset's perturbation vocabulary.

```bash
python scripts/infer.py --data-name norman --checkpoint norman_dymoe --perturbation CEBPA+ctrl --device cuda:0
```

The script writes **`pred_dymoe_<perturbation>.npz`** to the current directory. The file contains a mean predicted expression vector plus individual predictions for 32 sampled control cells (tune with `--num-cells`; cells are processed in forward passes of `--batch-size`, default 8). Running on CPU works via `--device cpu`, but is much slower.

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--checkpoint` | *(required)* | Directory containing `config.pkl` and `model.pt` |
| `--perturbation` | *(required)* | e.g. `CEBPA+ctrl` or `CEBPA+JUN` |
| `--num-cells` | `32` | Number of control cells to predict for |
| `--batch-size` | `8` | Inference cells per forward pass |
| `--device` | `auto` | `auto`, `cpu`, `cuda:N` |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L68-L78), [infer.py](/scripts/infer.py#L25-L77), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L424-L491)

## The Complete First-Run Pipeline

The following flow shows everything that happens from a fresh clone to your first prediction file. Notice that the only network downloads are the expression dataset (once) — embeddings are already in the repo, and the graph cache makes subsequent runs fast.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[git clone + pip install] --> B[python scripts/train.py<br/>--data-name norman]
    B --> C{./data/norman/<br/>exists?}
    C -->|No| D[Auto-download processed<br/>GEARS-format ZIP from<br/>Harvard Dataverse]
    D --> E[Extract perturb_processed.h5ad<br/>into ./data/norman/]
    C -->|Yes| F[Load h5ad]
    E --> F
    F --> G{cell_graphs.pkl<br/>cache exists?}
    G -->|No| H[Build PyG graph objects<br/>and save cache]
    G -->|Yes| I[Load cache]
    H --> I
    I --> J[Select embedding:<br/>gene_embeddings_norman_512.npy<br/>+ 2 common files]
    J --> K[Train: 25 epochs,<br/>MoE fusion, dynamic router]
    K --> L[Save checkpoint:<br/>config.pkl + model.pt]
    L --> M[python scripts/infer.py<br/>--checkpoint norman_dymoe<br/>--perturbation CEBPA+ctrl]
    M --> N[Write pred_dymoe_CEBPA_ctrl.npz<br/>mean vector + 32 cell predictions]
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L36-L78), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L150-L215), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L420-L422), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L488-L490)

## How the Data Flows Through the Model at a High Level

During every forward pass, each perturbed cell-graph sample receives three embedding streams, which are fused and decoded into a predicted expression profile:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs
        KG["KG embedding<br/>(gene_2_kge_comgcn,<br/>128-d)"]
        SG["scGPT embedding<br/>(dataset-aligned .npy,<br/>512-d)"]
        GI["Gene interaction<br/>GNN features"]
    end
    subgraph ResidualMoEFusion
        R["Soft router<br/>(input-dependent weights)"]
        E1["KG expert"]
        E2["scGPT expert"]
        E3["Interaction expert"]
        BASE["Residual base branch"]
    end
    DEC["Prediction decoder"] --> OUT["Predicted<br/>post-perturbation<br/>expression"]
    KG --> E1
    SG --> E2
    GI --> E3
    R --> E1 & E2 & E3
    E1 & E2 & E3 --> FUSED["Fused representation"]
    BASE --> FUSED
    FUSED --> DEC
```

The Quick Start commands never touch these internals — the defaults (`use_moe_fusion=True`, `router_mode="dynamic"`, `ablation_mode="full"`) are applied automatically. To learn how each piece works, follow the Deep Dive links below.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L96-L114), [README.md](/README.md#L7-L15), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L73-L146)

## Troubleshooting Common First-Run Issues

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Embedding file not found: ./embeddings/...` | Running from a directory other than the repo root, or embeddings deleted | `cd DyMoE-Pert` before running; keep all files in `./embeddings/` |
| `CUDA was requested but is unavailable` / `torch.cuda.is_available() is False` | CPU-only PyTorch build installed | Reinstall PyTorch 2.3.0 with the CUDA build matching your driver |
| `--multi-gpu needs at least two GPU ids` | Fewer than 2 valid IDs passed | Pass at least two IDs, e.g. `--device-ids 0,1` |
| First run is slow / uses lots of disk | Dataset downloading + graph cache construction (one-time) | Expected behavior; subsequent runs load `cell_graphs.pkl` from cache |
| `Required file not found: <checkpoint>/config.pkl` | Checkpoint directory name wrong, or training did not finish | Confirm training printed "checkpoint saving completed"; pass the exact `--model-save-name` |
| Gene name rejected in `--perturbation` | Gene not in the dataset's perturbation vocabulary | Use genes present in the selected dataset (e.g. Norman genes like `CEBPA`, `JUN`) |

Sources: [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L79-L105), [infer.py](/scripts/infer.py#L47-L54), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L198-L215), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L150-L153)

# Dataset and Embedding Setup



This page explains everything DyMoE-Pert needs on disk before training can start: the perturbation **expression datasets** (downloaded automatically in GEARS format) and the **gene embedding files** shipped in the `embeddings/` directory. You will learn what each file is, where it must live, how the first run downloads and caches data, and how the training script wires these files into the model. No expression dataset is committed to the repository — only the fixed gene embeddings are bundled — so understanding this page is the prerequisite for your first successful `train.py` run.

## The Three Inputs at a Glance

A DyMoE-Pert training run consumes exactly three kinds of inputs, and they live in two places: a `./data/` directory that gets populated on first use, and the pre-shipped `./embeddings/` directory. The expression data describes *what happened to each cell* (which genes were perturbed and how expression changed), while the embeddings describe *who the perturbed genes are* in two complementary mathematical spaces: a biological knowledge-graph space (128-dimensional) and an scGPT foundation-model space (512-dimensional).

![DyMoE-Pert model architecture: multimodal feature embedding, dynamic residual mixture-of-experts fusion, and expression prediction](https://github.com/zhyzhy12512/DyMoE-Pert/blob/main/figures/dymoe_architecture.png?raw=true)

The following diagram shows how these inputs flow from their sources into the model at training time:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph DV["Harvard Dataverse (auto-download)"]
        ZIP["Dataset ZIP<br/>perturb_processed.h5ad"]
        EG["essential_all_data_pert_genes.pkl"]
    end
    subgraph REPO["Repository (already bundled)"]
        KG["gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz<br/>(KG, 128-dim)"]
        PE["gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz<br/>(pert embeddings)"]
        SC["gene_embeddings_&lt;dataset&gt;_512.npy<br/>(scGPT, 512-dim)"]
    end
    subgraph DISK["./data/ after first run"]
        H5["perturb_processed.h5ad"]
        CG["data_pyg/cell_graphs.pkl<br/>(graph cache)"]
        SP["splits/*.pkl<br/>(split cache)"]
    end
    ZIP --> H5
    EG --> GO["GO filtering"]
    H5 --> CG
    H5 --> SP
    CG --> LD["PertData dataloader"]
    SP --> LD
    LD --> M["scPert_Model"]
    KG --> M
    PE --> M
    SC --> M
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L36-L50), [scripts/train.py](scripts/train.py#L119-L135)

## Supported Datasets and Their Download Sources

The loader recognizes exactly five dataset names, matching the five benchmark datasets from the manuscript (Norman, Dixit, Adamson, and the filtered essential-gene subsets of Replogle K562 and RPE1). Each name maps to a processed GEARS-format ZIP hosted on Harvard Dataverse; the Replogle ZIPs are explicitly noted in code as *filtered subsets*, not the complete screens. You never need to call a download function yourself — the loader fetches and extracts them the first time you train.

| `--data-name` | Processed data ZIP (Harvard Dataverse) | Dataset-aligned scGPT embedding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `norman` | dataverse.harvard.edu/api/access/datafile/6154020 | `gene_embeddings_norman_512.npy` |
| `adamson` | dataverse.harvard.edu/api/access/datafile/6154417 | `gene_embeddings_adamson_512.npy` |
| `dixit` | dataverse.harvard.edu/api/access/datafile/6154416 | `gene_embeddings_dixit_512.npy` |
| `replogle_k562_essential` | dataverse.harvard.edu/api/access/datafile/7458695 | `gene_embeddings_replogle_k562_essential_512.npy` |
| `replogle_rpe1_essential` | dataverse.harvard.edu/api/access/datafile/7458694 | `gene_embeddings_replogle_rpe1_essential_512.npy` |

The mapping in the left column is enforced twice: once as the `choices` of the `--data-name` CLI argument, and once inside `PertData.load`, which raises a `ValueError` for any other name unless you supply a custom data path. The two replogle entries carry code comments stating "This is not the complete dataset and has been filtered," so do not expect them to reproduce full-screen analyses.

Sources: [scripts/train.py](scripts/train.py#L12-L23), [models/ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L150-L171), [README.md](README.md#L40-L48)

## The Bundled Embedding Files

Unlike the expression data, the embedding files are committed to the repository, so a fresh clone already contains everything embedding-related. There are two categories. The **two common files** are shared across all datasets: a knowledge-graph embedding table produced upstream with a ComGCN-style encoder (its arrays are 128-dimensional, which you can verify against `kg_input_dim=128` in the model), and a perturbation-gene embedding table. The **five dataset-aligned files** are per-dataset scGPT gene embeddings of fixed dimension 512, generated from an scGPT checkpoint for this project.

| File in `embeddings/` | Type | Dimension | Consumed by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz` | Common, knowledge-graph (keys: `gene_names`, `embeddings`) | 128 | KG expert input |
| `gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz` | Common, perturbation gene embeddings | 512 | Perturbation embedding lookup |
| `gene_embeddings_norman_512.npy` | Dataset-aligned scGPT | 512 | scGPT expert input |
| `gene_embeddings_adamson_512.npy` | Dataset-aligned scGPT | 512 | scGPT expert input |
| `gene_embeddings_dixit_512.npy` | Dataset-aligned scGPT | 512 | scGPT expert input |
| `gene_embeddings_replogle_k562_essential_512.npy` | Dataset-aligned scGPT | 512 | scGPT expert input |
| `gene_embeddings_replogle_rpe1_essential_512.npy` | Dataset-aligned scGPT | 512 | scGPT expert input |

For genes that are absent from the scGPT checkpoint vocabulary, the generation process substituted deterministic random fallback vectors, so every gene in a dataset has a usable 512-dim row — no missing-value handling is needed at training time. The fixed 512 dimension is hard-coded as `'embedding_size': 512` in the model config and as `scgpt_input_dim=512` in the fusion module, so you cannot swap in embeddings of a different width without code changes.

> [!TIP]
> The two common embedding files are opened with **hard-coded relative paths** (`"./embeddings/..."`) inside the model constructor, not via the CLI. This is exactly why the README instructs you to run all commands from the repository root — launching `train.py` from another directory will fail with a `FileNotFoundError` even though `--embedding-dir` is set correctly.

Sources: [models/model.py](models/model.py#L370-L390), [models/model.py](models/model.py#L96-L107), [models/scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L327-L335), [README.md](README.md#L50-L50)

## First-Run Data Download, Extraction, and Caching

When you call `PertData.load(DataName="norman")`, the loader resolves the Dataverse URL, downloads the ZIP with a progress bar, and extracts it under `./data/norman/`. The download helper writes to a `.part` temporary file first and only renames it into place after a complete transfer, which prevents corrupt partial files from poisoning later runs. Once extracted, the loader reads `perturb_processed.h5ad` with scanpy — this single AnnData file is the canonical expression dataset.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["train.py starts"] --> B{"data/<name>/ exists?"}
    B -- no --> C["dataverse_download<br/>(.part temp file + progress bar)"]
    C --> D["zip_data_download_wrapper<br/>extract ZIP into ./data/"]
    B -- yes --> E["Found local copy..."]
    D --> F["sc.read_h5ad<br/>perturb_processed.h5ad"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["set_pert_genes<br/>download essential gene list if needed"]
    G --> H["GO filter: drop perturbations<br/>not in GO graph"]
    H --> I{"data_pyg/cell_graphs.pkl<br/>exists?"}
    I -- no --> J["Build PyG graph per cell<br/>(slow first run)"]
    I -- yes --> K["Load cached pickle"]
    J --> L["Save cell_graphs.pkl"]
    L --> M["Ready for prepare_split"]
    K --> M
```

After this step the local layout looks like the tree below — the caches mean your **second** run of the same dataset is dramatically faster, because graph construction and splitting are the expensive parts:

```
data/
├── norman/                          # extracted dataset
│   ├── perturb_processed.h5ad       # expression + condition labels
│   ├── data_pyg/
│   │   └── cell_graphs.pkl          # one PyG graph object per cell
│   └── splits/
│       ├── norman_simulation_77_0.75.pkl        # condition->set assignment
│       └── norman_simulation_77_0.75_subgroup.pkl
└── essential_all_data_pert_genes.pkl  # shared perturbation-gene universe
```

Sources: [models/ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L131-L215), [models/utils.py](models/utils.py#L51-L97), [models/ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L198-L215)

## Supporting Files: Essential Gene List and GO Filtering

Two auxiliary downloads round out the data setup. First, `set_pert_genes` fetches the **essential perturbation gene list** (`essential_all_data_pert_genes.pkl`, Dataverse file 6934320) to define the universe of perturbable genes and builds the perturbation-to-index mapping `node_map_pert` used throughout training and inference. Second, during `load`, every perturbation condition is checked with `filter_pert_in_go`; conditions whose constituent genes are absent from the GO-derived perturbation graph are **dropped from the AnnData object entirely** before any graphs are built, and the dropped names are printed so you can see exactly what was removed.

A third helper, `get_go_auto`, exists in the utilities and downloads `gene2go.pkl` (Dataverse file 6153417) to compute GO similarity edges when a dataset needs its own gene-similarity network built. You will not interact with these files directly, but knowing they arrive lazily explains why the very first run also downloads small `.pkl` files alongside the main dataset ZIP.

Sources: [models/ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L99-L129), [models/ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L187-L196), [models/utils.py](models/utils.py#L119-L150)

## Wiring It Together: CLI Arguments for Data and Embeddings

`scripts/train.py` exposes four arguments that control the data and embedding setup, and it applies a simple but important resolution chain: the dataset name selects the embedding file automatically, `--embedding-dir` provides the directory, and `--embedding-file` can override the automatic choice entirely. Before any model work begins, the script validates the resolved embedding path with `os.path.exists` and raises a descriptive `FileNotFoundError` if it is missing — a deliberate early-failure design so you never lose training time to a typo.

| Argument | Default | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--data-name` | `norman` | Which of the five datasets to download/load and which embedding file is auto-selected |
| `--data-path` | `./data` | Root directory for downloads, caches, and splits |
| `--embedding-dir` | `./embeddings` | Directory searched for the dataset-aligned scGPT file |
| `--embedding-file` | `None` | Optional override of the automatic `<dataset>_512.npy` mapping |

After validation, `train.py` constructs `PertData(args.data_path)`, calls `load` and `prepare_split` (default seed 77), builds the dataloaders, and finally passes the resolved `embedding_path` into the `scPert` wrapper, which stores it for model construction. The split options (`--split`, `--seed`) cache their results on disk as shown earlier, so changing the seed creates a *new* cached split file rather than overwriting the old one.

> [!TIP]
> The `--embedding-file` override only replaces the **dataset-aligned scGPT array**. The two common `.npz` files are unaffected by any CLI flag because they are read from fixed paths inside `scPert_Model.__init__` — treat them as immovable infrastructure.

Sources: [scripts/train.py](scripts/train.py#L21-L54), [scripts/train.py](scripts/train.py#L101-L105), [scripts/train.py](scripts/train.py#L119-L135)

## How the Model Loads the Embedding Tensors

Inside `scPert_Model.__init__`, three `np.load` calls convert your files into registered PyTorch buffers (non-trainable tensors that move with the model). The KG file provides `loaded_embeddings` plus a `gene_to_index` dictionary mapping gene symbols to rows; the common perturbation file provides `pert_embeddings` plus `pert_to_index`; and your dataset-aligned scGPT file becomes `gene_emb`, looked up via the CLI-resolved `embedding_path`. Together they feed two downstream consumers: the `pert_dense` layer, which expects a **640-dimensional** concatenated vector (128 + 512) when MoE fusion is disabled, and the `ResidualMoEFusion` module, which receives the two modalities *separately* through its 128-dim KG projector and 512-dim scGPT projector.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph FILES["Files on disk"]
        F1["gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz"]
        F2["gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz"]
        F3["gene_embeddings_&lt;dataset&gt;_512.npy"]
    end
    F1 -- "np.load → buffer" --> B1["loaded_embeddings (128-d)<br/>+ gene_to_index"]
    F2 -- "np.load → buffer" --> B2["pert_embeddings<br/>+ pert_to_index"]
    F3 -- "np.load(embedding_path) → buffer" --> B3["gene_emb (512-d)"]
    B1 --> MOE["ResidualMoEFusion<br/>kg_projector: 128→hidden"]
    B3 --> MOE2["ResidualMoEFusion<br/>scgpt_projector: 512→hidden"]
    B1 -- "concat 128+512 = 640" --> PD["pert_dense (no-MoE path)"]
    B3 -- "concat" --> PD
    MOE --> OUT["fused perturbation representation"]
    MOE2 --> OUT
    PD -.->|"alternative path"| OUT
```

This layout is the reason the configuration pins `'embedding_size': 512` and why the fusion module rejects any `kg_input_dim` other than 128 at construction time — the embedding files and the architecture dimensions are contractually locked together. The internal fusion behavior (how the router weighs the KG expert against the scGPT expert) is covered in [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design).

Sources: [models/model.py](models/model.py#L348-L414), [models/model.py](models/model.py#L96-L130), [models/scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L327-L354)

## Troubleshooting Your First Setup

Most setup failures fall into four patterns, all with unambiguous fixes. The table below maps each symptom you are likely to see to its root cause in the code and the corrective action.

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FileNotFoundError: Embedding file not found: ./embeddings/...` | `--embedding-dir` changed or dataset-aligned `.npy` missing | Restore the file under `embeddings/` or pass `--embedding-file` with a valid path |
| `FileNotFoundError` mentioning `gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz` despite correct CLI flags | Model reads the two common files via hard-coded relative paths | Run `python scripts/train.py` from the repository root |
| Run stalls at start with a progress bar and no model output | First run downloads + extracts the dataset ZIP, builds per-cell graph cache | Wait; re-runs hit `cell_graphs.pkl` and the split cache and start quickly |
| `ValueError: data attribute is either norman, adamson, dixit...` | `--data-name` not among the five supported keys | Use exactly one of the names in the dataset table |
| Training runs but very slowly on laptop | No GPU detected, fell back to CPU | Pass `--device cuda:0` if available; README warns CPU mode is much slower |

Note that disk space matters on the first run as well: the README explicitly cautions that the first run takes time and disk space to download, process the dataset, and build graph caches — the Replogle essential subsets are the smallest, while Norman/Dixit/Adamson are moderate, full processed screens.

Sources: [scripts/train.py](scripts/train.py#L102-L105), [models/model.py](models/model.py#L370-L390), [models/ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L182-L185), [README.md](README.md#L78-L79)

## Where to Go Next

With data and embeddings in place, your natural next steps follow the catalog. To actually launch a run — including the memory-conscious Norman command and the four-GPU benchmark configuration — continue to [Training and Prediction Commands](4-training-and-prediction-commands). To understand *why* the loader builds one graph per cell and what `cell_graphs.pkl` contains, read [GEARS-Format Data Pipeline](12-gears-format-data-pipeline). For a deep dive into how the KG (128-d) and scGPT (512-d) tables were produced and how the MoE consumes them, see [Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings](13-knowledge-graph-and-scgpt-embeddings). Finally, to control exactly which perturbations a model is allowed to see (the seed-77 simulation split cached in `splits/`), continue to [Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split](14-perturbation-splits-and-simulation-split).


# Training and Prediction Commands



This page is your operational guide for running DyMoE-Pert end to end. The repository exposes exactly **two command-line entry points**: `scripts/train.py`, which trains a model and saves a checkpoint, and `scripts/infer.py`, which loads that checkpoint and predicts the expression outcome of a perturbation you name. Everything else — the data loader, the model class, and the training loop — lives in the `models/` package and is invoked *by* these scripts, not run directly. By the end of this page you will be able to launch a single-GPU or four-GPU training run and turn its checkpoint into per-perturbation predictions.

![DyMoE-Pert model architecture](https://github.com/zhyzhy12512/DyMoE-Pert/blob/main/figures/dymoe_architecture.png?raw=true)

> [!TIP]
> Always run both commands from the repository root directory. `scripts/train.py` appends the current directory to `sys.path` to import the `models` package, and the two common embedding files are read from relative paths under `./embeddings/` — running from elsewhere breaks imports and file lookup.

## How the Two Commands Fit Together

Both scripts follow the same three-phase lifecycle, differing only in whether phase two is *learning* or *loading*. The diagram below traces the full journey from command invocation to output files:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph TRAIN["python scripts/train.py"]
        A[Parse CLI arguments] --> B[PertData: download dataset<br/>from Harvard Dataverse]
        B --> C[prepare_split<br/>simulation split, seed 77]
        C --> D[get_dataloader<br/>train / val / test loaders]
        D --> E[scPert.model_initialize<br/>build model with MoE config]
        E --> F[scPert.train<br/>epochs, lr, optional multi-GPU]
        F --> G[save_model<br/>config.pkl + model.pt]
    end

    subgraph INFER["python scripts/infer.py"]
        H[Parse CLI arguments<br/>--checkpoint, --perturbation] --> I[PertData: load dataset<br/>split=no_test]
        I --> J[scPert.load_pretrained<br/>config.pkl + model.pt]
        J --> K[scPert.predict<br/>sample control cells]
        K --> L[pred_dymoe_GENE1_GENE2.npz]
    end

    G -.checkpoint directory.-> J
```

The checkpoint directory is the only contract between the two commands: `train.py` writes it, `infer.py` consumes it. Notably, both scripts share an identical `EMBEDDING_FILES` mapping that ties each `--data-name` to its dataset-aligned embedding file, so you never specify embedding paths manually for supported datasets.

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L71-L153), [infer.py](infer.py#L25-L76), [README.md](README.md#L52-L79)

## Training a Model

### Canonical Commands

The README documents two production-ready invocations. For a **memory-conscious single-GPU run on Norman** — the recommended starting point for beginners:

```bash
python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --device cuda:0 --batch-size 4 --test-batch-size 4 --model-save-name norman_dymoe
```

For the **four-GPU configuration used in the reported benchmark runs**:

```bash
python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --multi-gpu --device-ids 0,1,2,3 --model-save-name norman_dymoe
```

To train on a different dataset, change `--data-name` to any of: `norman`, `adamson`, `dixit`, `replogle_k562_essential`, or `replogle_rpe1_essential`. The script automatically selects the matching embedding file from its internal mapping.

| Scenario | Command pattern | Key difference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single GPU (low memory) | `--device cuda:0 --batch-size 4 --test-batch-size 4` | Small explicit batch sizes |
| Multi-GPU benchmark | `--multi-gpu --device-ids 0,1,2,3` | PyG DataParallel with DataListLoader |
| Other dataset | `--data-name adamson` | Embedding file auto-resolved |
| Quick experiment | No flags beyond `--data-name` | 25 epochs, batch size 64 defaults |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L54-L66), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L12-L18)

### Step-by-Step: What Happens When You Run train.py

Each numbered step below corresponds to verified code paths in the scripts:

1. **Environment setup** — The script enables expandable CUDA memory segments to reduce fragmentation, then imports the `models` package from the repository root.
2. **Dataset acquisition** — `PertData.load()` downloads the processed GEARS-format ZIP from Harvard Dataverse into `./data/<dataset-name>/` on first run, then reuses the local copy afterward. Expression datasets are *not* shipped with the repository.
3. **Graph caching** — On the first run, cell-level PyTorch Geometric graph objects are built and cached to `data_pyg/cell_graphs.pkl`; subsequent runs load this cache directly.
4. **Split preparation** — `prepare_split(split="simulation", seed=77)` by default partitions perturbations into train/val/test sets, caching the split as a pickle file.
5. **Dataloader construction** — Three loaders are created (train/val/test); with `--multi-gpu`, a `DataListLoader` replaces the standard loader.
6. **Model initialization** — `scPert` is constructed with the embedding path, then `model_initialize()` builds the model with MoE fusion always enabled (`use_moe_fusion=True` is forced).
7. **Training loop** — `scPert.train()` runs the optimizer, tracks the best model by validation top-20 DE MSE, and evaluates on the test set afterward.
8. **Checkpoint saving** — `save_model()` writes `config.pkl` (full configuration) and `model.pt` (weights of the best model) into your `--model-save-name` directory.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "First run only"
        DL[Download dataset ZIP] --> GC[Build cell graph cache]
    end
    subgraph "Every run"
        S[Recreate split<br/>or load cached split] --> L[Build dataloaders] --> T[Train 25 epochs<br/>track best val DE-MSE] --> TS[Test evaluation<br/>subgroup analysis] --> SV[Save checkpoint]
    end
    GC --> S
```

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L150-L215), [train.py](train.py#L119-L153), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L533-L744)

### Training Parameter Reference

All flags below are parsed by `scripts/train.py`. Defaults match the main DyMoE-Pert configuration reported in the manuscript.

| Parameter | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--data-name` | `norman` | Dataset key; choices are the five supported names |
| `--data-path` | `./data` | Where datasets are downloaded/cached |
| `--embedding-dir` | `./embeddings` | Directory containing gene embedding files |
| `--embedding-file` | *(auto)* | Override the dataset-aligned `.npy` embedding |
| `--device` | `auto` | `auto`, `cpu`, `cuda`, or `cuda:N` |
| `--batch-size` | `64` | Training cells per step |
| `--test-batch-size` | *(= batch size)* | Eval-time batch size; lower it to save memory |
| `--hidden-size` | `64` | Model hidden dimension |
| `--epochs` | `25` | Training epochs |
| `--lr` | `0.001` | Learning rate for AdamW |
| `--seed` | `77` | Split seed (model weights are seeded at 0 internally) |
| `--split` | `simulation` | Perturbation split strategy |
| `--model-save-name` | `<data-name>_model_FINAL` | Output checkpoint directory |
| `--multi-gpu` | off | Enable PyG DataParallel training |
| `--device-ids` | `0,1,2,3` | Comma-separated GPU ids for `--multi-gpu` |
| `--moe-hidden-dim` | *(follows hidden-size)* | Inner dimension of the MoE fusion module |
| `--moe-dropout` | `0.1` | Dropout inside the MoE fusion |
| `--moe-balance-weight` | `0.0` | Weight of the router balance loss |
| `--moe-ablation-mode` | `full` | `full`, `base_only`, `no_interaction`, `experts_only` |
| `--moe-router-mode` | `dynamic` | `dynamic` or `fixed_uniform` (E3 control) |
| `--no-moe-router-stats` | off | Suppress router statistics logging |

> [!TIP]
> Two flags interact in a non-obvious way: if you select `--moe-router-mode fixed_uniform` **or** `--moe-ablation-mode base_only`, the script silently forces `--moe-balance-weight` to `0.0` regardless of what you passed, because a fixed router and a base-only configuration make the balance loss meaningless.

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L21-L54), [train.py](train.py#L73-L75), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L320-L325)

## Predicting a Perturbation

### The Prediction Command

Prediction requires a checkpoint directory produced by training. A single-gene perturbation on Norman:

```bash
python scripts/infer.py --data-name norman --checkpoint norman_dymoe --perturbation CEBPA+ctrl --device cuda:0
```

A **double-gene perturbation** uses the `GENE1+GENE2` form, for example `--perturbation CEBPA+JUN`. Both gene names must exist in the selected dataset's perturbation vocabulary — you cannot invent gene combinations that the dataset loader has never seen.

The script writes `pred_dymoe_<perturbation>.npz` to your current directory (with `+` replaced by `_`). The archive contains both the **mean predicted expression vector** across sampled cells and the **individual predictions for all 32 sampled control cells**, so you can compute uncertainty yourself.

### Prediction Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--checkpoint` | *(required)* | Directory containing `config.pkl` and `model.pt` |
| `--perturbation` | *(required)* | Format `GENE+ctrl` or `GENE1+GENE2` |
| `--data-name` | `norman` | Dataset key, must match the checkpoint's training data |
| `--data-path` | `./data` | Dataset cache location |
| `--embedding-dir` | `./embeddings` | Embedding file location |
| `--device` | `auto` | Falls back to `cpu` if no CUDA device |
| `--num-cells` | `32` | Control cells sampled for the prediction |
| `--batch-size` | `8` | Cells per inference forward pass |

Sources: [infer.py](scripts/infer.py#L25-L35), [README.md](README.md#L68-L79)

### How Prediction Works Internally

Before predicting, `infer.py` validates three paths (embedding file, `config.pkl`, `model.pt`) and fails fast with a clear error if any is missing. It then loads the dataset with `split="no_test"` — this split creates only train/val loaders and skips test-set construction, because inference needs the dataset purely for its gene vocabulary and control-cell pool, not for evaluation. The `load_pretrained` method rebuilds the model from the saved configuration and restores the weights, automatically stripping any `module.` prefix that DataParallel training added to parameter names.

The `predict()` call samples `--num-cells` control cells, constructs one input graph per cell with your chosen perturbation attached, runs batched forward passes under `torch.no_grad()`, and averages the outputs into the mean prediction.

Sources: [infer.py](infer.py#L47-L72), [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L460-L461), [scpert.py](scpert.py#L357-L397), [scpert.py](scpert.py#L424-L491)

## Checkpoint Anatomy

The checkpoint directory is intentionally minimal — two files capture everything needed to reproduce the model:

| File | Written by | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `config.pkl` | `save_model()` | Full model configuration: hidden sizes, MoE flags, perturbation vocabulary, gene/node mappings |
| `model.pt` | `save_model()` | State dict of the **best** model (selected by validation top-20 DE MSE), with parallel-wrapping removed |

A critical subtlety for beginners: the saved weights are not necessarily from the final epoch. During training, a deep copy of the model is updated only when validation top-20 DE MSE improves, so `model.pt` always holds the best-validation checkpoint.

> [!TIP]
> Checkpoints saved from multi-GPU runs store **unwrapped** parameter names — `save_model` explicitly removes the DataParallel `module.` prefix before saving. This means a checkpoint trained on four GPUs loads seamlessly into a single-GPU or CPU inference session with no manual state-dict surgery.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L399-L422), [scpert.py](scpert.py#L660-L666), [scpert.py](scpert.py#L386-L393)

## Multi-GPU Training Constraints

The `--multi-gpu` flag activates PyTorch Geometric's `DataParallel` wrapper across your listed GPUs. Three validation rules are enforced *before* training starts, so misconfigurations fail immediately with explicit errors rather than mid-run:

| Rule | Failure message trigger |
| --- | --- |
| CUDA must be available | `--multi-gpu` with no CUDA devices raises immediately |
| At least two GPU ids required | A single id in `--device-ids` is rejected |
| `--device` must equal first `--device-ids` entry | e.g. `--device cuda:1 --device-ids 0,1` raises |

GPU ids are validated against `torch.cuda.device_count()`, so requesting `cuda:3` on a two-GPU machine fails at argument-checking time. The underlying distributed mechanics (batch splitting, gradient synchronization) are handled inside `scPert.train()` and are covered in detail in [Multi-GPU Parallel Training](16-multi-gpu-parallel-training).

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L79-L101), [scpert.py](scpert.py#L560-L573)

## Troubleshooting Common Command Failures

Errors you are most likely to hit as a first-time user, mapped to their verified causes and fixes:

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Embedding file not found: ./embeddings/...` | Missing or misplaced `.npy` embedding file | Verify `embeddings/` directory contents; check `--embedding-dir` |
| `Required file not found: .../config.pkl` | `--checkpoint` points to an empty or wrong directory | Point to the directory `train.py` created via `--model-save-name` |
| `CUDA was requested but is unavailable` | No CUDA-capable driver or CPU-only PyTorch build | Install a CUDA-matched PyTorch 2.3.0 build, or use `--device cpu` |
| `--multi-gpu needs at least two GPU ids` | Only one id passed to `--device-ids` | List two or more ids, e.g. `--device-ids 0,1` |
| `--device must match the first --device-ids entry` | Mismatched device arguments | Set `--device cuda:0` when using `--device-ids 0,...` |
| Prediction fails on a gene name | Perturbation absent from the dataset's perturbation vocabulary | Use genes from the chosen dataset; check dataset docs |
| First run seems to hang | Dataset ZIP download + graph cache construction in progress | Expected on first run; subsequent runs load local caches |

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L79-L105), [infer.py](infer.py#L47-L54), [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L198-L215)

## Where to Go Next

You now know how to drive both commands. The natural progression through this documentation:

- **Before training**: confirm your dataset and embedding files are in place with [Dataset and Embedding Setup](3-dataset-and-embedding-setup), and try the end-to-end install path in [Quick Start](2-quick-start).
- **Understanding what you trained**: the flags `--moe-ablation-mode`, `--moe-router-mode`, and `--moe-balance-weight` manipulate the fusion architecture — see [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design) and [Ablation Modes Framework](9-ablation-modes-framework) for what each mode structurally removes.
- **Interpreting the training log**: the epoch metrics (Overall MSE, Top 20 DE MSE) and the simulation-split subgroup analysis printed after testing are explained in [Metrics and DE Gene Analysis](18-metrics-and-de-gene-analysis).
- **Going deeper on what the commands invoke**: [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration), [Unseen Perturbation Inference](17-unseen-perturbation-inference), and the exhaustive flag semantics in [Configuration Reference](19-configuration-reference).

# Architecture Overview



DyMoE-Pert predicts how genetic perturbations reshape single-cell expression profiles — including perturbations never observed during training. Its defining architectural idea is that the representation of a perturbed gene should not be fused from biological knowledge-graph (KG) and scGPT foundation-model sources by one fixed rule. Instead, a **dynamic residual mixture-of-experts (MoE)** block learns, per input, how to weight three complementary experts on top of a shared residual base branch. This page gives a end-to-end map of the system: the major components, how data and embeddings flow through them, and where each deep-dive continues. All behavior described here is verified against the code in `models/` and `scripts/`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L19), [model.py](models/model.py#L96-L110)

## The System in One Picture

The published architecture figure summarizes the three-stage design: multimodal perturbation embedding, dynamic MoE fusion, and expression prediction on top of a control-expression baseline.

![DyMoE-Pert model architecture: multimodal feature embedding, dynamic residual mixture-of-experts fusion, and expression prediction](https://github.com/zhyzhy12512/DyMoE-Pert/blob/main/figures/dymoe_architecture.png?raw=true)

The following diagram translates that figure into the concrete modules you will find in the code. A prediction is produced per cell-graph sample: gene context is built from dataset-aligned embeddings, the perturbation condition string is resolved into per-gene fused embeddings by the MoE block, both signals are combined and refined by a transformer stack, and the decoder outputs a **delta** that is added to the control expression vector.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    X["Control expression vector x<br/>(pert_data.x)"]:::data
    KG["KG embedding · 128-d<br/>gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz"]:::data
    SG["scGPT embedding · 512-d<br/>gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz"]:::data
    GE["Dataset-aligned gene embeddings · 512-d<br/>gene_embeddings_&lt;dataset&gt;_512.npy"]:::data

    subgraph GENECTX["Gene context encoder"]
        GD["gene_dense: 512 → 64"] --> GA["Gene self-attention<br/>softmax(gene·geneᵀ/√h) then context matmul,<br/>projected + residual"]
    end

    subgraph MOE["ResidualMoEFusion (models/model.py)"]
        P1["kg_projector: 128 → 64"]:::proj
        P2["scgpt_projector: 512 → 64"]:::proj
        E1["KG expert"]:::expert
        E2["scGPT expert"]:::expert
        E3["Interaction expert<br/>[z_kg, z_sc, z_kg⊙z_sc, |z_kg−z_sc|]"]:::expert
        R["Soft router: 128 → 64 → 3<br/>softmax → per-input weights α"]:::router
        BASE["Residual base branch<br/>base_mlp on [z_kg, z_sc]"]:::base
        SUM["Σ αᵢ·hᵢ + h_base → LayerNorm"]:::combine
    end

    COMBO["Combo handling: pert_fuse MLP<br/>+ mean over perturbed genes"]:::combo
    ADD["Add: gene context + perturbation embedding<br/>(scaled by learnable emb_scale)"]
    TRN["8 × ImprovedTransformerLayer<br/>(chunked attention, residual ×0.5)"]:::backbone
    DEC["final_mlp → output_layer → Δ"]:::backbone
    OUT["prediction = x + Δ"]:::result

    GE --> GD
    KG --> P1 --> E1
    SG --> P2 --> E2
    P1 --> E3
    P2 --> E3
    P1 --> R
    P2 --> R
    P1 --> BASE
    P2 --> BASE
    E1 --> SUM
    E2 --> SUM
    E3 --> SUM
    R --> SUM
    BASE --> SUM
    SUM --> COMBO
    GA --> ADD
    COMBO --> ADD
    X --> OUT
    ADD --> TRN --> DEC --> OUT

    classDef data fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2b6cb0
    classDef expert fill:#fff5e6,stroke:#c05621
    classDef router fill:#fde8e8,stroke:#c53030
    classDef base fill:#e9f7ef,stroke:#276749
    classDef result fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6b46c1
```

Every arrow above corresponds to a specific line range in `models/model.py`, which is the single file containing all trainable architecture. The orchestration wrapper (`models/scpert.py`) and the entry points (`scripts/train.py`, `scripts/infer.py`) configure and drive these modules rather than adding new computation.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L678-L760), [README.md](README.md#L34-L37)

## Repository Layout and Module Responsibilities

The codebase is deliberately flat: two Python packages, three fixed embedding assets, and one architecture figure. `models/` holds the entire model and data stack, while `scripts/` contains only thin command-line wrappers.

```
DyMoE-Pert/
├── embeddings/            # fixed runtime gene representations (KG + scGPT)
├── figures/
│   └── dymoe_architecture.png
├── models/
│   ├── model.py           # ResidualMoEFusion + scPert_Model (all trainable modules)
│   ├── scpert.py          # scPert wrapper: init, train/eval loop, save/load, MoE stats
│   ├── ProcePertdata.py   # PertData: GEARS-format loading, splits, cell graphs
│   ├── data_utils.py      # DataSplitter, DE-gene helpers
│   ├── inference.py       # evaluate, metrics, deeper/non-dropout analyses
│   ├── utils.py           # downloads, GeneSimNetwork, co-expression graph, loss_fct
│   └── __init__.py
├── scripts/
│   ├── train.py           # CLI: dataset → PertData → scPert training
│   └── infer.py           # CLI: checkpoint + perturbation → predicted expression
└── requirements.txt
```

| Module | Responsibility | Key symbols |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `models/model.py` | All trainable architecture: MoE fusion, gene context, transformer backbone, decoder | `ResidualMoEFusion`, `scPert_Model`, `ImprovedTransformerLayer`, `MemoryEfficientMultiheadAttention` |
| `models/scpert.py` | Experiment wrapper: model lifecycle, parallelism unwrapping, MoE aux-loss injection, stats logging | `scPert`, `_moe_balance_loss`, `_format_moe_stats` |
| `models/ProcePertdata.py` | Dataset download, GEARS-format loading, split assignment, PyG `Data` construction | `PertData` |
| `models/utils.py` | Downloads, GO-similarity and co-expression graph construction, composite loss | `GeneSimNetwork`, `get_similarity_network`, `loss_fct` |
| `scripts/train.py` | CLI that wires dataset, dataset-aligned embedding file, and MoE configuration | `EMBEDDING_FILES`, `parse_args` |

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L23-L58), [utils.py](models/utils.py#L343-L400), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L12-L54)

## Three Embedding Sources Feed the Model

`scPert_Model.__init__` registers three distinct embedding assets as buffers, and the forward pass treats them with different roles. The KG and scGPT files are **condition-independent** and shared across all datasets; the third file is **dataset-aligned** and supplies the base representation for every gene in the dataset's feature space.

| Source | File | Dimension | Role in the model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Knowledge-graph embeddings | `embeddings/gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz` | 128 | Per-perturbed-gene biological prior, routed through the KG expert |
| scGPT-derived perturbation embeddings | `embeddings/gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz` | 512 | Foundation-model prior per perturbed gene, routed through the scGPT expert |
| Dataset-aligned gene embeddings | `embeddings/gene_embeddings_<dataset>_512.npy` | 512 | Base gene features for the whole transcriptomic context (`gene_emb`) |

Lookup is name-based with graceful fallback: `'ctrl'` maps to zero vectors (128-d for KG, 512-d for scGPT), known genes index into the registered buffers, and unknown gene names receive **deterministic random embeddings** generated from a SHA1-seeded generator — a 640-dim random vector where the first 128 dims serve KG and the remaining 512 serve scGPT. This determinism means unseen perturbations always produce identical embeddings across runs and machines, which is essential for reproducible inference on unseen combinations.

> [!TIP]
> Because lookup falls back to deterministic random vectors instead of raising errors, a typo in a gene name silently produces a plausible prediction instead of a crash — always validate perturbation names against the dataset vocabulary before interpreting results.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L371-L390), [model.py](models/model.py#L636-L671), [README.md](README.md#L64-L68)

## The Forward Pass: From Perturbation String to Predicted Expression

`scPert_Model.forward` processes a batch of PyG cell graphs in five stages. Each stage is small and independently verifiable, and the whole pass is contained in fewer than 90 lines.

| Stage | Operation | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Gene context | Dataset-aligned 512-d embeddings → `gene_dense` (512→64) → softmax gene-gene attention → context aggregation → residual add | `model.py` L684-L693 |
| 2. Perturbation embedding | For each perturbed gene: KG + scGPT lookup → MoE fusion; single-gene conditions duplicate the fused vector so both "slots" of a combo are symmetric; combos pass through `pert_fuse` and are averaged before broadcasting to all `num_genes` positions | `model.py` L695-L730 |
| 3. Control handling | `'ctrl'` conditions receive a learned `control_emb`; a sum-based mask also substitutes `control_emb` wherever the perturbation matrix is all-zero; the result is scaled by the learnable `emb_scale` | `model.py` L700-L736 |
| 4. Refinement | `layer_norm1(gene_emb + pert_emb)` → dropout → 8 transformer layers, each applied with a **scaled residual** (`×0.5`) → `layer_norm2` | `model.py` L739-L747 |
| 5. Delta decoding | `final_mlp` (64→256→128→64) → `output_layer` (→1) → **residual add of control expression `x`** → reshape per sample | `model.py` L748-L757 |

Two design decisions deserve emphasis. First, the model is a **residual predictor**: the decoder learns a per-gene correction on top of the measured control expression rather than absolute expression, which anchors predictions to realistic baselines. Second, the interaction expert consumes an explicitly crafted cross-modal feature — the concatenation of the two projected embeddings, their elementwise product, and their absolute difference — giving the router a candidate expert that is specialized for nonlinear cross-source structure rather than either source alone.

> [!TIP]
> The 0.5 scaling on each transformer residual (`combined_emb = combined_emb + layer_output * 0.5`) halves the effective learning-rate of the attention stack; when tuning training hyperparameters, treat the backbone as intrinsically conservative rather than raising the global LR to compensate.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L684-L757), [model.py](models/model.py#L296-L297)

## The Dynamic Residual MoE Fusion Block

`ResidualMoEFusion` is the conceptual core of DyMoE-Pert, and it is intentionally rigid in structure — it hard-codes exactly three experts — while remaining flexible in behavior through two orthogonal switches: `router_mode` (`dynamic` vs `fixed_uniform`) and `ablation_mode` (`full`, `base_only`, `no_interaction`, `experts_only`). Ablation switches are implemented as parameter freezing plus masked routing rather than separate model classes, so every variant shares one code path and one checkpoint format.

The forward flow is compact: project both inputs to `hidden_dim`, run the base MLP on their concatenation, run each expert, compute router logits from the same concatenated input, softmax into weights, take the weighted sum of expert outputs, and add the base branch before a final `LayerNorm`. When `return_aux=True` — the default path in this fork — the module also returns a dictionary carrying router logits, raw and applied weights, the balance loss, the active-expert mask, and per-expert outputs, which the wrapper aggregates and logs.

| Component | Input → Output | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Projectors | 128→64 and 512→64, GELU + LayerNorm | Bring heterogeneous modalities to a shared space |
| Base branch | `base_mlp` on `[z_kg, z_sc]` (128→64) | Always-available shared multimodal representation (the "residual" in the name) |
| Three experts | 64→64 each; interaction expert 256→64 | Specialized transformations: KG prior, scGPT prior, cross-modal interactions |
| Soft router | `[z_kg, z_sc]` → 3 logits → softmax | Input-dependent fusion weights; initialized near-uniform via tiny-weight init |
| Balance loss | MSE of mean applied weights vs uniform 1/3 | Optional regularizer against expert collapse; weight forced to 0 for fixed-uniform or `base_only` modes |

The near-zero initialization of the router's final linear layer (weights ~ N(0, 10⁻³), bias zero) means that at the start of training, softmax over logits near zero yields weights close to 1/3 each — the model begins as a uniform mixture and learns to specialize. The internals of routing, balance loss, and the ablation framework each have dedicated pages: [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design), [Expert Specialization: KG, scGPT, Interaction](7-expert-specialization-kg-scgpt-interaction), [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss), and [Ablation Modes Framework](9-ablation-modes-framework).

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L96-L167), [model.py](models/model.py#L239-L271), [model.py](models/model.py#L273-L345)

## The Backbone: Gene Context, Chunked Attention, and the Decoder

Upstream of the MoE block, the gene context encoder applies a lightweight attention-like operation over all genes in the dataset: gene embeddings are normalized via scaled dot-product (`/√hidden_size`), softmaxed into a gene-gene interaction matrix, multiplied back onto the embeddings to produce a context vector, projected through `gene_interaction_layer`, and residually added. This gives every gene's representation awareness of the rest of the transcriptome before any perturbation signal arrives.

The refinement stack uses eight custom `ImprovedTransformerLayer`s whose attention is **chunked** (`MemoryEfficientMultiheadAttention`, chunk size 256): queries, keys, and values are processed in fixed-size slices along the sequence dimension and concatenated, bounding peak memory for large gene panels at the cost of extra kernel launches. Each layer is a standard pre/post-norm transformer block — LayerNorm around a multi-head attention sublayer and a 4×-expansion GELU feed-forward — applied with the scaled residual described above.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L26-L93), [model.py](models/model.py#L393-L445), [model.py](models/model.py#L689-L693)

## Orchestration: The `scPert` Wrapper and the Training Entry Point

The `scPert` class in `models/scpert.py` is the stateful experiment manager. `model_initialize` assembles the config dictionary — including all `moe_*` switches — instantiates `scPert_Model`, and keeps a CPU deepcopy as `best_model`. Checkpoints are two files: `config.pkl` (the full keyword config) and `model.pt` (the unwrapped state dict, so checkpoints saved under `DataParallel` remain portable; `load_pretrained` conversely strips any `module.` prefix when loading). Module-level `torch.manual_seed(0)` in `scpert.py` pins model initialization deterministically.

Training-time integration of the MoE happens in three places. The wrapper's `_moe_balance_loss` adds `moe_balance_weight × balance_loss` to the base prediction loss (returning the balance term separately for logging) and skips it entirely when the weight is ≤ 0. `_format_moe_stats` renders a rich single-line diagnostic — applied and raw per-expert alphas, their min/max, routing entropy, active experts, and resolved ablation/router modes — from the merged aux dictionary that `scPert_Model` produces via `_merge_moe_aux`. Finally, `scripts/train.py` hard-sets `use_moe_fusion = True` and maps `--data-name` to its dataset-aligned embedding file, so every run through the CLI trains the full DyMoE configuration; the README's default config additionally sets `moe_balance_weight` to 0.0, making the balance term diagnostics-only unless explicitly raised.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L271-L355), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L357-L422), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L64-L77), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L112-L169), [model.py](models/model.py#L492-L631), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L71-L117)

## Where to Go Next

This page deliberately stayed at the map level; each region of the diagram now has a dedicated exploration path within the Deep Dive catalog. To follow the data flow in code order, proceed to [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design) for the fusion block's structure, then [Expert Specialization: KG, scGPT, Interaction](7-expert-specialization-kg-scgpt-interaction) and [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss) for the dynamic-routing machinery, and [Ablation Modes Framework](9-ablation-modes-framework) for the experimental variants. For the backbone and output path, continue with [Gene Interaction GNN Layers](10-gene-interaction-gnn-layers) and [Prediction Decoder and Loss](11-prediction-decoder-and-loss). If you instead want the upstream story — how GEARS-format data, the GO similarity graph, and the perturbation splits are produced before anything reaches `scPert_Model.forward` — jump to [GEARS-Format Data Pipeline](12-gears-format-data-pipeline), [Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings](13-knowledge-graph-and-scgpt-embeddings), and [Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split](14-perturbation-splits-and-simulation-split). For operational concerns, [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration), [Multi-GPU Parallel Training](16-multi-gpu-parallel-training), and [Unseen Perturbation Inference](17-unseen-perturbation-inference) cover the lifecycle beyond this page.


# Residual Fusion Design



This page explains the **residual mixture-of-experts fusion** that DyMoE-Pert uses to merge two heterogeneous perturbation representations — a 128-dimensional knowledge-graph embedding and a 512-dimensional scGPT embedding — into a single vector consumed by the prediction backbone. The core object is `ResidualMoEFusion` in `models/model.py`: a base MLP trunk, three expert branches, and a soft router, combined through an explicit residual add followed by layer normalization. We cover the fusion equation, the role of the base branch, the dense weighted-sum aggregation, the structural ablation variants, and how the module plugs into `scPert_Model` and the training loop. Router mechanics and expert internals are covered by their own pages and only summarized here.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L96-L110), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## The Fusion Contract: Trunk Plus Routed Deltas

The entire design reduces to one line executed in `ResidualMoEFusion.forward`:

```python
output = self.output_norm(h_base + expert_output)   # model.py L311
```

where `expert_output` is a router-weighted sum of the three expert outputs (`model.py#L305-L306`) and `h_base` is the output of a dedicated base MLP. Expressed as a pipeline:

```text
z_kg   = kg_projector(kg_embedding)               # 128-d → hidden_dim
z_sc   = scgpt_projector(scgpt_embedding)         # 512-d → hidden_dim
h_base = base_mlp(concat(z_kg, z_sc))             # 2·hidden_dim → output_dim
h_kg   = kg_expert(z_kg)                          # hidden_dim → output_dim
h_sc   = scgpt_expert(z_sc)                       # hidden_dim → output_dim
h_int  = interaction_expert([z_kg, z_sc, z_kg⊙z_sc, |z_kg−z_sc|])
w      = softmax(router(concat(z_kg, z_sc)))      # 3 weights, sum to 1
output = LayerNorm(h_base + w_kg·h_kg + w_sc·h_sc + w_int·h_int)
```

Three properties of this contract matter architecturally. First, it is a **dense** mixture: all three experts are evaluated for every input and their outputs are blended by weights that sum to 1 — there is no top-k sparsity or hard dispatch. Second, the trunk `h_base` carries no router weight and cannot be scaled down; it is either fully present or structurally removed (the `experts_only` ablation). Third, the experts act as **modulation deltas** on top of the trunk, mirroring the identity-shortcut logic of residual networks: even if every expert output were zero, a valid representation still flows to the output through `h_base`.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L273-L312), [model.py](models/model.py#L299-L306), [README.md](README.md#L11)

## Stage One: Reconciling Heterogeneous Modalities

Before any fusion can happen, the two input modalities must be made commensurable. The raw inputs are asymmetric — 128 dimensions from the ComGCN-trained knowledge-graph embeddings versus 512 dimensions from scGPT — so concatenating them directly (as the non-MoE fallback does, producing a 640-dimensional vector) would force the downstream network to cope with unbalanced scale and information density. `ResidualMoEFusion` instead runs each modality through its own projector: a `Linear → GELU → Dropout → LayerNorm` stack that maps both inputs to a shared `hidden_dim` space (`kg_projector` and `scgpt_projector`).

The terminal `LayerNorm` in each projector is significant for the fusion contract: it bounds the scale of `z_kg` and `z_sc` before they enter both the router (whose softmax is scale-sensitive) and the interaction expert (whose elementwise product `z_kg ⊙ z_sc` grows quadratically with input magnitude). The shared `hidden_dim` defaults to the backbone's `hidden_size` (64) unless `moe_hidden_dim` overrides it, and the expert/base final layers project from `hidden_dim` to `output_dim`, which is pinned to `self.hidden_size` so the fused vector drops directly into the perturbation pipeline.

| Stage | Module | Input → Output | Role in the fusion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Projector | `kg_projector` (Linear→GELU→Dropout→LayerNorm) | 128 → `hidden_dim` | Normalize KG modality into shared space |
| Projector | `scgpt_projector` (Linear→GELU→Dropout→LayerNorm) | 512 → `hidden_dim` | Normalize scGPT modality into shared space |
| Trunk | `base_mlp` (Linear→GELU→Dropout→Linear) | 2·`hidden_dim` → `output_dim` | Residual base `h_base` |
| Expert | `kg_expert` | `hidden_dim` → `output_dim` | KG-specific delta |
| Expert | `scgpt_expert` | `hidden_dim` → `output_dim` | scGPT-specific delta |
| Expert | `interaction_expert` | 4·`hidden_dim` → `output_dim` | Cross-modal, non-additive delta |
| Router | `router` (2·`hidden_dim` → `hidden_dim` → 3) | 2·`hidden_dim` → 3 logits | Input-dependent mixture weights |
| Output | `output_norm` (LayerNorm) | `output_dim` → `output_dim` | Stabilize the fused result |

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L119-L130), [model.py](models/model.py#L296), [model.py](models/model.py#L408-L414), [model.py](models/model.py#L415-L429)

## The Base Branch: A Trunk, Not a Fourth Expert

A subtle but deliberate design decision is that `base_mlp` is architecturally separated from the experts. It consumes exactly the same input as the router — `base_input = concat(z_kg, z_sc)` — so it has access to the full multimodal signal, but unlike the experts it is **outside** the routing mixture. There is no learnable weight that can attenuate `h_base`; the only ways to remove it are the coarse, structural ones: freezing (via the ablation framework, which disables gradients) or full bypass (`experts_only`, where the forward path skips the base MLP entirely and computes `LayerNorm(expert_output)`).

This asymmetry encodes an inductive bias: shared multimodal information should always reach the output, while expert contributions should be *earned* through routing. In practice the trunk also functions as the model's fallback behavior — the `base_only` ablation, which freezes experts and router, reduces the whole module to `LayerNorm(h_base)` and is used as the control condition demonstrating what the routed deltas add. The contrast between `base_only` and `full` is therefore a direct measurement of the experts' marginal value over the residual trunk.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L132-L137), [model.py](models/model.py#L278-L288), [model.py](models/model.py#L307-L312), [model.py](models/model.py#L178-L187)

## End-to-End Data Flow

The diagram below shows one forward pass through `ResidualMoEFusion`. Prerequisites for reading it: `z_kg`/`z_sc` are the projected modality vectors from the previous section; `h_base` is the trunk output; the router's softmax produces weights over exactly three experts; and the residual add plus final LayerNorm produce the fused embedding whose width equals the backbone's `hidden_size`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    KG["KG embedding (128-d)"] --> P1["kg_projector"]
    SC["scGPT embedding (512-d)"] --> P2["scgpt_projector"]
    P1 --> ZK["z_kg (hidden_dim)"]
    P2 --> ZS["z_sc (hidden_dim)"]
    ZK --> CAT["base_input = concat(z_kg, z_sc)"]
    ZS --> CAT
    CAT --> BASE["base_mlp → h_base"]
    CAT --> R["router → logits → softmax"]
    ZK --> E1["kg_expert → h_kg"]
    ZS --> E2["scgpt_expert → h_sc"]
    ZK --> E3["interaction_expert → h_int"]
    ZS --> E3
    R --> W["router_weights (sum = 1)"]
    E1 --> SUM["dense weighted sum: Σ wᵢ·hᵢ"]
    E2 --> SUM
    E3 --> SUM
    W --> SUM
    BASE --> ADD["residual add: h_base + Σ wᵢ·hᵢ"]
    SUM --> ADD
    ADD --> LN["output_norm (LayerNorm)"]
    LN --> OUT["fused embedding (output_dim = hidden_size)"]
    style ADD fill:#e8f4e8,stroke:#2d7a2d
```

The forward method also builds an auxiliary dictionary (`return_aux=True`) exposing the router logits, the pre- and post-ablation routing weights, the per-expert outputs, the balance loss, and boolean flags describing which structural components were active.
