This aux payload is the sole interface through which training-time regularization and router diagnostics observe the fusion internals — the fused tensor itself is otherwise opaque to the rest of the model.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L273-L345), [model.py](models/model.py#L317-L344)

## Expert Stack: The Inputs to the Weighted Sum

For the fusion equation to be meaningful, every term in the weighted sum must share the output dimension — and they do: all three experts emit `output_dim`-wide vectors, which is what makes `torch.stack([h_kg, h_sc, h_interaction], dim=-2)` followed by a weighted sum well-formed. The experts differ in their *inputs*, not their widths. `kg_expert` sees only the projected KG vector, `scgpt_expert` sees only the projected scGPT vector, and `interaction_expert` sees an explicitly engineered 4·`hidden_dim` feature vector combining both projections, their elementwise product, and their absolute difference — the only place in the fusion module where non-additive cross-modal interactions are computed explicitly.

| Expert | Input features | Transformation | Signal captured |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `kg_expert` | `z_kg` | Linear→GELU→Dropout→Linear | Relation-structure knowledge from the KG embedding |
| `scgpt_expert` | `z_sc` | Linear→GELU→Dropout→Linear | Foundation-model expression priors |
| `interaction_expert` | `[z_kg, z_sc, z_kg⊙z_sc, \|z_kg−z_sc\|]` | Linear(4h→h)→GELU→Dropout→Linear | Multiplicative and asymmetry effects between modalities |

The depth of each expert's specialization — what each branch actually learns on real perturbation data — is the subject of [Expert Specialization: KG, scGPT, Interaction](7-expert-specialization-kg-scgpt-interaction); here we only note the interface contract that the fusion depends on: homogeneous outputs, heterogeneous inputs.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L138-L155), [model.py](models/model.py#L290-L297), [model.py](models/model.py#L305-L306)

## Soft, Dense Aggregation and Its Initialization

The aggregation step — stack, broadcast weights, sum — implements what the code calls the "dynamic" router mode. Because it is soft and dense, gradient flow reaches every expert on every sample; the router learns a per-perturbation blend rather than a discrete assignment. A second mode, `fixed_uniform`, replaces the softmax output with constant 1/3 weights, converting the module into a strict control where the only learned specialization lives in the expert weights themselves; additionally, a trained dynamic model can be evaluated with uniform routing at inference time via `set_inference_router_mode("fixed_uniform")`, a lever used to disentangle routing contributions from expert contributions without retraining.

> [!TIP]
> The router's final linear layer is initialized with weight std = 1e-3 and zero bias (model.py#L164-L166). Softmax over near-zero logits is almost exactly uniform, so **training begins at h_base + (1/3)(h_kg + h_sc + h_int)** — the residual trunk dominates early optimization and expert specialization emerges gradually as the router's logits grow. This is the initialization counterpart of the residual contract.

| Property | Soft dense mixture (this design) | Hard top-k routing (not used) | Fixed uniform (control mode) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gradient reach | All experts per sample | Only selected experts | All experts, no routing signal |
| Compute cost | Always 3 expert evaluations | Lower (~k evaluations) | Always 3 evaluations |
| Failure mode | Weight collapse to one expert | Unstable expert switching | None (no collapse possible) |
| Interpretability | Continuous per-sample weights | Discrete assignments | Weights are constants |

The balance loss that guards against weight collapse — a mean-squared penalty pulling per-expert average routing weights toward uniformity — is computed inside the module but its optimization role belongs to [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss).

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L156-L166), [model.py](models/model.py#L239-L262), [model.py](models/model.py#L264-L271), [model.py](models/model.py#L169-L172)

## Ablation Geometry: How Each Variant Rewrites the Residual Equation

The `ablation_mode` constructor argument defines four structural variants, each of which is a different reading of the fusion equation. Crucially, these are not just flag checks in the forward pass — the constructor also **freezes parameters** (`requires_grad = False`) for components that are bypassed, so optimizers built over `requires_grad`-filtered parameters skip them entirely.

| Mode | Base trunk | Expert stack | Router behavior | Effective equation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `full` | Active, trained | All 3, trained | Softmax over 3 | `LN(h_base + Σ₃ wᵢhᵢ)` |
| `base_only` | Active, trained | Frozen, bypassed | Bypassed | `LN(h_base)` |
| `no_interaction` | Active, trained | KG + scGPT only | Softmax over 2 active experts, renormalized to sum 1 | `LN(h_base + w₁h_kg + w₂h_sc)` |
| `experts_only` | Disabled | All 3, trained | Softmax over 3 | `LN(Σ₃ wᵢhᵢ)` |

Two implementation details deserve attention. In `no_interaction`, the interaction expert's output is replaced with a **zero tensor that is detached** (`torch.zeros_like(h_kg).detach()`), so stale gradients can never flow into the frozen expert even if its parameters were later unfrozen; the router then softmaxes over only the active slice of its logits and scatters the renormalized weights back into a 3-wide vector, preserving the stack shape of the weighted sum. In `experts_only`, the residual add is removed rather than the base weighted to zero — meaning the fused output loses its trunk anchor entirely, which is the harshest test of whether routed deltas alone can carry the representation. The experimental purpose of these variants is documented in [Ablation Modes Framework](9-ablation-modes-framework).

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L178-L204), [model.py](models/model.py#L243-L253), [model.py](models/model.py#L293-L294), [model.py](models/model.py#L285-L312)

## Integration: Where Fusion Sits in `scPert_Model`

`scPert_Model` owns one `ResidualMoEFusion` instance, built only when `use_moe_fusion` is true (the training CLI sets it unconditionally). The integration point is `_fuse_pert_embedding`, which is called **once per perturbed gene** inside the forward loop: for a combination like `GENE1+GENE2`, each gene's 128-d KG embedding and 512-d scGPT embedding are fused independently, and the resulting per-gene vectors are then stacked, passed through `pert_fuse`, and averaged into the graph-level perturbation embedding. When `use_moe_fusion` is false, the same call site falls back to raw concatenation plus the `pert_dense` MLP (accepting the 128+512 = 640-d vector directly) — which is precisely the baseline the residual MoE design replaces.

> [!TIP]
> The residual design is a failure-containment mechanism at the system level: if routing weights collapse toward a degenerate state during training, the fused output degrades gracefully toward trunk-only behavior (essentially `base_only`) rather than toward garbage. The downstream pipeline never needs a special case for a broken router.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph FWD["scPert_Model.forward — once per perturbed gene"]
        G1["get_gene_embedding → KG 128-d"] --> FUSE["_fuse_pert_embedding"]
        G2["get_pert_embedding → scGPT 512-d"] --> FUSE
    end
    FUSE --> MOE["ResidualMoEFusion.forward"]
    MOE -->|"fused vector (hidden_size)"| FUSE
    MOE -->|"aux dict"| AUXL["moe_aux_list (per call)"]
    FUSE --> PF["pert_fuse + mean over combo genes"]
    PF --> OUT["joins gene embeddings in the backbone"]
    AUXL --> MERGE["_merge_moe_aux across batch"]
    MERGE --> BL["mean balance_loss → training loss"]
```

The merged aux statistics (router weight tensors stacked across every fusion call in the batch, plus a batch-level routing entropy) are returned alongside predictions whenever `moe_return_router_stats` is enabled, and the trainer unwraps them through `_split_model_output` — a small compatibility shim that lets the same code path serve both the `(output, aux)` tuple and the plain-tensor legacy return.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L415-L429), [model.py](models/model.py#L478-L490), [model.py](models/model.py#L697-L730), [model.py](models/model.py#L758-L760), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L58-L61)

## Training-Time Coupling

The fusion module does not add its own loss; it *reports* one. Each forward returns `balance_loss` inside the aux dict, `_merge_moe_aux` averages it across all fusion calls in the batch, and the trainer's `_moe_balance_loss` helper adds `λ · balance_loss` to the task loss before backward. λ (`moe_balance_weight`) defaults to 0.0 in the training CLI — matching the manuscript's main configuration — while the model-level default is 0.01; in either case λ is **forced to 0.0** when the router is `fixed_uniform` or the ablation is `base_only`, because in those regimes the routing distribution contains no learnable degree of freedom to regularize. Note also that the optimizer is constructed over `requires_grad`-filtered parameters only, which is how the ablation freezing described earlier removes bypassed components from training at zero runtime cost.

The full optimization treatment of the balance term — its gradient dynamics and interaction with the task loss — is covered in [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss); the surrounding loop mechanics are in [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration).

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L317-L321), [model.py](models/model.py#L364-L367), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L64-L77), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L573-L611), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L40-L41), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L73-L75)

## Design Rationale: Residual Fusion vs. the Alternatives

Placing the design in context clarifies why each element exists. The module's true baseline is the non-MoE fallback (`pert_dense` over the raw 640-d concatenation), and its theoretical alternative is a pure MoE without a trunk. The residual middle ground buys gradient stability and graceful degradation at the cost of a permanently active trunk that experts can only modulate, never replace.

| Dimension | Residual MoE (this design) | Plain concat + MLP (fallback) | Pure MoE, no trunk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gradient path at initialization | Trunk + near-uniform expert mix (well-conditioned) | Single path | Only routed path, random specialization |
| Router collapse consequence | Degrades toward trunk-only behavior | N/A | Output collapses to one expert |
| Non-additive combinatorial signal | Explicit (interaction expert features) | Implicit, learned late (if at all) | Only if an expert models it |
| Input-dim asymmetry (128 vs 512) | Explicit normalization before fusion | Raw concat, scale imbalance | Requires projectors regardless |
| Parameter overhead | Trunk + 3 experts + router | One MLP | Experts + router only |

The manuscript-level claim attached to this architecture — that its clearest advantage appears on combinatorial perturbations whose single-gene effects were never observed — depends on both the interaction expert's explicit cross-modal features and the residual trunk keeping training stable while those features are learned.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L408-L414), [model.py](models/model.py#L478-L481), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## Summary and Reading Path

The residual fusion design in DyMoE-Pert is best understood as a **contract**: a fixed, always-on multimodal trunk (`h_base`) plus three homogeneous expert deltas blended by a near-uniformly-initialized soft router, summed and normalized as `LayerNorm(h_base + Σ wᵢhᵢ)`. The projectors reconcile 128-d and 512-d inputs into a common scale-normalized space; the dense mixture keeps every expert in the gradient path; the structural ablations (`base_only`, `no_interaction`, `experts_only`) each rewrite a specific part of the equation for controlled comparison; and the aux dictionary cleanly separates the fused tensor from the routing diagnostics consumed by training.

To continue through the Deep Dive catalog in dependency order: the experts themselves are dissected in [Expert Specialization: KG, scGPT, Interaction](7-expert-specialization-kg-scgpt-interaction); the router's dynamics and the balance loss are treated in [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss); the ablation experiments built on the variants above are in [Ablation Modes Framework](9-ablation-modes-framework); and how the fused embedding is consumed downstream is covered in [Prediction Decoder and Loss](11-prediction-decoder-and-loss).


# Expert Specialization: KG, scGPT, Interaction


This page dissects the three specialized experts inside DyMoE-Pert's `ResidualMoEFusion` module: the **KG expert**, the **scGPT expert**, and the **Interaction expert**. Each expert processes a distinct view of the perturbation representation, and their division of labor is the mechanism by which the model fuses knowledge-graph priors with foundation-model gene embeddings. We cover expert construction, modality-specific input sourcing, the interaction expert's feature-crossing design, and how specialization is shaped to remain a *soft mixture* rather than a hard gate. Routing mechanics and the balance loss formulation are treated in depth in [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss); the residual summation structure is covered in [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design).

## Architectural Position of the Experts

The experts live in `ResidualMoEFusion`, instantiated inside `scPert_Model` only when `use_moe_fusion` is enabled. The constructor enforces exactly three experts and validates the router and ablation modes up front, establishing the fixed expert topology this page describes. The fusion module receives two heterogeneous tensors — a 128-dim knowledge-graph embedding and a 512-dim scGPT embedding — and returns a single `hidden_size`-dim vector that replaces the naive concatenation pathway.

Two modality projectors normalize this dimensional asymmetry *before* expert computation: `kg_projector` maps 128 → `hidden_dim` and `scgpt_projector` maps 512 → `hidden_dim`, each via Linear → GELU → Dropout → LayerNorm. This design decision matters for expert specialization: every expert — including the cross-modal one — operates on a shared latent geometry rather than raw, differently-scaled embedding spaces.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Inputs["Raw Modality Inputs"]
        KG["KG embedding (128-d)"]
        SC["scGPT embedding (512-d)"]
    end
    subgraph Projection["Modality Projection"]
        KP["kg_projector<br/>128 → hidden"] --> ZK["z_kg"]
        SP["scgpt_projector<br/>512 → hidden"] --> ZS["z_sc"]
    end
    KG --> KP
    SC --> SP
    subgraph Experts["Three Specialized Experts"]
        E1["kg_expert<br/>input: z_kg"]
        E2["scgpt_expert<br/>input: z_sc"]
        E3["interaction_expert<br/>input: [z_kg, z_sc,<br/>z_kg ⊙ z_sc, |z_kg − z_sc|]"]
    end
    ZK --> E1
    ZS --> E2
    ZK --> E3
    ZS --> E3
    subgraph Routing["Soft Router"]
        R["router on [z_kg, z_sc]<br/>→ 3 softmax weights"]
    end
    ZK --> R
    ZS --> R
    R --> E1
    R --> E2
    R --> E3
    E1 --> OUT["Σ wᵢ·hᵢ → residual add"]
    E2 --> OUT
    E3 --> OUT
```

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L96-L130), [model.py](models/model.py#L415-L427)

## Expert Comparison: Inputs, Capacity, and Roles

All three experts share the same *output* contract — a `Linear(hidden_dim → hidden_dim) → GELU → Dropout → Linear(hidden_dim → output_dim)` trunk — so the router can treat them as interchangeable contributors to a weighted sum. Their differentiation is entirely in the **input feature space** and the **input width**. The interaction expert is the only expert that sees both modalities and the only one whose first layer is 4× wider, reflecting its four concatenated feature blocks.

| Expert | Input features | Input width | Cross-modal? | Architectural role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `kg_expert` | `z_kg` | `hidden_dim` | No | Unimodal KG pathway |
| `scgpt_expert` | `z_sc` | `hidden_dim` | No | Unimodal scGPT pathway |
| `interaction_expert` | `[z_kg, z_sc, z_kg ⊙ z_sc, \|z_kg − z_sc\|]` | `4 × hidden_dim` | Yes | Explicit feature crossing |

The interaction expert's feature construction at forward time is `[z_kg, z_sc, z_kg * z_sc, |z_kg - z_sc|]` — concatenation, Hadamard product, and absolute difference. The product term supplies a bilinear coupling (coordinates that co-activate across modalities), while the absolute-difference term supplies a disagreement signal (coordinates where the knowledge-graph prior and the scGPT prior diverge). This is the standard NLI/decomposition-style feature-crossing recipe applied to embedding fusion, and it is why this expert can model *relationships between* sources rather than either source alone.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L138-L155), [model.py](models/model.py#L296-L297)

## KG Expert: Input Sourcing and Edge Cases

The KG expert's input originates in `get_gene_embedding`, backed by the buffer loaded from `embeddings/gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz` at model construction. Lookup follows a strict three-tier policy: control perturbations receive a 128-dim zero vector; genes present in the KG vocabulary receive their stored ComGCN knowledge-graph embedding; out-of-vocabulary genes receive the first 128 dims of a deterministic fallback vector.

The fallback is worth understanding precisely. `get_random_embedding` derives a seed from the SHA-1 hash of the gene name, generating a seeded 640-dim Gaussian vector scaled by `1/√640`. The KG pathway slices `[:128]` and the scGPT pathway (below) slices `[128:]` of the *same* vector — so an unseen gene still produces two coherent, deterministic modality inputs without any file dependency. Determinism via name-hashed seeding guarantees the same gene always maps to the same embedding across processes and multi-GPU workers, which is essential for reproducible inference on unseen perturbations.

> [!TIP]
> The two OOV slices `[:128]` and `[128:]` come from one seeded 640-dim vector. This means unseen genes have *correlated* KG and scGPT fallback embeddings by construction — the interaction expert's product term will see consistent structure even for out-of-vocabulary genes, rather than independent noise per modality.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L370-L377), [model.py](models/model.py#L636-L648), [model.py](models/model.py#L651-L658)

## scGPT Expert: Input Sourcing and Edge Cases

The scGPT expert's input comes from `get_pert_embedding`, backed by `embeddings/gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz` loaded as the `pert_embeddings` buffer. Its policy mirrors the KG expert's tiered lookup — `ctrl` maps to a 512-dim zero vector, known genes index directly into the buffer, and unknown genes slice `[128:]` of the shared deterministic fallback. Both controls and fallbacks preserve the contract that `scgpt_projector` always receives a valid 512-dim tensor.

At training/inference time, the forward loop resolves *one fused embedding per perturbation gene* in a combo (e.g., both genes of `GENE_A+GENE_B`), calling `get_gene_embedding` and `get_pert_embedding` per gene and passing them to `_fuse_pert_embedding`. With MoE enabled, `_fuse_pert_embedding` delegates to `ResidualMoEFusion` and appends the returned aux dict to a batch-level list; with MoE disabled, it degrades to plain concatenation through `pert_dense` — the exact ablation baseline the experts replace. Single-gene perturbations duplicate their fused embedding so the subsequent `pert_fuse` averaging step sees a pair.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L379-L390), [model.py](models/model.py#L660-L671), [model.py](models/model.py#L697-L730), [model.py](models/model.py#L478-L490)

## How Specialization Emerges: Soft Mixture by Design

The experts are not hard-gated; the router computes softmax weights over all three and the fused output is the weighted sum `Σ wᵢ·hᵢ`, added residually to the base pathway. Specialization therefore manifests as *learned weight distribution*, not expert selection. Three mechanisms shape this distribution toward a healthy soft mixture:

1. **Near-uniform router initialization.** The router's final layer is initialized with weight std `1e-3` and zero bias, so at step zero every expert receives an approximately equal weight — no expert is privileged from birth.
2. **Balance loss pressure.** Per batch, the mean router weight per expert is pulled toward `1/N` via MSE. This term enters training through `_moe_balance_loss` as `base_loss + moe_balance_weight × balance_loss`, with a default weight of `0.01` — zeroed automatically when the router is `fixed_uniform` or the ablation is `base_only`, since uniform weighting needs no regularization. The loss is computed **only over active experts**, so ablations renormalize rather than penalize.
3. **Mask-aware renormalization.** In `no_interaction` mode, the interaction expert's output is replaced with detached zeros and softmax is recomputed over the two remaining active experts, redistributing the full weight budget instead of leaving orphaned mass.

This is a deliberate anti-collapse design: the combination of near-uniform init, small balance weight, and soft summation keeps all three experts contributing, with specialization emerging gradually as gradient pressure shifts weights per input. The cost is that per-sample routing is *dense* — no expert is ever fully skipped — trading compute efficiency for stability.

> [!TIP]
> Because `no_interaction` zeroes the interaction expert *inside the weighted sum*, the frozen expert contributes exactly nothing while its router slot remains valid — this is cleaner than masking the expert output post-hoc, since the router's renormalized weights preserve a proper probability simplex over active experts.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L156-L166), [model.py](models/model.py#L264-L271), [model.py](models/model.py#L239-L262), [model.py](models/model.py#L293-L294), [model.py](models/model.py#L305-L311), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L64-L77), [model.py](models/model.py#L364-L366)

## Observing Specialization: Expert Telemetry

The training wrapper surfaces empirical specialization through `_format_moe_stats`, which emits per-epoch router diagnostics: `applied_alpha_*` (post-mask, post-inference-mode weights averaged over the batch), `raw_alpha_*` (pre-ablation softmax weights), per-expert `alpha_min`/`alpha_max`, and router **entropy**. Reading these logs is the practical way to verify expert behavior: a `full` run should show all three alphas near `0.333` early (uniform init) and diverging as specialization develops, while entropy below `ln(3) ≈ 1.0986` quantifies the departure from uniform routing.

| Telemetry field | Meaning | Healthy signal |
|---|---|---|
| `applied_alpha_{kg,scgpt,interaction}` | Batch-mean weight actually applied | Non-degenerate; not collapsed to one expert |
| `raw_alpha_*` | Weights before ablation masking | Divergence from uniform = learned routing |
| `alpha_min` / `alpha_max` | Weight range per expert across batch | Wide range = input-dependent routing |
| `entropy` | Mean routing entropy | Between ~0.5 and 1.1 nats — neither collapsed nor frozen |
| `balance` | Balance loss value | Trending down without hitting zero |

The aux dict that feeds these logs is assembled in `ResidualMoEFusion.forward` with `return_aux=True`, carrying per-forward `expert_outputs` for each expert plus router logits, weights, and balance loss; the model-level `_merge_moe_aux` then stacks these across all pert-genes in the batch. This telemetry loop is how you empirically validate that the KG expert, scGPT expert, and interaction expert are each earning their share of the mixture.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L112-L169), [model.py](models/model.py#L318-L344), [model.py](models/model.py#L492-L631)

## Interplay with Ablation Modes

Expert participation is governed by the ablation framework, which freezes parameters and zeroes outputs rather than deleting modules — keeping checkpoints structurally comparable across configurations. In `base_only`, all three experts and the router are frozen and the fusion collapses to the base MLP; in `no_interaction`, only the interaction expert is disabled (the direct ablation of this page's cross-modal hypothesis); in `experts_only`, the base MLP is disabled and the output is the experts' weighted sum alone. Each mode also stamps an integer ID and an `active_expert_mask` into the aux dict so downstream logs and loss computation stay consistent. Full parameter-freezing semantics and the experimental rationale for each mode are documented in [Ablation Modes Framework](9-ablation-modes-framework).

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L178-L204), [model.py](models/model.py#L189-L237)

## Summary and Reading Path

Expert specialization in DyMoE-Pert follows a precise contract: **shared output shape, differentiated inputs, soft routing**. The KG and scGPT experts are structurally identical unimodal pathways over projected 128-d and 512-d embeddings respectively; the interaction expert is the sole cross-modal component, distinguished by its 4×-wide first layer over concatenated, element-wise-product, and absolute-difference features. Specialization is cultivated — not imposed — through near-uniform router init, a small balance loss on active experts, and dense soft weighting.

To continue the Deep Dive into the Dynamic MoE Fusion Core:

- [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design) — how the expert mixture integrates with the base pathway
- [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss) — full routing math and regularization analysis
- [Ablation Modes Framework](9-ablation-modes-framework) — experimental configurations isolating each expert's contribution
- [Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings](13-knowledge-graph-and-scgpt-embeddings) — provenance and construction of the expert inputs


# Soft Router and Balance Loss



This page documents the soft routing mechanism and the auxiliary balance loss inside DyMoE-Pert's `ResidualMoEFusion` module. While [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design) explains *why* a base MLP is additive with expert outputs and [Expert Specialization](7-expert-specialization-kg-scgpt-interaction) explains *what* each expert computes, this page focuses on the third pillar: *how mixing coefficients are produced, constrained, and monitored*. We cover the router topology, the dense soft-max weighting scheme, the two routing modes (`dynamic` and `fixed_uniform`), the mean-squared deviation balance loss, its activation guards, and the telemetry pipeline that surfaces router behavior during training.

## Router Architecture: Input, Topology, and Cold-Start Initialization

The router is a two-layer MLP defined as `Linear(2·hidden_dim → hidden_dim) → GELU → Dropout → Linear(hidden_dim → 3)`. Its input is deliberately restricted to the **base branch representation**: `base_input = cat([z_kg, z_sc], dim=-1)`, the concatenation of the KG-projected (128→hidden) and scGPT-projected (512→hidden) embeddings. The interaction features (`z_kg * z_sc`, `|z_kg - z_sc|`) feed the interaction expert but are **excluded from router input**, keeping the gating decision a function of source-magnitude evidence rather than of the interaction construct itself.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L156-L161), [model.py](/models/model.py#L274-L276), [model.py](/models/model.py#L296-L299)

The final linear layer is initialized with `normal_(mean=0, std=1e-3)` and zero bias. Because softmax over near-zero logits yields weights ≈ 1/3 per expert, training **cold-starts at uniform mixing** and must learn any deviation from the data gradient. This initialization is complementary to the balance loss: the loss penalizes drift *away* from uniform, while the init guarantees the drift starts at zero rather than at an arbitrary random split.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L163-L167)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    KG["KG embedding (128-d)"] --> P1["kg_projector"]
    SC["scGPT embedding (512-d)"] --> P2["scgpt_projector"]
    P1 --> ZK["z_kg"]
    P2 --> ZS["z_sc"]
    ZK & ZS --> BI["base_input = cat(z_kg, z_sc)"]
    BI --> R["router MLP (2 layers)"]
    R --> L["logits (3,)"]
    L --> SM["softmax → router_weights (α_kg, α_sc, α_int)"]
    ZK --> E1["kg_expert → h_kg"]
    ZS --> E2["scgpt_expert → h_sc"]
    ZK & ZS --> XI["interaction features"] --> E3["interaction_expert → h_int"]
    SM -- "α-weighted sum" --> EO["expert_output"]
    BI --> B["base_mlp → h_base"]
    EO & B --> N["output_norm(h_base + expert_output)"]
    SM -.->|mean over batch| BL["balance loss = MSE vs 1/3"]
```

## Soft Weight Computation: Dense Mixing over Three Experts

Weight computation is **dense and soft**: `raw_router_weights = softmax(router_logits, dim=-1)` produces a probability vector over all three experts, and the expert outputs are fused via `sum(router_weights.unsqueeze(-1) * expert_stack, dim=-2)` where `expert_stack = stack([h_kg, h_sc, h_interaction], dim=-2)`. There is **no top-k sparsification, no capacity factor, and no token dropping** — all three experts execute on every perturbation token, and the router selects only the mixture ratio. This makes the compute cost constant per token and eliminates the load-balancing failure mode specific to hard routing (expert overflow), reducing the balance loss's role from "load distribution enforcement" to "specialization regularization."

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L299-L306)

The module enforces exactly three experts (`num_experts != 3` raises), so the softmax support is fixed. Validation also restricts `router_mode` to the two supported values at construction time, and `scPert_Model` mirrors the same validation when reading `moe_router_mode` from args.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L109-L112), [model.py](/models/model.py#L358-L363)

## Routing Modes: Dynamic vs Fixed-Uniform Controls

`_compute_router_weights` is the single decision point that maps logits to applied weights, and it resolves four scenarios in priority order. In `dynamic` training mode the raw softmax is used directly. In `fixed_uniform` mode — described in `--moe-router-mode` help as a "strict fixed-uniform E3 control" — the router is numerically bypassed with constant `1/num_experts` weights, making the MoE degenerate into a fixed average of the three experts while keeping parameters otherwise identical. The third scenario applies `fixed_uniform` **only at inference** (`inference_router_mode`), toggled post-training via `set_inference_router_mode`, enabling an ablation where training used learned routing but evaluation uses uniform mixing. The fourth scenario handles the `no_interaction` ablation: softmax is computed over only the *active* experts' logits (KG, scGPT), then re-scattered into the full 3-slot vector with the interaction slot zero-filled, guaranteeing the masked expert contributes exactly zero to the mixture.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L239-L262), [model.py](/models/model.py#L169-L172), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L47-L53)

| Scenario | Condition | Applied weights | Router gradients | Balance loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dynamic training | `router_mode="dynamic"`, training | `softmax(logits)` | Flows | Active |
| Fixed-uniform control | `router_mode="fixed_uniform"` | Constant `1/3` | N/A (bypassed) | Force-zeroed |
| Inference fixed-uniform | `not training` + `inference_router_mode="fixed_uniform"` | Constant `1/3` | N/A | N/A (eval only) |
| No-interaction ablation | `ablation_mode="no_interaction"` | `softmax` over active subset, zero-filled | Flows to active slots | Active over 2 experts |

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L243-L262)

## The Balance Loss: Formulation and Semantics

`_compute_balance_loss` computes the **mean squared deviation of batch-average routing weights from the uniform target**:

1. Slice the applied `router_weights` to active experts: `active_weights = router_weights[..., active_expert_mask]`.
2. Reduce over all non-expert dimensions (the per-perturbation batch axis): `mean_router_weight = active_weights.mean(...)`, a vector of length = number of active experts.
3. Target is `full_like(mean, 1/K)` where `K = active_weights.shape[-1]`.
4. Return `mean((mean_router_weight - target)²)` — a scalar.

This is a direct uniformity regularizer on **soft mixture coefficients**, not the Switch-Transformer-style importance×load product. Two semantic consequences follow. First, because the reduction is over the mean of weights (not the mean of argmax assignments), the loss penalizes *aggregate* expert under-use even when individual tokens are highly specialized — a router that sends every token entirely to one expert but alternates experts across the batch can still satisfy it. Second, because it operates on `router_weights` (post-mask, post-mode resolution) rather than `raw_router_weights`, the loss automatically degrades to the correct target when `no_interaction` re-normalizes over two experts (target becomes 1/2, not 1/3), and returns exactly zero when the expert mask is empty (`base_only`).

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L264-L271), [model.py](/models/model.py#L197-L204)

> [!TIP]
> The balance loss consumes **applied** weights, not raw logits. This is why fixed-uniform mode can zero the loss safely: with constant 1/3 weights the MSE is identically zero anyway, and `_empty_router_aux` returns a detached zero tensor for `base_only` where no router exists at all.

## Balance Loss Activation Guards and Weighting

The loss participates in training only when explicitly weighted, and three independent guards enforce its deactivation in configurations where it would be meaningless. `scPert_Model.__init__` stores `moe_balance_weight` (default `0.01`) from args, then force-zeroes it when `router_mode == "fixed_uniform"` or `ablation_mode == "base_only"`. The CLI parser defaults `--moe-balance-weight` to `0.0` (opt-in at the script level) and re-applies the same guard. `scPert.model_initialize` performs the identical guard a third time before writing the value into the serialized config — so a saved checkpoint's config never contains an active balance weight for a uniform-router or base-only model, keeping [Configuration Reference](19-configuration-reference) semantics reproducible across `load_pretrained`.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L364-L366), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L40), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L74-L75), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L320-L325)

## Router Telemetry: Aux Metadata Aggregation

When `return_aux=True`, `ResidualMoEFusion.forward` returns a metadata dictionary alongside the fused embedding: `router_logits`, `raw_router_weights` (pre-mask softmax), `router_weights` (post-mask applied), `balance_loss`, mode flags (`router_mode_fixed_uniform`, `inference_router_mode_fixed_uniform`), integer-coded ablation mode, `active_expert_mask`, `active_expert_names`, `base_enabled`, `router_enabled`, and the raw per-expert outputs. Because `scPert_Model.forward` may invoke the fusion module once **per perturbation gene** in a combo perturbation (via `_fuse_pert_embedding`, appending each aux dict to `moe_aux_list`), the per-sample aux dicts are merged by `_merge_moe_aux`: weights stack along a new leading dimension, `balance_loss` is averaged across the per-gene calls, and a companion diagnostic — **router entropy** `−Σ α·log(α)` averaged over tokens — is computed to measure how peaked the routing distribution is.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L317-L345), [model.py](/models/model.py#L478-L490), [model.py](/models/model.py#L578-L631), [model.py](/models/model.py#L610-L616)

Degenerate configurations get structurally valid empty telemetry rather than `None`: `_empty_router_aux` (for `base_only`) and the two early-exit branches of `_merge_moe_aux` produce zero-shaped tensors and scalar zeros, with `router_enabled=False`. This invariant lets downstream logging and multi-GPU code treat aux as always-a-dict.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L212-L237), [model.py](/models/model.py#L492-L577)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F["ResidualMoEFusion.forward (per pert gene)"] -->|return_aux=True| A1["aux dict: logits, weights, balance_loss, masks"]
    A1 --> L["moe_aux_list.append(aux)"]
    L --> M["_merge_moe_aux over N pert genes"]
    M --> BL["balance_loss = mean over aux entries"]
    M --> H["router_entropy = mean of -Σ α·log α"]
    M --> S["stacked weights/logits + mode flags"]
    BL --> T["_moe_balance_loss: loss += w · balance_loss"]
    T --> B["loss.backward()"]
    S --> P["_format_moe_stats → console telemetry"]
```

## Training-Time Integration: Loss Composition and Logging

Inside the training loop, `pred, moe_aux = _split_model_output(model(model_batch))` separates predictions from telemetry. The task loss is computed by `loss_fct` (the prediction objective detailed in [Prediction Decoder and Loss](11-prediction-decoder-and-loss)), then `_moe_balance_loss(task_loss, moe_aux, self.model)` composes the final objective: it unwraps any `PyGDataParallel` wrapper to read `moe_balance_weight` from the underlying module (essential because attribute lookups on a DataParallel shell fail), converts the aux balance value to the base loss's dtype/device, and returns `base_loss + balance_weight · balance_loss` together with the raw balance scalar for logging. Gradients then flow through a single `backward()` with `clip_grad_value_(1.0)`.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L64-L77), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L597-L612)

Every 50 steps, the loop logs three things: the combined loss with the task-loss and weighted-balance breakdown, and a formatted router-statistics line from `_format_moe_stats`. The stats line distinguishes **applied** alphas (post-mask/post-mode, what actually weighted the experts: `applied_alpha_kg/scgpt/interaction`) from **raw** alphas (the unmasked softmax), and reports per-expert min/max ranges plus entropy — the minimal observable set needed to diagnose expert collapse (min/max compressing toward a one-hot pattern) versus healthy specialization. The formatted string also echoes the effective ablation mode, router mode, active expert names, and the numeric balance value.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L615-L631), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L112-L169)

| Telemetry field | Source | Diagnostic question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| `applied_alpha_{kg,scgpt,interaction}` | mean of post-mask `router_weights` | Which experts does the model actually use? |
| `raw_alpha_{...}` | mean of pre-mask softmax | How would routing look without ablation masking? |
| `alpha_min` / `alpha_max` | per-expert extremes over batch | Is routing degenerate (min≈0, max≈1) or soft? |
| `entropy` | `−Σ α·log(α+1e-8)` | How peaked is the routing distribution? |
| `balance` | averaged `_compute_balance_loss` | How far is batch-average usage from uniform? |

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L130-L168), [model.py](/models/model.py#L610-L616)

## Design Trade-offs

The soft-dense design trades compute for stability and observability. The comparison below positions this router against the two hard-routing failure modes it avoids, and clarifies what the balance loss can and cannot enforce.

| Property | DyMoE soft router | Top-k hard router (typical MoE) |
|---|---|---|
| Experts executed per token | All 3 | k of N |
| Load-balance failure mode | Weight collapse (α → one-hot) only | Weight collapse **and** capacity overflow / token dropping |
| Balance loss role | Regularize mean mixture toward uniform | Enforce expert invocation counts (load) |
| Router gradient | Dense through softmax and all experts | Sparse through selected experts only |
| Ablation masking | Zero-fill weight slot + renormalize softmax | Expert simply never dispatched |

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L299-L306), [model.py](/models/model.py#L264-L271)

Three costs are worth noting for advanced users. **(1) Expressivity ceiling:** a soft router cannot realize exclusive expert routing — every perturbation embedding always receives contributions from all three experts, so specialization manifests as weight ratios, not selection. **(2) Balance-loss granularity:** the MSE-on-batch-mean formulation constrains only the *first moment* of the weight distribution; it cannot prevent individual tokens from being one-hot as long as the batch averages to uniform. **(3) Guard redundancy is a feature:** the balance weight is zeroed at three layers (model init, CLI, `model_initialize`) — an intentional belt-and-suspenders pattern ensuring the serialized config, the runtime attribute, and the effective training objective always agree, which matters when reproducing `fixed_uniform` control experiments from checkpoints. For how these controls feed the ablation study, continue to [Ablation Modes Framework](9-ablation-modes-framework); for the wiring of these arguments into the training entry point, see [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration) and [Multi-GPU Parallel Training](16-multi-gpu-parallel-training); for eval-time routing behavior, see [Unseen Perturbation Inference](17-unseen-perturbation-inference).

> [!TIP]
> When running a `dynamic` training followed by `set_inference_router_mode("fixed_uniform")`, the balance loss has already done its job during training; the eval-time uniform override is a *post-hoc* control that isolates the router's learned contribution — the `_format_moe_stats` `applied_alpha_*` fields will all read exactly 0.333333, confirming the override took effect.


# Ablation Modes Framework



The Ablation Modes Framework is the mechanism that lets a single `ResidualMoEFusion` module be trained and evaluated as four structurally different models: the complete DyMoE-Pert fusion, a baseline-only variant, an experts-without-interaction variant, and an experts-without-base-branch variant. Rather than maintaining four separate model classes, the framework encodes the structural decision as one validated string (`ablation_mode`) and propagates its consequences through parameter freezing, forward-path branching, router weight renormalization, balance-loss computation, and runtime observability metadata. This page explains how those pieces work together; the design of the experts themselves is covered in [Expert Specialization: KG, scGPT, Interaction](7-expert-specialization-kg-scgpt-interaction) and the fusion arithmetic in [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design).

The single source of truth is the `ablation_mode` argument of `ResidualMoEFusion`, which is validated at construction time against the closed set `("full", "base_only", "no_interaction", "experts_only")`. Any other value raises a `ValueError` immediately, so an invalid ablation study can never start silently training the wrong architecture.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L96-L117)

## The Four Structural Variants

Each mode removes exactly one architectural hypothesis from the full model, which is what makes the resulting comparisons interpretable. `full` is the complete residual MoE: a base MLP branch plus three weighted expert outputs. `base_only` disables all experts and the router, reducing the fusion to the base MLP over concatenated projected KG and scGPT features. `no_interaction` keeps the base branch and the KG/scGPT experts but cuts the cross-modal interaction expert, testing whether explicit KG×scGPT interaction features matter. `experts_only` keeps the router and all three experts but removes the base MLP, testing whether the residual base branch is necessary.

| Mode | Base branch | KG expert | scGPT expert | Interaction expert | Router | What it isolates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `full` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | — (reference model) |
| `base_only` | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | Value of the entire MoE path |
| `no_interaction` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ (renormalized) | Value of the cross-modal interaction expert |
| `experts_only` | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | Value of the residual base branch |

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L113-L117), [model.py](models/model.py#L278-L312)

## Structural Enforcement: Freezing and Active-Expert Masking

The framework's first design decision is that a mode is enforced structurally, not by runtime `if` checks scattered through training code. During `__init__`, `_apply_ablation_freezing()` walks the submodules that the mode disables and sets `requires_grad=False` on every parameter. `base_only` freezes the three experts and the router; `no_interaction` freezes only the interaction expert; `experts_only` freezes only the base MLP. The training loop then builds its optimizer exclusively from parameters with `requires_grad=True`, and raises a `RuntimeError` if a mode left nothing trainable — so frozen components receive neither gradient updates nor optimizer state, rather than merely being multiplied by zero.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L167), [model.py](models/model.py#L174-L187), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L573-L576)

The second enforcement mechanism is the active-expert mask, produced by `_active_expert_mask_tensor()`. It encodes the mode as a boolean triple over `(kg, scgpt, interaction)`: `[False, False, False]` for `base_only`, `[True, True, False]` for `no_interaction`, and `[True, True, True]` otherwise (`experts_only` keeps all three experts active even though the base is frozen). Every downstream consumer — router renormalization, balance loss, and the aux metadata dict — derives its behavior from this one mask instead of re-testing the mode string, which is the pattern that keeps the four variants consistent.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L197-L204)

> [!TIP]
> Because freezing happens in `__init__` and the optimizer is built from `requires_grad` afterwards, an ablated checkpoint contains optimizer state only for active components. When you load such a checkpoint with `load_pretrained`, the `config.pkl` restores `moe_ablation_mode` and re-instantiates the same frozen structure — you cannot accidentally run a `base_only` checkpoint through the full architecture.

## Forward-Path Divergence per Mode

Inside `forward()`, the mode selects among three distinct computation paths. For `base_only`, the method short-circuits after the base MLP and returns `output_norm(h_base)` immediately; if `return_aux=True`, it attaches a synthesized "empty router" aux dict (`_empty_router_aux`) with zero-length router-weight tensors and zero balance loss, so callers always see a uniform aux interface regardless of mode. For `experts_only`, `h_base` is set to `None` and the final fusion is `output_norm(expert_output)` with `base_enabled=False`. For `full` and `no_interaction`, the standard residual path runs: `output = output_norm(h_base + expert_output)`.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L273-L312)

The `no_interaction` mode has one subtle behavior worth noting explicitly: it does not delete the interaction expert from the expert stack. Instead, `h_interaction` is replaced by `torch.zeros_like(h_kg).detach()` — a detached zero tensor — and the stack of three expert outputs is still assembled. This keeps tensor shapes identical across modes (a property that matters for the multi-GPU data-parallel path, where replicas must produce matching output structures) while guaranteeing the interaction branch contributes exactly nothing to the weighted sum.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    IN["kg_embedding + scgpt_embedding"] --> PROJ["kg_projector / scgpt_projector"]
    PROJ --> BASE["base_mlp(cat[z_kg, z_sc])"]

    PROJ --> MODE{"ablation_mode"}

    MODE -- "base_only" --> ONLYBASE["output = norm(h_base)<br/>experts + router bypassed"]
    MODE -- "no_interaction" --> ZINT["h_interaction = 0 (detached)"]
    MODE -- "experts_only" --> NOBASE["h_base = None"]
    MODE -- "full" --> FUSION

    PROJ --> E1["kg_expert"]
    PROJ --> E2["scgpt_expert"]
    PROJ --> E3["interaction_expert"]
    E3 -- "no_interaction" --> ZINT

    E1 & E2 & ZINT --> STACK["expert stack [h_kg, h_sc, h_int]"]
    BASE --> ROUTER["router -> alpha (renormalized over active experts)"]
    ROUTER --> STACK

    STACK --> FUSION["output = norm(h_base + Σ α·h)<br/>(experts_only: norm(Σ α·h))"]
```

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L285-L311), [model.py](models/model.py#L293-L297)

## Router Renormalization and Balance Loss under Ablation

The router softmax is mode-aware in exactly one place. For `no_interaction`, `_compute_router_weights()` slices the router logits down to the two active experts (`router_logits[..., active_expert_mask]`), applies softmax (or uniform 0.5/0.5 weights under `fixed_uniform` routing), and then scatters the result back into a length-3 tensor with zeros in the interaction slot. This means the two surviving experts compete for weights that sum to 1 across the active set only — the interaction expert never receives stray probability mass. All other router-mode interactions (`fixed_uniform`, inference-time uniform routing) are orthogonal to the ablation framework and are detailed in [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss).

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L239-L262)

Balance loss is likewise computed over the active expert subset only: `_compute_balance_loss()` selects `router_weights[..., active_expert_mask]` and penalizes deviation of the per-expert mean weight from `1 / num_active`. For `no_interaction` the target is therefore 0.5 per surviving expert; for `full` and `experts_only` it is 1/3. For `base_only` — where there are no active experts — the method returns a zero scalar, and the aux dict for that mode reports `router_enabled=False`. One deliberate safety rule ties the loss together: whenever the mode is `base_only` (or the router mode is `fixed_uniform`), `moe_balance_weight` is forcibly zeroed in both `scPert_Model.__init__` and `scPert.model_initialize`, so a meaningless balance penalty can never enter the total loss.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L264-L271), [model.py](models/model.py#L364-L366), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L320-L325)

## Observability: Aux Metadata and Log Stats

Every forward pass under MoE fusion emits an auxiliary dictionary, and the ablation framework populates it with self-describing metadata rather than leaving the caller to infer the variant. The aux dict carries `moe_ablation_mode` as a stable integer id (`full=0, base_only=1, no_interaction=2, experts_only=3`), the `active_expert_mask` boolean triple, `active_expert_names` (inactive slots encoded as `-1`), and the boolean flags `base_enabled` and `router_enabled`. In multi-GPU training, `_merge_moe_aux()` aggregates these tensors across per-replica aux lists — stacking mode ids and masks, OR-ing the `base_enabled`/`router_enabled` flags — so the merged stats remain valid under PyG `DataParallel`.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L212-L237), [model.py](models/model.py#L318-L344), [model.py](models/model.py#L590-L631)

The training loop turns this metadata into human-readable ablation diagnostics. `_mode_from_aux()` decodes the integer id back to its name, `_active_expert_names_from_aux()` extracts the surviving expert list, and `_format_moe_stats()` prints a periodic log line containing the mode, active experts, base/router enablement flags, the applied vs. raw per-expert router weights (`applied_alpha_*` / `raw_alpha_*`), their min/max ranges, and router entropy. Under `base_only` this collapses to a compact `router_status=disabled` line, since the router-weight tensors are empty. These logs are the practical tool for confirming that an ablation run is really running the intended structure.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L86-L109), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L112-L169), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L629-L631)

> [!TIP]
> The `moe_ablation_mode` id travels through the aux dict as a *tensor*, not a Python string. That is what allows `_merge_moe_aux` to verify consistency across data-parallel replicas (`ablation_modes.stack(...)`), and it means custom tooling that inspects aux dicts should decode via `_mode_from_aux` rather than comparing raw values.

## Configuring Modes: From CLI to Checkpoint

The configuration surface is deliberately small — one CLI flag, one config key, one constructor argument — with validation duplicated at each layer. `scripts/train.py` exposes `--moe-ablation-mode` with the four allowed choices (default `full`) and always forces `use_moe_fusion=True`, so the ablation framework is exercised on every training run of the provided scripts. The value flows into `scPert.model_initialize` (which re-validates and persists it into `config.pkl`) and finally into `scPert_Model`, which passes it to `ResidualMoEFusion`. At inference time there is no override: `scripts/infer.py` calls `load_pretrained`, and the checkpoint's stored mode silently reconstructs the same architecture.

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L41-L52), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L73-L75), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L320-L349), [infer.py](scripts/infer.py#L69)

A typical ablation comparison therefore consists of four training runs differing in exactly one flag:

```bash
python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --model-save-name norman_full            # full
python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --model-save-name norman_base            # base_only
python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --model-save-name norman_nointer         # no_interaction
python scripts/train.py --data-name norman --model-save-name norman_expertsonly     # experts_only
```

| Layer | Key / flag | Allowed values | Default | Enforcement point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CLI (`train.py`) | `--moe-ablation-mode` | `full`, `base_only`, `no_interaction`, `experts_only` | `full` | argparse `choices` |
| Wrapper (`scPert.model_initialize`) | `moe_ablation_mode` | same set | `full` | `ValueError` + balance-weight zeroing |
| Model (`scPert_Model`) | `moe_ablation_mode` (config) | same set | `full` | `ValueError` in `__init__` |
| Fusion (`ResidualMoEFusion`) | `ablation_mode` | same set | `full` | `ValueError` + `_apply_ablation_freezing()` |
| Checkpoint (`config.pkl`) | `moe_ablation_mode` | persisted value | — | restored by `load_pretrained` |

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L137-L146), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L357-L397)

The following diagram summarizes how one string propagates through the system, from CLI to frozen parameters to logged diagnostics:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLI["--moe-ablation-mode<br/>(scripts/train.py)"] --> INIT["scPert.model_initialize<br/>validate + zero balance weight"]
    INIT --> CFG["config.pkl<br/>(moe_ablation_mode persisted)"]
    INIT --> MODEL["scPert_Model<br/>re-validate config"]
    MODEL --> FUSION["ResidualMoEFusion<br/>freeze disabled submodules"]
    FUSION --> FWD["forward():<br/>mode-specific path"]
    FWD --> AUX["aux dict:<br/>mode id, expert mask,<br/>base/router enabled"]
    AUX --> LOG["_format_moe_stats:<br/>mode + active experts + α weights"]
    CFG --> LOAD["load_pretrained<br/>(infer.py restores mode)"]
    LOAD --> MODEL
```

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L21-L54), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L586-L594), [model.py](models/model.py#L348-L368)

## Interpreting the Ablation Study

Because each mode deletes exactly one hypothesis, the resulting metric deltas have direct architectural interpretations. Comparing `full` against `base_only` quantifies the entire MoE contribution; `full` vs. `no_interaction` isolates the cross-modal interaction expert's value on KG×scGPT features; `full` vs. `experts_only` quantifies how much the residual base branch stabilizes fusion. Note that `experts_only` and `base_only` change the trainable parameter count as well as the architecture, so differences in absolute MSE partly reflect capacity — the log lines described above (`base_enabled`, `router_enabled`, per-expert α statistics) let you distinguish "the expert received no weight" from "the component was absent." For the evaluation settings that make these comparisons meaningful (simulation split subgroups, unseen-perturbation regimes), see [Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split](14-perturbation-splits-and-simulation-split) and [Unseen Perturbation Inference](17-unseen-perturbation-inference).

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L132-L161), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L153-L169)

Natural next steps in this Deep Dive sequence: [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design) for the `h_base + Σ α·h` arithmetic being ablated, [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss) for the routing modes that interact with `no_interaction`, and [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration) for how the loss-weighting hooks shown here fit into the full epoch cycle.

# Gene Interaction GNN Layers



This page documents the gene-interaction machinery of DyMoE-Pert: how gene–gene relational structure is *constructed* offline (GO and co-expression graphs), and how it is *consumed* inside the `scPert_Model` backbone, which replaces classical sparse message passing with a dense, attention-style interaction block followed by a transformer stack. The model retains PyG-compatible graph artifacts for data-pipeline compatibility while computing interactions densely at run time — a deliberate architectural deviation from the GEARS lineage it inherits.

## Design Rationale: From Sparse Message Passing to Dense Interaction

The single most important verifiable fact about this subsystem: `models/model.py` imports only `torch`, `numpy`, `torch.nn`, `torch.nn.functional`, `logging`, and `hashlib` — there is **no `torch_geometric` import** in the model backbone itself, even though the data pipeline (`ProcePertdata.py`, `utils.py`) is heavily PyG-based. The forward pass accesses only `pert_data.x` (gene expression) and `pert_data.pert` (condition label), never `edge_index` or `pert_idx`.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L1-L7), [model.py](/models/model.py#L678-L693)

This means the "GNN" role in DyMoE-Pert is fulfilled by two cooperating mechanisms: (1) a **dense scaled dot-product interaction block** that computes an implicit, fully-connected gene adjacency per batch, and (2) an **8-layer transformer stack** whose attention matrices act as learned, content-dependent adjacency matrices over gene tokens. Pre-built graphs (GO, co-expression) still exist upstream in the data pipeline and shape which genes enter the graph, but message passing over their sparse `edge_index` is no longer part of the computation path.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L684-L693), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L44-L56)

## Gene Interaction Graph Construction

Two relational sources can be materialized before training, both converging into the `GeneSimNetwork` container that converts a pandas edge list into PyG tensors. The `get_similarity_network` dispatcher selects between them via the `network_type` argument (`'co-express'` or `'go'`).

Sources: [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L241-L265), [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L162-L195)

| Property | GO Graph | Co-expression Graph |
|---|---|---|
| Similarity metric | Jaccard index of GO term sets | Absolute Pearson correlation of expression |
| Edge condition | `score > 0.1` | Top-k per gene AND `importance > threshold` (default 0.4) |
| Edge weight (`importance`) | Jaccard score | Pearson correlation magnitude |
| Data basis | `gene2go` annotation pickles (downloaded from Dataverse) | Control-condition cells in the training split |
| Computation | Parallelized per-gene via multiprocessing `Pool` | Vectorized `np_pearson_cor` + `argsort` top-k |
| Default K | 20 (`num_similar_genes_go_graph`) | 20 (`num_similar_genes_co_express_graph`) |

Sources: [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L197-L239), [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L267-L319), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L250-L269)

The co-expression builder computes the Pearson correlation matrix over control cells from the *training split only* (preventing leakage), zeroes NaNs, takes absolute values, then retains the top `k+1` correlations per gene row and filters by threshold, caching the result as a CSV keyed by split/seed/threshold/k.

Sources: [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L293-L319), [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L41-L48)

`GeneSimNetwork.__init__` performs the final conversion: a `networkx.DiGraph` is built with `importance` edge attributes, all genes in `gene_list` are added as nodes (isolated nodes become legal), and edges are exported as `self.edge_index` (a `torch.long` tensor of `(src, dst)` pairs mapped through `node_map`) plus `self.edge_weight` (a float tensor of importance values). This container is what the GEARS-inherited pipeline would feed to PyG — in DyMoE-Pert it survives as a structural artifact and a gene-set selector.

Sources: [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L176-L195)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Offline["Offline graph construction (utils.py)"]
        A["gene2go annotations"] -->|"Jaccard > 0.1"| B["GO edge list"]
        C["Control cells<br/>(train split)"] -->|"Pearson abs,<br/>top-k, threshold"| D["Co-expression edge list"]
        B --> E["GeneSimNetwork"]
        D --> E
        E -->|"edge_index, edge_weight"| F["PyG-compatible artifacts<br/>(gene-set / node identity)"]
    end
    subgraph Online["In-model dense interaction (model.py)"]
        G["scGPT gene embeddings<br/>(512-d)"] --> H["gene_dense projection"]
        H --> I["Scaled dot-product<br/>G x G matrix"]
        I --> J["softmax + aggregate"]
        J --> K["gene_interaction_layer MLP"]
        K --> L["Residual add"]
    end
    F -.->|"gene universe selection"| Online
```

The diagram requires one clarification: the dashed arrow is an *indirect* coupling. The offline graphs and `set_pert_genes` logic determine the gene universe and perturbation vocabulary the dataset exposes; the in-model block then operates densely over that universe without touching sparse edges at run time.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L99-L120), [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L162-L195)

## The In-Model Interaction Block

Inside `scPert_Model.forward`, gene embeddings are materialized per sample, projected, and interacted in three steps. First, the shared 512-dimensional scGPT gene embedding matrix (`gene_emb`, registered as a buffer) is repeated `num_graphs` times and projected through `gene_dense` (Linear 512→hidden, LayerNorm, ReLU, Dropout 0.1), then reshaped to `(num_graphs, num_genes, hidden)`.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L382-L405), [model.py](/models/model.py#L684-L687)

Second, the interaction itself is a scaled dot-product over the gene axis:

```python
gene_interaction = torch.matmul(gene_emb, gene_emb.transpose(-2, -1)) / (self.hidden_size ** 0.5)
gene_interaction = F.softmax(gene_interaction, dim=-1)
gene_context = torch.matmul(gene_interaction, gene_emb)
```

This produces, for every sample independently, a `(num_genes × num_genes)` attention matrix — a dense, content-dependent surrogate for the sparse adjacency matrices that `GeneSimNetwork` would have supplied — followed by one-hop aggregation (`gene_context`) where each gene's representation becomes an importance-weighted mixture of all genes.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L689-L691)

Third, the aggregated context passes through `gene_interaction_layer` (Linear hidden→hidden, LayerNorm, ReLU, Dropout 0.1) and is added residually: `gene_emb = gene_emb + gene_context`. The residual form means a gene that receives no useful relational signal retains its raw projected embedding unchanged — soft degradation rather than information loss.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L393-L398), [model.py](/models/model.py#L692-L693)

| Tensor | Shape | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `gene_emb` (after `gene_dense`) | `(num_graphs, num_genes, hidden)` | Per-gene projected representation |
| `gene_interaction` | `(num_graphs, num_genes, num_genes)` | Implicit dense adjacency / attention |
| `gene_context` | `(num_graphs, num_genes, hidden)` | One-hop relational aggregation |

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L684-L692)

> [!TIP]
> The interaction block is quadratic in gene count: `matmul` allocates a `(B × G × G)` matrix at fp32 precision. For the essential-gene panels used here (~5,000 genes) this is ~100 MB per 1,000-cell batch; scaling to genome-wide panels would require the chunked strategy used in the attention layers below.

## Transformer Backbone: Implicit Multi-Hop Propagation

One aggregation hop is insufficient to model indirect perturbation effects (A → B → C cascades). The backbone therefore stacks **8 `ImprovedTransformerLayer` modules**, each combining self-attention over the gene axis with a 4× expansion feed-forward network (GELU, Dropout 0.1) and pre-activation-style residual + LayerNorm. Conceptually, each attention layer performs one additional learned message-passing round whose edge weights are recomputed from current node states — a fully-connected, content-adaptive generalization of `GNNConv` layers.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L68-L93), [model.py](/models/model.py#L442-L445)

Two implementation details deserve attention. The attention itself, `MemoryEfficientMultiheadAttention` (8 heads), processes queries, keys, and values in slices of `chunk_size=256` along the sequence dimension, materializing only `(chunk × chunk)` attention blocks instead of the full `(G × G)` score matrix — bounding peak memory per layer independently of gene count. And the forward loop applies a fixed damping factor: `combined_emb = combined_emb + layer_output * 0.5`, halving each layer's contribution to stabilize deep stacking with BatchNorm/LayerNorm interactions.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L26-L66), [model.py](/models/model.py#L743-L745)

> [!TIP]
> The `0.5` output scaling combined with the final `layer_norm2` means the effective magnitude of the 8-layer stack is normalized after accumulation — you can tune depth without rescaling learning rates, but ablating the scaling factor will destabilize training at 8 layers.

Perturbation signals enter this gene graph *after* the interaction block: the fused perturbation embedding (MoE or concatenation path) is broadcast across all gene positions and summed with `gene_emb` under `layer_norm1` and dropout, so every downstream attention round mixes perturbation-conditioned node states. The decoder-side details are covered on the [Prediction Decoder and Loss](11-prediction-decoder-and-loss) page; the perturbation fusion itself on [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss).

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L695-L740)

The backbone terminates with `final_mlp` (three Linear+LayerNorm+ReLU+Dropout blocks shrinking 4×→2×→1× hidden size), a per-gene scalar `output_layer`, and a baseline residual: the prediction is `output + x`, meaning the network learns the *perturbation delta* over control expression rather than absolute expression — the same inductive bias GEARS uses.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L748-L757)

## Configuration Reference

The `tunable_parameters` API still exposes GEARS-era GNN knobs (`num_go_gnn_layers`, `num_gene_gnn_layers`) that flow into `model_initialize`'s config dict. Because the current backbone contains no PyG conv layers, these keys are accepted for compatibility with the data pipeline and experiment bookkeeping but do not instantiate any module — treat `hidden_size`, graph-construction thresholds, and MoE options as the operative controls.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L250-L269), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L327-L349)

| Parameter | Default | Actual effect in current backbone |
|---|---|---|
| `hidden_size` | 64 | Width of `gene_dense`, interaction block, transformer stack |
| `num_go_gnn_layers` | 1 | Legacy config key; no module instantiated |
| `num_gene_gnn_layers` | 1 | Legacy config key; no module instantiated |
| `num_similar_genes_go_graph` | 20 | Shapes offline GO edge list (k-NN per gene) |
| `num_similar_genes_co_express_graph` | 20 | Shapes offline co-expression edge list |
| `coexpress_threshold` | 0.4 | Pearson cutoff for offline co-expression edges |
| Transformer depth | 8 (hard-coded) | Number of implicit message-passing rounds |
| Attention `chunk_size` | 256 (hard-coded) | Peak-memory bound for attention scores |

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L271-L335), [model.py](/models/model.py#L442-L445), [model.py](/models/model.py#L27)

## Sparse GNN vs. Dense Interaction: Trade-off Analysis

For an advanced audience, the central architectural question is what is gained and lost by replacing GEARS' two-graph sparse message passing (GCN over GO + co-expression `edge_index`) with dense dot-product interaction plus transformer mixing.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L684-L693), [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L162-L195)

| Dimension | GEARS-style sparse GNN | DyMoE-Pert dense interaction |
|---|---|---|
| Topology constraint | Fixed k-NN graphs; no A↔B edge means no message | Fully connected; all pairs considered every forward |
| Edge weights | Static (`importance` from GO/co-expression) | Dynamic, recomputed from current representations |
| Compute scaling | `O(E·H)` in edges | `O(G²·H)` in gene pairs |
| Multi-hop | Depth = number of conv layers (typically 1–2) | 8 attention rounds with per-hop rewiring |
| Unknown-gene handling | Requires a node in the graph | No graph membership needed at run time |
| Inductive bias | Strong relational prior (biology-curated edges) | Weak prior; relational knowledge must be learned |

Sources: [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L267-L319), [model.py](/models/model.py#L689-L690), [model.py](/models/model.py#L743-L745)

The dense design trades the biological prior of curated edges for two practical wins relevant to this repository's goals: unseen perturbations and unseen genes need no graph edits (only the deterministic fallback embedding shown in [Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings](13-knowledge-graph-and-scgpt-embeddings)), and cross-dataset transfer avoids per-dataset graph rebuilding beyond the cached CSV artifacts. The cost is a quadratic interaction matrix and the loss of an explicit constraint that messages flow only between biologically related genes — which is precisely what the transformer's content-dependent attention is trusted to rediscover.

Sources: [model.py](/models/model.py#L636-L658), [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L285-L291)

## Next Steps

To continue along the model-backbone track, proceed to [Prediction Decoder and Loss](11-prediction-decoder-and-loss) for the output head, direction loss, and focal/weighted MSE terms built on top of this backbone's residual output. To understand what feeds the gene axis before the interaction block, see [Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings](13-knowledge-graph-and-scgpt-embeddings); for how perturbation signals are routed into `combined_emb`, see [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss), and for the graph artifacts' role in train/test splits, see [Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split](14-perturbation-splits-and-simulation-split).


# Prediction Decoder and Loss



This page explains how DyMoE-Pert converts the backbone's fused gene-perturbation representation into per-gene expression predictions, and how the composite training loss supervises that conversion. It covers the decoder head (`final_mlp` + `output_layer`), the delta-prediction residual design, the five loss terms inside `loss_fct`, and the final loss assembly performed by the training loop. The router/balance internals themselves are covered in [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss), while the upstream backbone that feeds this decoder is described in [Gene Interaction GNN Layers](10-gene-interaction-gnn-layers).

## Decoder Architecture: A Shared MLP Head with Scalar Projection

After the 8-layer transformer backbone produces `combined_emb` with shape `[batch, num_genes, hidden_size]`, the prediction head is applied uniformly to every gene token. The `final_mlp` first **expands** the representation to `4×hidden`, then contracts through `2×hidden` back to `hidden`, using LayerNorm + ReLU + Dropout at each intermediate stage. A final single-unit `output_layer` (`Linear(hidden_size, 1)`) collapses each gene's vector into one scalar — the predicted expression change for that gene.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["combined_emb\n[B, num_genes, H]"] --> B["final_mlp\nH → 4H → 2H → H"]
    B --> C["output_layer\nLinear H → 1"]
    C --> D["Δ prediction\n[B·G, 1]"]
    F["x: baseline expression\n[B·G, 1]"] --> E{"residual add"}
    D --> E
    E --> G["pred\n[num_graphs, num_genes]"]
```

Note that despite the config exposing a `decoder_hidden_size` parameter (a legacy of the GEARS/scPert lineage), the actual decoder geometry is derived entirely from `hidden_size` — every dimension in `final_mlp` and `output_layer` scales from `self.hidden_size`. The head is **shared across genes**: there are no gene-specific decoder weights, so all genes pass through identical transformations.

| Stage | Module | Shape transformation | Normalization / Activation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Head expansion | `final_mlp` block 1 | `H → 4H` | LayerNorm + ReLU + Dropout(0.1) |
| Head contraction | `final_mlp` block 2 | `4H → 2H` | LayerNorm + ReLU + Dropout(0.1) |
| Head core | `final_mlp` block 3 | `2H → H` | linear (no activation) |
| Scalar projection | `output_layer` | `H → 1` | linear |
| Residual recombination | `Δ + x` | `[B·G, 1] + [B·G, 1]` | none |

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L448-L460), [model.py](models/model.py#L749-L751)

## The Delta Paradigm: Predicting Perturbation Effects, Not Absolute Expression

The decoder does not predict raw expression values. Instead, the scalar produced by `output_layer` is interpreted as a **deviation from baseline**, added element-wise to the input expression `x` before the tensor is reshaped back into `[num_graphs, num_genes]` via `split`/`stack` plumbing. This design mirrors the GEARS-style formulation: the network only needs to model the perturbation-induced change, which is sparse and low-magnitude compared to absolute expression levels, so the burden of representing baseline biology is shifted entirely onto the input features.

> [!TIP]
> The single-scalar `output_layer` means the model predicts a per-gene Δ only — there is no variance head in this implementation. The `saved_logvar_sum` attribute inherited from the scPert base class exists but is never populated in this pipeline; any uncertainty-style outputs you see in ancestor projects are absent here.

This delta formulation also has a direct consequence for the loss design: since `pred ≈ y` in absolute space, loss terms that reference `ctrl` (focal weighting, direction loss) compare predictions against control expression to recover the *effect direction and magnitude*, not the raw value.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L754-L757), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L234)

## Composite Loss: Five Terms Under One Per-Perturbation Loop

The entire supervision signal is produced by `loss_fct` in `models/utils.py`. Its structure is a loop over the **unique perturbations** present in the batch: cells sharing a perturbation label are grouped via `pert_idx`, and all five loss terms are evaluated per group. Two inputs enable perturbation-aware masking: `ctrl` is the dataset-level mean control expression per gene (computed once in `scPert.__init__`), and `dict_filter` maps each perturbation to the indices of its non-zero differentially-expressed genes (extracted from `adata.uns['non_zeros_gene_idx']`), so the loss for a perturbation is computed **only on genes it actually affects**.

| Loss term | Formula sketch | Default weight | Activation guard |
|---|---|---|---|
| Focal MSE | `mean((pred−y)² · sigmoid(\|y−ctrl\|)^γ)`, γ=2 | 1.0 | always |
| Weighted MSE | `mean(w_gene · (pred−y)²)`, key genes boosted | 1.0 | `class_weights_indices` provided |
| Direction | `mean(\|sign(y−ctrl) − sign(pred−ctrl)\|)` | `direction_lambda=1e-3` | `ctrl` not None |
| Cosine | `1 − mean cos(pred, y)` | `cosine_lambda=0.1` | always |
| L1 | `Σ‖θ‖₁` over trainable params | `l1_lambda=1e-5` | `model_params` provided |

The per-group sums are accumulated and finally **normalized by the number of unique perturbations** in the batch (`losses / len(set(perts))`), which stabilizes gradients across batches of varying perturbation diversity.

Sources: [utils.py](models/utils.py#L343-L421), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L237-L243)

## Focal MSE and Class Weighting: Amplifying Strong Perturbations

The focal term implements magnitude-aware reweighting: the weight is `sigmoid(|y − ctrl|)^γ`, so genes whose true expression deviates strongly from control approach weight 1.0, while unaffected genes receive only `0.5^γ = 0.25`. With γ=2, squared-error contributions are concentrated on the perturbed state that actually matters, which combats the dominance of thousands of near-zero-error genes in high-dimensional expression regression.

The weighted MSE term operates on a different axis — **gene identity rather than effect size**. `calculate_class_weights` builds a per-gene weight vector with a base of 1.0, multiplies the weights of genes listed in `important_genes_indices` by `boost_factor=5`, and normalizes so the mean weight stays at 1. These indices come from the `key_genes` argument of `scPert.train()`, letting users emphasize biologically privileged genes (e.g., DE genes) during training.

| Property | Focal MSE | Weighted MSE |
|---|---|---|
| Weighting axis | per-sample effect magnitude | per-gene identity |
| Weight source | dynamic: `sigmoid(\|y − ctrl\|)` | static: user-supplied gene index list |
| Default strength | γ = 2 | boost_factor = 5 |
| Failure mode addressed | error dilution across unaffected genes | under-fitting on key genes |

Sources: [utils.py](models/utils.py#L380-L397), [utils.py](models/utils.py#L422-L427), [utils.py](models/utils.py#L429-L453)

## Direction and Cosine Terms: Preserving Perturbation Semantics

The **direction loss** penalizes sign disagreements: it computes `|sign(y − ctrl) − sign(pred − ctrl)|`, which yields 0 when the predicted change points the same way as the true change and 2 when it flips. This is the term that enforces up/down-regulation correctness — a prediction can be numerically close under MSE yet still get the sign wrong on weak effects, and this term catches exactly those cases. The **cosine loss** complements it by comparing the flattened per-cell prediction and target vectors, rewarding predictions that match the overall *shape* of the perturbation response profile regardless of scale.

| Term | What it captures | Strength | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direction | sign of change vs control | enforces regulation polarity | magnitude-blind; small weight (1e-3) keeps it a tie-breaker |
| Cosine | global response profile shape | scale-invariant alignment | cannot penalize magnitude error alone; relies on MSE companions |

Sources: [utils.py](models/utils.py#L399-L412)

## L1 Regularization: A Global Sparsity Prior

The final task-loss term is optional L1 regularization over **all trainable parameters**, not just decoder weights. `loss_fct` iterates over `model_params` and accumulates `torch.norm(param, 1)`, scaled by `l1_lambda=1e-5`. Because the training loop passes a generator over `self.model.parameters()` filtered by `requires_grad`, this acts as a mild network-wide sparsity prior alongside AdamW's `weight_decay`, rather than a decoder-local constraint.

Sources: [utils.py](models/utils.py#L414-L421)

## Loss Assembly in the Training Step
