The training loop in `scPert.train()` orchestrates the final composition. Each step performs: forward pass returning `pred` plus a `moe_aux` dictionary → `loss_fct` producing `task_loss` → `_moe_balance_loss` adding the MoE router regularizer → backward, value-clipping, and optimizer step. The balance term is added **outside** the task loss with weight `moe_balance_weight` (default 0.01), and is silently forced to zero when the router runs in `fixed_uniform` mode or the ablation mode is `base_only` — in those configurations the router contributes nothing to learn, so no load-balancing pressure is needed.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["forward: pred, moe_aux"] --> B["loss_fct\n(focal + weighted MSE + direction + cosine + L1)"]
    B --> C["task_loss\nnormalized per unique pert"]
    A --> D["moe_aux.balance_loss"]
    C --> E["_moe_balance_loss\ntotal = task + w·balance"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["loss.backward()"]
    F --> G["clip_grad_value_(1.0)"]
    G --> H["AdamW + OneCycleLR step"]
```

> [!TIP]
> When debugging "why doesn't the MoE balance term appear in training logs", check the config combination first: `moe_balance_weight` is programmatically reset to 0.0 for `fixed_uniform` router or `base_only` ablation modes, and `_moe_balance_loss` also returns unchanged when the weight is ≤ 0 or `moe_aux` lacks a `balance_loss` key.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L603-L615), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L64-L77), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L348-L349)

## Component Interaction Summary

The decoder and loss form a tightly coupled pair: the scalar-per-gene delta head defines what the loss compares (absolute predictions in expression space), while the loss's `ctrl`-relative terms recover perturbation semantics from those absolute predictions. Model selection is driven by validation `mse_de` (top-20 DE gene MSE), which directly reflects the focal/weighted weighting philosophy applied at evaluation time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Model["scPert_Model (models/model.py)"]
        FE["Embedding fusion +\nTransformer backbone"] --> DEC["final_mlp + output_layer\n+ residual Δ"]
    end
    subgraph Loss["loss_fct (models/utils.py)"]
        L["focal MSE + weighted MSE\n+ direction + cosine + L1"]
    end
    subgraph Trainer["scPert.train (models/scpert.py)"]
        B["_moe_balance_loss"]
        O["AdamW + OneCycleLR\nclip_grad_value_(1.0)"]
    end
    DEC -- "pred [B, G]" --> L
    L -- "task_loss" --> B
    FE -- "moe_aux.balance_loss" --> B
    B -- "total loss" --> O
    O -- "gradients" --> Model
```

To continue exploring this pipeline: the router regularizer referenced above is detailed in [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss); the loop that consumes this loss end-to-end, including validation and checkpointing, is covered in [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration); and the downstream metric definitions (`mse_de`, `pearson_delta`) that mirror these loss priorities are explained in [Metrics and DE Gene Analysis](18-metrics-and-de-gene-analysis).


# GEARS-Format Data Pipeline



The GEARS-Format Data Pipeline is DyMoE-Pert's ingestion layer: it converts public perturbation-seq datasets — already serialized in the [GEARS](https://github.com/snap-stanford/GEARS) `h5ad` convention — into per-cell PyTorch Geometric (`torch_geometric.data.Data`) objects that the Dynamic MoE model consumes directly. This page explains the complete data path: dataset acquisition, AnnData preprocessing, cell-graph construction, caching, and DataLoader assembly, ending at the exact handoff point where model training begins. Split *semantics* (which perturbations land in train/val/test) are covered in [Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split](14-perturbation-splits-and-simulation-split), and the gene-embedding files attached to this pipeline are detailed in [Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings](13-knowledge-graph-and-scgpt-embeddings).

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L23-L97), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L119-L126)

## Pipeline at a Glance

The pipeline is orchestrated by a single class, `PertData` (in `models/ProcePertdata.py`), driven by three sequential calls from the training script: `load()` → `prepare_split()` → `get_dataloader()`. Each stage is cached to disk, so a dataset is only downloaded, graphified, or split once; subsequent runs short-circuit by detecting local artifacts. The full flow from remote download to a batch-ready PyG `DataLoader` looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["train.py --data-name"] --> B["PertData.load()"]
    B --> C{"data_pyg/<br/>cell_graphs.pkl<br/>exists?"}
    C -- "No" --> D["Download zip from<br/>Harvard Dataverse"]
    D --> E["Read perturb_processed.h5ad<br/>(scanpy AnnData)"]
    E --> F["set_pert_genes()<br/>+ filter conditions in pert graph"]
    F --> G["create_dataset_file()<br/>1 PyG Data per cell"]
    G --> H["Pickle cell_graphs.pkl"]
    C -- "Yes" --> I["Load pickled graphs"]
    H --> I
    I --> J["prepare_split()<br/>condition -> train/val/test map"]
    J --> K["get_dataloader()<br/>group graphs per split"]
    K --> L["train / val / test<br/>PyG DataLoaders"]
    L --> M["scPert(pertData,<br/>embedding_path=...)"]
```

Every arrow in this diagram maps to verifiable code: the three-call orchestration appears verbatim in the training entry point, and each internal stage is a named method on `PertData`.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L131-L215), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L268-L417), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L419-L491), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L119-L126)

## The GEARS-Format Contract

"GEARS format" in this repository means a specific on-disk layout under your `--data-path` directory. For each dataset named `D`, the loader expects (or creates) the folder `data/D/` containing a `perturb_processed.h5ad` AnnData file plus a `data_pyg/` cache directory, and — after splitting — a `splits/` directory of pickle files. The AnnData must expose two conventions the code hard-depends on: `adata.obs['condition']` holding perturbation labels such as `ctrl`, ` gene1+ctrl`, or `gene1+gene2`, and `adata.var['gene_name']` holding the gene symbol per column.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L170-L180), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L237-L241), [data_utils.py](/models/data_utils.py#L57-L60)

Condition strings are parsed uniformly via helpers in `models/utils.py`: `parse_any_pert` decomposes any condition into its constituent genes, treating `X+ctrl` as a single perturbation and `X+Y` as a combo of two. This string protocol is what allows one pipeline to serve single-gene and combinatorial perturbation datasets without format changes.

Sources: [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L16-L39)

## Loading Built-in Datasets

`PertData.load()` recognizes five canonical GEARS dataset names and resolves each to a Harvard Dataverse file ID. The five names are precisely the five `EMBEDDING_FILES` keys in `scripts/train.py`, which is why the `--data-name` CLI argument is constrained to that set — the pipeline guarantees that the dataset and its pre-computed 512-d gene embedding file stay aligned.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L150-L165), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L12-L18)

| Dataset name | Organism / cell line focus | Dataverse artifact | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `norman` | Combined perturbation screen | datafile/6154020 | Combo-perturbation generalization |
| `adamson` | Single-gene perturbation screen | datafile/6154417 | Single-perturbation generalization |
| `dixit` | Single-gene perturbation screen | datafile/6154416 | Single-perturbation generalization |
| `replogle_k562_essential` | Filtered essential-gene subset | datafile/7458695 | Large-scale single-perturbation |
| `replogle_rpe1_essential` | Filtered essential-gene subset | datafile/7458694 | Large-scale single-perturbation |

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L154-L165)

The download path is deliberately resilient: `dataverse_download` streams the file with a progress bar and writes to a `.part` suffix that is atomically `os.replace`d on success (so interrupted downloads never leave corrupt files), and `zip_data_download_wrapper` skips work entirely when a local copy exists. This mirrors the caching philosophy applied at every later stage of the pipeline.

Sources: [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L51-L77), [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L80-L97)

## From AnnData to Per-Cell PyG Graphs

This is the conceptual heart of the pipeline. GEARS reframes each cell as a *graph* whose nodes are genes; DyMoE-Pert inherits this framing so that its GNN backbone and MoE fusion modules can operate on gene-level features. For every unique condition in `adata.obs['condition']`, `create_dataset_file()` calls `create_cell_graph_dataset()`, which emits one `torch_geometric.data.Data` object per cell and stores the result as a dict: `condition → list[Data]`.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L618-L627), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L549-L616)

Each `Data` object carries five fields, constructed inside `create_cell_graph`:

| Field | Construction | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `x` | `torch.Tensor(X).T` → shape `(num_genes, 1)` | Gene-node feature matrix; **genes are nodes**, each with one scalar expression feature |
| `pert_idx` | Indices of perturbed genes from `get_pert_idx()`; `[-1]` for ctrl | Which gene nodes were perturbed |
| `y` | `torch.Tensor(y)` | Post-perturbation expression vector (the prediction target) |
| `de_idx` | Indices of top-20 DE genes for the condition; `[-1]*20` if unavailable | Genes used for DE-focused evaluation |
| `pert` | The condition string itself | Human-readable label threaded through training/inference |

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L519-L547), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L583-L593)

> [!TIP]
> The input/target pairing is the subtle part: for a non-control condition, each perturbed cell's expression becomes the label `y`, while the input `x` is a *randomly sampled control cell* (with `num_samples=1` by default). The model therefore learns the mapping `control expression + perturbation identity → perturbed expression` — the perturbation signal enters only through `pert_idx`, never through `x`. For `ctrl` conditions, `x = y` is the same cell, teaching the identity function.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L594-L608)

The top-20 DE genes attached as `de_idx` come from `adata.uns['rank_genes_groups_cov_all']`, which the preprocessing stage computes per condition against its cell-type-matched control. If that key is absent (custom datasets that skip DE calculation), the pipeline degrades gracefully to a single dummy `-1` marker rather than failing.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L571-L593)

## Preprocessing Annotations Stored in `adata.uns`

When a dataset is loaded fresh, most of the evaluation-relevant metadata already lives inside the GEARS `h5ad`. But when you process a *new* dataset via `new_data_process()`, two functions in `models/data_utils.py` rebuild that metadata. `get_DE_genes` derives `dose_val`, `control`, and `condition_name` columns and runs a covariate-stratified differential expression scan (`rank_genes_groups_by_cov` with `n_genes = len(adata.var)`, i.e., ranking *all* genes), storing the full ranking in `adata.uns['rank_genes_groups_cov_all']`.

Sources: [data_utils.py](/models/data_utils.py#L15-L54), [data_utils.py](/models/data_utils.py#L57-L70), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L250-L253)

`get_dropout_non_zero_genes` then computes per-condition mean expression versus control and derives four masks that downstream metric code depends on: genes that are non-zero post-perturbation, genes that are "true zeros" (zero in both perturbed and control, i.e., not dropouts), the union of those (`non_dropouts`), and the top-20 DE genes restricted to each mask. These land in `adata.uns` under four keys:

| `adata.uns` key | Content | Primary consumer |
|---|---|---|
| `rank_genes_groups_cov_all` | Full per-condition DE gene ranking | `de_idx` in cell graphs; metrics |
| `top_non_dropout_de_20` | Top-20 DE genes excluding dropout artifacts | DE gene analysis |
| `non_dropout_gene_idx` | All non-dropout gene indices | DE gene analysis |
| `non_zeros_gene_idx` / `top_non_zero_de_20` | Non-zero gene indices / top-20 | Loss filtering, metrics |

Sources: [data_utils.py](/models/data_utils.py#L72-L132)

Note the tight coupling: `scPert` later reads `non_zeros_gene_idx` to build its per-perturbation `dict_filter`, which the loss function uses to restrict directional and weighted losses to genes that are actually observable post-perturbation. This is a concrete example of how preprocessing metadata propagates all the way into the training objective.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L237-L244), [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L393-L407)

## Perturbation Gene Filtering (`set_pert_genes`)

Before graph construction, `load()` calls `set_pert_genes()` to decide which genes can legally appear in the perturbation graph, then drops every condition not fully representable in it. Three modes are supported: a custom essential-gene pickle passed via `gene_set_path`; a *small* graph limited to genes present in the dataset itself (`default_pert_graph=False`); or the *default* large GEARS gene universe downloaded from Dataverse (`essential_all_data_pert_genes.pkl`). Conditions failing the check are reported and filtered out of the AnnData before any graph is built.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L99-L129), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L187-L196)

The method also registers `pert_names` (the unique perturbable genes) and `node_map_pert` (gene → perturbation-node index), which are distinct from the *expression* gene index `node_map` built later in `get_dataloader()`. Keeping these two index spaces separate is essential — perturbation identity and expression nodes must not be conflated when the model embeds perturbations via 512-d vectors.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L128-L129), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L440-L441)

## On-Disk Artifact Layout and Caching

After a successful first run, your data directory encodes the pipeline's full state, and every artifact is a cache: delete one and only that stage recomputes.

```
data/                          # --data-path
├── <dataset_name>/            # e.g. norman/
│   ├── perturb_processed.h5ad     # AnnData: expression + obs/uns metadata
│   ├── data_pyg/
│   │   └── cell_graphs.pkl         # dict: condition -> list[torch_geometric Data]
│   └── splits/
│       ├── <ds>_<split>_<seed>_<frac>.pkl        # set2conditions
│       └── <ds>_simulation_<seed>_<frac>_subgroup.pkl
├── essential_all_data_pert_genes.pkl   # default perturbation gene universe
└── gene2go.pkl                          # GO annotations (graph construction)
```

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L166-L172), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L198-L215), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L328-L346)

> [!TIP]
> The `cell_graphs.pkl` cache is a double-edged sword: it makes warm startup near-instant, but it is keyed only by file existence — not by dataset content. If you edit the `h5ad` (e.g., re-filter conditions) without deleting `data_pyg/cell_graphs.pkl`, the loader will silently serve stale graphs. Always clear `data_pyg/` after modifying an AnnData in place.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L202-L215)

## DataLoader Assembly (`get_dataloader`)

The final stage converts `set2conditions` (the split map produced by `prepare_split()`, detailed in [Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split](14-perturbation-splits-and-simulation-split)) into concrete loaders. It first rebuilds `node_map` — gene symbol → column index — then gathers each split's cell graphs by concatenating the per-condition graph lists, and wraps them in PyTorch Geometric loaders with deliberately asymmetric shuffle semantics:

| Split | Loader | shuffle | drop_last |
|---|---|---|---|
| train | `DataLoader` / `DataListLoader` | `True` | `True` |
| val | same class | `True` | `False` |
| test | same class | `False` | `False` |

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L440-L490)

The loader class itself is conditional: `get_dataloader(..., use_data_list_loader=True)` selects `DataListLoader`, which yields *lists* of `Data` objects instead of a fused `Batch`. This is the exact mechanism behind `--multi-gpu` in the training script — per-GPU replica lists bypass PyG's single-process batching, as covered in [Multi-GPU Parallel Training](16-multi-gpu-parallel-training). The training-side consumer (`_prepare_train_batch`) accepts both shapes, re-fusing lists into a `Batch` only when not running under PyG `DataParallel`.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L436-L438), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L122-L126), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L44-L55)

Special split modes also alter the loader set: `no_split` returns only a `test_loader` (used for pure inference runs), and `no_test` returns `train_loader` + `val_loader` only. This is how the pipeline supports evaluation-only and test-free experimental configurations without special-casing the training loop.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L445-L463), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L486-L490)

## Handoff to the Model

The pipeline terminates at the `scPert` constructor, which is the precise boundary between this page and [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration). `scPert.__init__` absorbs the entire `PertData` state machine: the dataloaders, the AnnData (with its `uns` metadata), both index maps (`node_map`, `node_map_pert`), the split bookkeeping (`set2conditions`, `subgroup`), and the derived lists `gene_list` / `pert_list`. It immediately computes `ctrl_expression` (mean control profile) and the per-perturbation `dict_filter` from the preprocessing metadata described above.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L177-L248)

In parallel, `scripts/train.py` resolves which 512-d gene-embedding file pairs with the loaded dataset via the `EMBEDDING_FILES` mapping and passes it as `embedding_path` — the entry point into the expert-fusion inputs described in [Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings](13-knowledge-graph-and-scgpt-embeddings). The invariant is structural: the row order of the embedding matrix must correspond to `pertData.gene_names`, which is why both artifacts must originate from the same dataset universe.

Sources: [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L101-L105), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L228-L235)

## Bringing Your Own Data in GEARS Format

`PertData.new_data_process()` is the sanctioned entry point for custom datasets. The requirements are a strict superset check on the AnnData contract: `condition` must exist in `adata.obs` and `gene_name` in `adata.var` — violations raise immediately rather than producing silent corruption. The method then runs the full preprocessing chain (DE genes → dropout masks → `h5ad` write → pert-gene filtering → PyG graphification) and leaves the result in exactly the same on-disk layout as a built-in dataset, so a custom dataset becomes indistinguishable from `norman` or `adamson` to every downstream consumer.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L217-L266)

For custom datasets, note the DE-calculation escape hatch: `skip_calc_de=True` skips the expensive `rank_genes_groups_by_cov` scan and the dropout analysis, at the cost of placeholder `de_idx` values in cell graphs (which affects DE-focused metrics, see [Metrics and DE Gene Analysis](18-metrics-and-de-gene-analysis)) and an empty `dict_filter` (which weakens the direction-aware loss). Use it only for quick smoke tests, never for reported results.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L250-L252), [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L576-L593)

Once processed and split, your custom dataset flows through `load(data_path=...)`, which detects a local folder layout instead of a Dataverse name and follows the identical cache-first path — the pipeline never distinguishes built-in from custom data after load time.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](/models/ProcePertdata.py#L174-L180)

## Where to Go Next

The pipeline deliberately stops at the dataloader boundary. To understand what happens to these cell graphs next: the split *strategies* (simulation subgroups, combo seen/unseen) that `prepare_split()` invokes are unpacked in [Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split](14-perturbation-splits-and-simulation-split); the 512-d embedding files that pair with each dataset name are analyzed in [Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings](13-knowledge-graph-and-scgpt-embeddings); and the training loop that iterates the loaders — including the MoE balance loss computed on each batch — is detailed in [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration).


# Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings



DyMoE-Pert does not learn gene representations from scratch. Instead, every forward pass is anchored by three externally precomputed embedding banks: **knowledge-graph (KG) embeddings** distilled from a ComGCN-trained biological knowledge graph, a **common perturbation embedding bank** aligned with the gene universe, and **dataset-specific scGPT embeddings** that provide a 512-dimensional functional prior for each gene. This page documents what these files contain, how they are loaded into `scPert_Model` as registered buffers, how per-gene lookups handle control and out-of-vocabulary names, and where each representation enters the network. The fusion *mechanics* (experts, router) are covered in [Expert Specialization: KG, scGPT, Interaction](7-expert-specialization-kg-scgpt-interaction); here we focus on the embedding assets themselves and their injection points.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L370-L390), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L12-L18)

## Embedding Inventory: Three Banks, Two Formats

The `embeddings/` directory holds two formats. The `.npz` files are NumPy archives with two arrays — `gene_names` (the lookup keys) and `embeddings` (the matrix) — produced offline by ComGCN training on a knowledge graph. The `.npy` files are flat 512-dimensional scGPT matrices whose row order implicitly corresponds to the dataset's gene list. All three are loaded once in the model constructor and registered as PyTorch buffers so they travel with the model on `.to(device)` calls without being treated as trainable parameters.

| File | Format | Dim | Model buffer | Lookup key | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz` | `.npz` (`gene_names` + `embeddings`) | 128 | `loaded_embeddings` | gene name (`gene_to_index`) | KG structural prior for the perturbed gene(s) |
| `gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz` | `.npz` (`gene_names` + `embeddings`) | 512 | `pert_embeddings` | pert gene name (`pert_to_index`) | common perturbation-side representation (note the double "s" in the filename) |
| `gene_embeddings_<dataset>_512.npy` | `.npy` | 512 | `gene_emb` | row position (gene index) | dataset-aligned scGPT base features for all genes |

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L370-L390), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L12-L18)

## Loading Paths: Parameterized vs Hardcoded

The two embedding families enter the model through different mechanisms. The **scGPT bank is fully parameterized**: `scripts/train.py` maps each supported dataset name to its embedding file via the `EMBEDDING_FILES` dictionary, resolves the final path from `--embedding-dir` (default `./embeddings`) and an optional `--embedding-file` override, and raises `FileNotFoundError` early if the file is missing. The resolved path is passed into `scPert`, stored as `self.embedding_path`, and finally handed to `scPert_Model(self.config, self.embedding_path)`, where it becomes the `gene_emb` buffer.

The **KG banks are hardcoded**: the constructor loads `./embeddings/gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz` and `./embeddings/gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz` with fixed relative paths, builds name→index dictionaries from the archived `gene_names`, and registers the matrices as float32 buffers. This means training must be launched from the repository root, and swapping KG banks requires editing `model.py` rather than passing a flag.

> [!TIP]
> The scGPT embedding dimension is enforced by config, not by inspection: `model_initialize` hardcodes `'embedding_size': 512` in the config dict, and `pert_dense`'s first layer expects exactly `640 = 128 + 512` inputs. Feeding a non-512-dim `.npy` will fail deep inside `nn.Linear` rather than at load time — validate your custom embedding file's shape before training.

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L12-L18), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L102-L105), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L235), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L327-L349), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L354-L355), [model.py](models/model.py#L370-L390)

## Concept Relationship Diagram: From Files to Forward Pass

The diagram below traces each embedding bank from disk to its consumption point inside `scPert_Model.forward`. Two independent gene streams exist: the scGPT `gene_emb` drives the **base gene branch** (identical for every cell in the batch), while the KG 128-dim vector and the common 512-dim perturbation vector are retrieved **per perturbed gene** and fused into a perturbation embedding that is broadcast across all gene positions.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph DISK["embeddings/"]
        NPZ1["gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz<br/>(names + 128-dim)"]
        NPZ2["gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz<br/>(names + 512-dim)"]
        NPY["gene_embeddings_&lt;dataset&gt;_512.npy<br/>(512-dim)"]
    end

    subgraph MODEL["scPert_Model buffers (non-trainable)"]
        B1["loaded_embeddings<br/>+ gene_to_index"]
        B2["pert_embeddings<br/>+ pert_to_index"]
        B3["gene_emb"]
    end

    NPZ1 -->|"np.load + register_buffer"| B1
    NPZ2 -->|"np.load + register_buffer"| B2
    NPY -->|"np.load(embedding_path)"| B3

    B3 -->|"repeat(num_graphs) → gene_dense<br/>512 → hidden"| GENE["Base gene branch<br/>+ interaction context"]
    B1 -->|"get_gene_embedding(pert)<br/>128-dim KG"| FUSE["Pert embedding fusion<br/>concat (640) or MoE"]
    B2 -->|"get_pert_embedding(pert)<br/>512-dim common"| FUSE

    FUSE -->|"pert_fuse → mean →<br/>repeat over genes"| PERT["pert_emb_matrix"]
    GENE --> ADD(("+"))
    PERT -->|"× emb_scale"| ADD
    ADD --> TR["8× Transformer layers<br/>→ final MLP → decoder"]
```

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L370-L390), [model.py](models/model.py#L684-L693), [model.py](models/model.py#L697-L740)

## KG Embeddings: 128-Dim Structural Priors with Deterministic Fallbacks

The KG bank `gene_2_kge_comgcn_final_common.npz` is queried through `get_gene_embedding(gene_name)` for each single gene inside a perturbation condition (combo perturbations like `A+B` are split on `+` first). Three outcomes exist, and together they make the model total over any gene name:

1. **`'ctrl'`** returns a 128-dimensional zero vector on the runtime device — control conditions carry no perturbation signal.
2. **Known gene** performs a dictionary lookup into `loaded_embeddings` and returns the pretrained 128-dim ComGCN vector directly (zero gradient flow — it is a buffer).
3. **Unknown gene** (not in the KG vocabulary — possible for novel perturbation targets in unseen-perturbation evaluation) falls back to `get_random_embedding`, which derives a seed from the SHA-1 hash of the gene name, generates a deterministic 640-dim Gaussian vector scaled by `1/√640`, and slices the first 128 dims for the KG slot.

The hash-seeding is the subtle design choice here: the same gene name always produces the same pseudo-embedding across processes, GPUs, and runs, so unseen genes get a stable, reproducible identity rather than a random one re-sampled per epoch.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L636-L648), [model.py](models/model.py#L651-L658), [model.py](models/model.py#L706-L711)

## scGPT Embeddings: Dataset Alignment and the Common Perturbation Bank

There are two scGPT-flavored assets, and they serve different branches. The **dataset-aligned bank** (`gene_embeddings_norman_512.npy`, `gene_embeddings_dixit_512.npy`, etc.) is selected by dataset name at training time and loaded as `gene_emb`. In `forward`, it is repeated once per cell graph in the batch, projected by `gene_dense` (512 → `hidden_size`), reshaped to `(num_graphs, num_genes, hidden)`, and enriched by a scaled dot-product interaction pass (`gene_interaction` softmax attention → `gene_context`) before residual addition. Because every row corresponds to a gene position, this bank encodes *what each gene is*, independent of which perturbation was applied.

The **common bank** (`gene_embeddingss_full_common.npz`) is queried per perturbed gene via `get_pert_embedding`. It mirrors the KG lookup pattern exactly — zeros(512) for `'ctrl'`, buffer lookup for known names — except its fallback slices `get_random_embedding(...)[128:]`, i.e., dims 128–640 of the same deterministic random vector used by the KG path. This guarantees that an unknown gene's KG fragment and scGPT fragment are complementary slices of one consistent vector rather than two unrelated samples.

| Scenario | KG path (`get_gene_embedding`) | scGPT/common path (`get_pert_embedding`) |
|---|---|---|
| Perturbed gene is `'ctrl'` | `zeros(128)` | `zeros(512)` |
| Name found in vocabulary | `loaded_embeddings[gene_to_index[name]]` | `pert_embeddings[pert_to_index[name]]` |
| Name unknown to both banks | `randn(640, seeded by SHA1(name))[:128]` | `randn(640, seeded by SHA1(name))[128:]` |

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L12-L18), [model.py](models/model.py#L387-L390), [model.py](models/model.py#L684-L693), [model.py](models/model.py#L660-L671)

## Consumption: Two Fusion Routes into `pert_emb_matrix`

For each perturbed condition, the 128-dim KG vector and the 512-dim common vector are combined through `_fuse_pert_embedding`, which implements two alternative routes depending on the `use_moe_fusion` flag:

| Route | Mechanism | Output dim | When used |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legacy concat | `torch.cat([kg, scgpt])` → `pert_dense` (640 → 2·hidden → hidden) | `hidden_size` | `use_moe_fusion=False` |
| Dynamic MoE | separate projectors (128→hidden, 512→hidden), 3 experts, softmax router | `hidden_size` | `use_moe_fusion=True` (default in `train.py`) |

The MoE route is the paper's contribution — its expert structure and router math are detailed in [Residual Fusion Design](6-residual-fusion-design) and [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss). What matters at the embedding level is that both routes reduce the two heterogeneous sources to a common `hidden_size` vector. Combo conditions produce one fused vector per gene, stack them, average through `pert_fuse`, and broadcast the result across all `num_genes` positions, scaled by the learnable scalar `emb_scale` before being added to the gene branch. Multiple perturbations therefore share one averaged perturbation embedding rather than occupying separate token slots — a design contrast with GEARS, discussed in [Positioning vs GEARS and scPert](20-positioning-vs-gears-and-scpert).

> [!TIP]
> Because `gene_emb` (scGPT) is shared across the entire batch and only `pert_emb_matrix` varies per cell, the expensive base-gene interaction pass runs identically for every graph in a batch — the model batches by repetition, not by per-cell gene features. If you profile training, expect the per-perturbation Python loop (one iteration per graph for embedding lookup) to dominate for small batches.

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L478-L490), [model.py](models/model.py#L415-L427), [model.py](models/model.py#L719-L740), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L73)

## Dimension Contract Summary

The whole embedding system hangs together through a handful of fixed dimensional contracts. Memorize these numbers when extending the pipeline with your own banks:

| Contract | Value | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| KG embedding dim | 128 | `kg_input_dim=128` in `ResidualMoEFusion`; `zeros(128)` for ctrl |
| scGPT gene dim | 512 | `scgpt_input_dim=512`; config `'embedding_size': 512` |
| Random fallback dim | 640 (=128+512) | `random_embedding_dim = 640`; sliced `[:128]` / `[128:]` |
| Concat fusion input | 640 | `pert_dense` first `nn.Linear(640, ...)` |
| Fused perturbation output | `hidden_size` (default 64) | both fusion routes; `pert_emb_matrix` width |

Sources: [model.py](models/model.py#L96-L107), [model.py](models/model.py#L400-L414), [model.py](models/model.py#L467), [model.py](models/model.py#L415-L427)

## Practical Workflow and Next Steps

To train on a supported dataset, the correct scGPT file is picked automatically from `EMBEDDING_FILES` — for example, `--data-name adamson` resolves to `embeddings/gene_embeddings_adamson_512.npy` under `--embedding-dir ./embeddings`, and the KG banks are picked up by their hardcoded paths. To use a custom dataset, generate a 512-dim scGPT matrix whose row order matches your `perturb_processed.h5ad` gene list and point `--embedding-file` at it; custom KG banks additionally require editing the two `np.load` calls in `model.py`. The full asset setup (downloads, file placement) is covered in [Dataset and Embedding Setup](3-dataset-and-embedding-setup), and how these embeddings behave when a perturbation gene is absent from every bank is treated in [Unseen Perturbation Inference](17-unseen-perturbation-inference).

Recommended reading order from here: proceed to [GEARS-Format Data Pipeline](12-gears-format-data-pipeline) to see how the AnnData that defines gene ordering is produced, then [Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split](14-perturbation-splits-and-simulation-split) to understand which gene names will hit the KG vocabulary during evaluation.


# Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split



This page explains how DyMoE-Pert partitions perturbation conditions into train, validation, and test sets, with particular depth on the default **simulation split** — a gene-level partitioning scheme that carves the test set into four generalization subgroups. It covers the split engine, the full split taxonomy, the subgroup-aware evaluation path, and the caching mechanism that makes splits reproducible across runs.

Splits operate on two granularity levels simultaneously. A *condition* is a measured perturbation such as `CEBPA+ctrl` (single) or `CEBPA+MEIS2` (combo), while the simulation split assigns conditions to sets by first partitioning the underlying *genes* into seen and out-of-distribution (OOD) pools. This design is what lets the benchmark measure extrapolation to entirely unseen genes rather than merely unseen condition labels.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L268-L317), [data_utils.py](models/data_utils.py#L135-L147)

## Split System Architecture

The split subsystem follows a three-layer separation of concerns. **Orchestration** lives in `PertData.prepare_split`, which validates the requested split name, manages the on-disk cache, and materializes results into two artifacts: a `set2conditions` dictionary mapping `train`/`val`/`test` to condition lists, and (for the simulation split) a `subgroup` dictionary. **Partitioning** lives in the `DataSplitter` class, which mutates `adata.obs` with a `split` column via gene-level or condition-level logic. **Consumption** happens in `get_dataloader`, which expands conditions into per-cell graph objects and feeds PyG loaders, and in `scPert`, which uses the subgroup dictionary for stratified test reporting.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    CLI["scripts/train.py --split --seed"] --> PS["PertData.prepare_split"]
    PS --> CACHE{"Split pickle in data/{dataset}/splits/ ?"}
    CACHE -->|"cache hit"| LOAD["Load set2conditions + subgroup"]
    CACHE -->|"cache miss"| DS["DataSplitter(adata, split_type, seen)"]
    DS -->|"simulation"| SIM["get_simulation_split"]
    DS -->|"simulation_single"| SIMS["get_simulation_split_single"]
    DS -->|"single / combo / no_test"| GSL["get_split_list"]
    SIM --> MAP["Write split column into adata.obs"]
    SIMS --> MAP
    GSL --> MAP
    MAP --> S2C["set2conditions: set name to condition list"]
    S2C --> DL["get_dataloader: train/val/test PyG loaders"]
    SIM -.->|"test_subgroup + val_subgroup"| SG["subgroup pickle, used by scPert evaluation"]
    DL --> SG
```

Split results are persisted for reproducibility. The cache file is named `{dataset}_{split}_{seed}_{train_gene_set_size}.pkl` under `data/<dataset>/splits/`; if it exists, `prepare_split` loads it instead of recomputing, and for `simulation` it additionally restores the sibling `_subgroup.pkl`. This means identical `split + seed + train_gene_set_size` triples are byte-identical across runs, which is essential when comparing ablation modes or router configurations against the same partition.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L310-L346), [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L405-L417), [data_utils.py](models/data_utils.py#L135-L198)

## The Split Taxonomy

`prepare_split` enforces a closed vocabulary of nine split modes. The two `simulation*` modes operate at gene granularity through dedicated `DataSplitter` methods; the `combo_seenN` family and `single` route through `get_split_list` with condition-level logic; the remaining modes are utility splits for training-only or inference-only workflows.

| Split | Routing inside `DataSplitter` | Test-set composition |
|---|---|---|
| `simulation` (default) | `get_simulation_split` | Four gene-level subgroups: `combo_seen0`, `combo_seen1`, `combo_seen2`, `unseen_single` |
| `simulation_single` | `get_simulation_split_single` | `unseen_single` only |
| `single` | `get_split_list`, `split_type='single'` | Random fraction of single perturbations; combos sharing those genes are excluded from training |
| `combo_seen0` | `get_split_list`, `seen=0` | Singles plus combos where **both** genes are held out |
| `combo_seen1` | `get_split_list`, `seen=1` | Singles plus combos with exactly one held-out gene |
| `combo_seen2` | `get_split_list`, `seen=2` | Random fraction of combos (both genes seen in training) |
| `no_test` | `get_split_list`, `split_type='no_test'` | None — only train/val loaders are produced |
| `no_split` | Bypasses the splitter; every condition labeled `test` | Everything, for prediction-only loading |
| `custom` | Loads a user pickle `{'train': [...], 'val': [...], 'test': [...]}` | Fully user-defined |

The `custom` mode is useful for replicating published splits or cross-paper comparisons: pass `split_dict_path` pointing to a pickled dictionary, and `prepare_split` adopts it wholesale without invoking the splitter at all.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L278-L325), [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L353-L403)

## Inside the Simulation Split

The simulation split begins by collecting every distinct perturbed gene across all non-control conditions, then sampling `train_gene_set_size` (default 0.75) of them — seeded by `seed` — as the **seen gene pool**. The remainder become the **OOD gene pool**. Conditions are then assigned by composing these pools with the perturbation's arity:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    ALL["Unique perturbed genes"] -->|"75% sampled with seed"| SEEN["Seen gene pool"]
    ALL -->|"remaining 25%"| OOD["OOD gene pool"]
    SEEN -->|"single perts"| TR["TRAIN"]
    SEEN -->|"combos with exactly one seen gene"| T1["TEST combo_seen1"]
    SEEN -->|"combos with both genes seen"| FS{"combo_seen2_train_frac = 0.75"}
    FS -->|"kept"| TR
    FS -->|"held out"| T2["TEST combo_seen2"]
    OOD -->|"single perts"| T3["TEST unseen_single"]
    OOD -->|"combos with zero seen genes"| T0["TEST combo_seen0"]
```

Each test subgroup probes a different generalization capability. The four subgroups are returned in a dictionary and persisted alongside the split:

| Subgroup | Membership rule | Generalization demanded |
|---|---|---|
| `combo_seen0` | Combos whose **both** constituent genes are OOD | New gene pair, both genes never seen — hardest setting |
| `combo_seen1` | Combos with exactly one seen gene (fully excluded from training) | Pairwise composition across the seen/OOD boundary |
| `combo_seen2` | Combos with both genes seen; 25% randomly held out | Combinatorial novelty only — the pair is new, the genes are not |
| `unseen_single` | Single-gene perturbations of OOD genes | Node-level extrapolation to unseen perturbation targets |

Two structural details matter for correctness. First, splitting is **two-stage**: after the test partition is computed, the training set itself is re-partitioned by the same gene-level splitter with 0.9/0.9 fractions to yield the validation set, and `'ctrl'` is explicitly re-appended to train before the split column is written — control cells always train regardless of composition. Second, the method asserts a complete, non-overlapping partition: `combo_seen1 + combo_seen0 + unseen_single + train + combo_seen2` must equal the total condition count, and random number generation is re-seeded immediately before the `combo_seen2` draw so the partition is deterministic even though it involves two sampling steps.

> [!TIP]
> Within the simulation split, `combo_seen1` perturbations are *always* excluded from training — there is no sampling fraction for them — while `combo_seen2` retention is directly tunable via `combo_seen2_train_frac`. Raising that fraction trades test-set size for more compositional training signal.

Sources: [data_utils.py](models/data_utils.py#L156-L166), [data_utils.py](models/data_utils.py#L231-L289), [data_utils.py](models/data_utils.py#L185-L198)

## The simulation_single Variant

`simulation_single` is the single-gene analogue: it samples the seen gene pool identically, assigns seen-gene singles to train and OOD-gene singles to test, and returns a single subgroup `{'unseen_single': ...}`. No combo perturbations participate, and the validation stage re-applies the same single-gene splitter with a 0.9 fraction. It suits datasets like Replogle K562/RPE1 where screens are single-gene only, keeping the OOD evaluation philosophy while dropping combinatorial subgroups.

Sources: [data_utils.py](models/data_utils.py#L167-L173), [data_utils.py](models/data_utils.py#L200-L229)

## Perturbation-Level Splits: single and combo_seenN

When `prepare_split` receives `single` or any `combo_seenN` name, it constructs `DataSplitter` with `split_type='combo'` and `seen` parsed from the split name's last character, delegating to `get_split_list`. This family operates directly on conditions: held-out genes are chosen randomly (scaled by the single-perturbation count times `combo_single_split_test_set_fraction`, default 0.1), then mapped back to the perturbations containing them via `get_perts_from_genes`, which classifies conditions into singles (`GENE+ctrl`) and combos (`GENEA+GENEB`).

The `seen` parameter controls how much *gene-level* novelty the test combos carry, with a `hold_outs` mechanism enforcing purity:

| Split | Test combos contain | Held out from training | Trade-off noted in code |
|---|---|---|---|
| `combo_seen0` | Both genes unseen | Every combo with any seen gene | Can shrink the dataset; `hold_outs=False` relaxes purity |
| `combo_seen1` | Exactly one unseen gene | Combos with two unseen genes | Same dataset-size caveat applies |
| `combo_seen2` | Random fraction of all combos | Nothing (all other combos stay in train) | No gene-level constraint |

In the `single` split, combos containing any held-out gene are dropped from training entirely rather than being tested — they fall outside both sets. The `no_test` mode is the degenerate case: conditions are divided into train/val at the condition level only, and downstream `scPert.train` detects the missing `test_loader` and terminates after validation without test evaluation.

Sources: [data_utils.py](models/data_utils.py#L291-L375), [data_utils.py](models/data_utils.py#L377-L399), [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L375-L398), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L660-L669)

## From Split Assignment to Dataloaders and Evaluation

Once the split column is written, `prepare_split` collapses it into `set2conditions` — a dictionary of unique condition lists per set — and `get_dataloader` expands each condition into its pre-built per-cell graph objects (one graph per cell, paired with random control cells as basal expression). Loader behavior differs by role, which is significant for reproducing benchmark numbers:

| Loader | Condition list | `shuffle` | `drop_last` | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `train_loader` | `set2conditions['train']` | `True` | `True` | Optimization epochs |
| `val_loader` | `set2conditions['val']` | `True` | `False` | Best-model selection (top-20 DE MSE) |
| `test_loader` | `set2conditions['test']` | `False` | `False` | Final deterministic evaluation |

The `no_split` mode is the exception: it labels every condition `test` and returns only a `test_loader`, which is the loading path used when running trained checkpoints on arbitrary conditions.

For `simulation` splits, evaluation becomes **stratified by generalization subgroup**. `scPert` copies the `subgroup` dictionary at construction, and after computing per-perturbation test metrics, iterates `test_subgroup` to average each metric within `combo_seen0`, `combo_seen1`, `combo_seen2`, and `unseen_single` — reported both to console and (optionally) wandb. The same stratification is applied to the deeper analysis metrics (Pearson on predicted deltas and non-dropout top-20 DE statistics). Before any of this, `prepare_split` prints the test composition per subgroup, giving an immediate sanity check on split size.

> [!TIP]
> The cache key includes `train_gene_set_size` and, when supplied, a joined string of `test_perts` — but *not* `combo_seen2_train_frac` or `combo_single_split_test_set_fraction`. Changing those latter parameters with the same seed can silently reuse a stale cache built with different fractions; clear `data/<dataset>/splits/` when experimenting with them.

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L400-L417), [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L419-L491), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L217-L235), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L681-L743)

## Driving Splits from the CLI

The training entry point exposes exactly two split-related flags: `--split` (default `simulation`) and `--seed` (default `77`) — the seed documented as the main benchmark configuration. Since `--split` has no `choices` restriction, any of the nine taxonomy names passes through to `prepare_split`'s validation. However, `scripts/train.py` calls `prepare_split` with only `split` and `seed`, so `train_gene_set_size`, `combo_seen2_train_frac`, `combo_single_split_test_set_fraction`, `test_perts`, and `custom` splits require direct `PertData` usage in Python — the CLI pins the documented 0.75/0.75/0.1 defaults.

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L33-L34), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L119-L121), [README.md](README.md#L54)

## Where to Go Next

The split system consumes the condition annotations and DE gene annotations produced upstream — see [GEARS-Format Data Pipeline](12-gears-format-data-pipeline) for how `condition` and `condition_name` columns are constructed, and [Knowledge-Graph and scGPT Embeddings](13-knowledge-graph-and-scgpt-embeddings) for how the perturbed genes indexed by splits receive their expert inputs. For how the val loader drives best-model selection and how subgroup metrics feed the full test report, continue to [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration) and [Metrics and DE Gene Analysis](18-metrics-and-de-gene-analysis). To predict individual conditions outside any split (the `no_split` pathway's typical consumer), see [Unseen Perturbation Inference](17-unseen-perturbation-inference), and for the complete flag reference, [Configuration Reference](19-configuration-reference).

# Training Loop Orchestration



This page dissects how a DyMoE-Pert training run is wired end-to-end: the CLI bootstrap in `scripts/train.py`, the `scPert` trainer class that owns the epoch lifecycle, and the per-step mechanics that fuse task loss with MoE balance loss under a single-GPU or PyG-DataParallel regime. The focus is strictly on *orchestration* — who calls whom, in what order, and with what state. For the mathematical content of the loss terms themselves, see [Prediction Decoder and Loss](11-prediction-decoder-and-loss); for router internals, see [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss).

## Orchestration Architecture: Three Layers of Control

The training system follows a deliberate three-layer separation: a **CLI bootstrap layer** that validates configuration and resolves hardware, a **trainer layer** (`scPert`) that owns all mutable training state (optimizer, scheduler, best-model snapshot), and a **compute layer** (`scPert_Model`) that remains a pure forward-pass graph emitting predictions plus an auxiliary MoE statistics dictionary. The trainer layer is the single source of truth — the model itself never adjusts its own learning rate, checkpoint state, or parallelism. This layering means the same `scPert.train()` method serves both interactive Python sessions and the CLI, and it is why `save_model` can serialize a consistent `(config.pkl, model.pt)` pair regardless of how the run was launched.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph L1["Layer 1 — CLI Bootstrap (scripts/train.py)"]
        A[parse_args] --> B[resolve_device]
        B --> C[Multi-GPU validation]
    end
    subgraph L2["Layer 2 — Trainer (models/scpert.py::scPert)"]
        D[PertData handoff<br/>__init__] --> E[model_initialize<br/>config + model + CPU best_model]
        E --> F[train<br/>optimizer / scheduler / epoch loop]
        F --> G[save_model<br/>config.pkl + model.pt]
    end
    subgraph L3["Layer 3 — Compute (models/model.py::scPert_Model)"]
        H[forward: pred, moe_aux]
    end
    subgraph SUP["Support Modules"]
        I[loss_fct<br/>models/utils.py]
        J[evaluate / compute_metrics<br/>models/inference.py]
    end
    C --> D
    F -->|pred, moe_aux| H
    F -->|task loss| I
    F -->|epoch-end eval| J
    F --> G
```

Note the direction of data flow in the diagram: the compute layer pushes `(pred, moe_aux)` upward, but all control signals (gradient clipping, LR stepping, best-model decisions) originate from the trainer. Supporting modules are stateless function libraries invoked *by* the trainer, never the reverse.

Sources: [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L70-L158), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L162-L248), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L533-L744)

## Bootstrap Phase: Configuration and Device Resolution

Execution begins in `main()`, which first normalizes the MoE configuration before any hardware decisions are made. Two CLI constraints are enforced eagerly: `--moe-router-mode fixed_uniform` or `--moe-ablation-mode base_only` forces `moe_balance_weight` to `0.0`, because both configurations make the balance term structurally meaningless. Device resolution then proceeds through `resolve_device`, which maps `auto` to `cuda:0` when CUDA is available and `cpu` otherwise; requesting a CUDA device that does not exist raises immediately rather than silently falling back. Multi-GPU requests are validated *before* data loading — the code requires `torch.cuda.is_available()`, at least two IDs in `--device-ids`, all IDs within range, and `--device` pinned to the first ID — so a misconfigured run fails in milliseconds instead of after dataset preprocessing. Finally, `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` is set at module import time (before `torch` is imported) to reduce fragmentation on long training runs.

| Parameter | Default | Orchestration Role |
|---|---|---|
| `--epochs` | 25 | Total epoch count passed to `scPert.train()` |
| `--lr` | 0.001 | Base learning rate for AdamW |
| `--batch-size` / `--test-batch-size` | 64 / inherits train | Train vs. evaluation loader sizes |
| `--multi-gpu` / `--device-ids` | off / `0,1,2,3` | Triggers PyG DataParallel + DataListLoader path |
| `--moe-balance-weight` | 0.0 | Weight of router balance loss; zeroed for fixed-uniform/base-only |
| `--moe-ablation-mode` | `full` | Structural ablation; `base_only` also zeroes balance weight |
| `--seed` | 77 | Passed to `prepare_split`, controls perturbation split |

Sources: [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L28-L67), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L70-L106), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L8-L9)

## Trainer Construction: Data Handoff and Model Initialization

The CLI then performs a strict sequence: `PertData` loads the GEARS-format dataset, `prepare_split` applies the perturbation split, and `get_dataloader` materializes train/val/test loaders — with `use_data_list_loader=args.multi_gpu` switching the train loader to PyG's `DataListLoader` when parallelism is requested. The `scPert` constructor receives the loaded `pert_data` object and extracts everything the training loop will need at loss and evaluation time: precomputed **control expression** (`ctrl_expression`, the mean of control cells moved to device), the per-perturbation **non-zero gene filter** (`dict_filter`), gene/pert index maps, and the dataset identity (`split`, `seed`) that later gates subgroup analysis. This eager extraction means the training loop never touches `adata` for loss computation — it operates on tensors already resident on the target device.

`model_initialize` is deliberately separated from the constructor so the same trainer can be re-configured (e.g., `load_pretrained` calls it after parsing a saved config). It validates the MoE mode strings again defensively, freezes the full configuration into `self.config` (including `embedding_size=512`), instantiates `scPert_Model` onto the device, and — critically — creates `self.best_model` as a **CPU deepcopy** of the freshly initialized model. This snapshot slot is reused by the training loop's checkpoint rule and by `save_model`, guaranteeing that serialized weights never carry parallel-wrapper prefixes.

Sources: [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L108-L132), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L217-L248), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L271-L355)

## Training Setup: Optimizer, Scheduler, and Parallel Wrapping

The `train()` method begins by fetching the train/val loaders and deciding the parallelism mode in one expression: parallelism requires *both* `use_parallel=True` and at least two device IDs — a single-GPU `device_ids=[0]` request deliberately degrades to the plain path rather than wrapping in DataParallel. When parallel, the model is wrapped in `torch_geometric.nn.DataParallel` with `output_device` pinned to the first ID; this wrapper is what makes the DataListLoader batch format (a Python list of `Data` objects) valid. Two state objects are then created in fixed order: a CPU `best_model` deepcopy of the wrapped model's *unwrapped* parameters, and the trainable-parameter list filtered by `requires_grad` — which also serves as a guard rail, raising `RuntimeError` if the model exposes no gradients.

The optimizer is AdamW with the CLI-provided `lr` and a fixed `weight_decay=1e-5`. The scheduler is `OneCycleLR` constructed with `max_lr=0.01` and `steps_per_epoch=len(train_loader)`, and it is stepped **once per epoch** (line 633), not per batch — an important deviation from OneCycle's typical per-step contract. Gradient updates are bounded by `nn.utils.clip_grad_value_` at `clip_value=1.0`, applied to the pre-collected `trainable_parameters` list rather than re-scanning `model.parameters()` each step.

> [!TIP]
> `OneCycleLR` is constructed with a hard-coded `max_lr=0.01` while the CLI `--lr` only sets AdamW's initial learning rate. Because the scheduler is stepped per *epoch* rather than per batch, the effective LR trajectory decouples from both values' textbook behavior — when reproducing or tuning runs, treat `--lr` and the scheduler's 0.01 peak as two independent knobs.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L556-L578), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L611-L612), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L633)

## The Epoch Loop: Step Anatomy

Each epoch executes a fixed five-stage step pattern, visualized below. Stage ordering is invariant: batch preparation happens *before* `zero_grad` so that device transfers never overlap with gradient state; the forward pass returns a `(pred, moe_aux)` tuple that `_split_model_output` normalizes into a 2-tuple even when MoE telemetry is disabled; and the composite loss is formed by adding `balance_weight × balance_loss` to the task loss only when the model actually emitted a balance term.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S0[batch from train_loader] --> S1{"Is batch a list?<br/>DataListLoader path"}
    S1 -->|Yes| S2a["cat y to device<br/>keep list for PyG DataParallel"]
    S1 -->|No| S2b["batch.to(device)<br/>single Batch"]
    S2a --> S3["optimizer.zero_grad<br/>forward → pred, moe_aux"]
    S2b --> S3
    S3 --> S4["loss_fct → task_loss<br/>per-perturbation focal + direction + cosine"]
    S4 --> S5{"moe_aux has<br/>balance_loss?"}
    S5 -->|Yes| S6["loss = task + weight × balance"]
    S5 -->|No| S7["loss = task_loss"]
    S6 --> S8["loss.backward<br/>clip_grad_value_ 1.0<br/>optimizer.step"]
    S7 --> S8
    S8 --> S9{"step % 50 == 0?"}
    S9 -->|Yes| S10["print loss + MoE router telemetry"]
    S9 -->|No| S0b[next step]
    S10 --> S0b
    S0b --> E1[epoch exhausted]
    E1 --> E2["scheduler.step"]
    E2 --> E3[evaluate train + val]
```

The task loss itself is computed by `loss_fct`, which loops over the *set of perturbations in the batch* and accumulates four components per perturbation — focal MSE (scaled by a sigmoid of `|target − ctrl|`), optionally class-weighted MSE over `key_genes`, a direction loss penalizing sign disagreement with control, and cosine similarity loss — plus an optional L1 penalty over model parameters, finally normalizing by the number of distinct perturbations. The training loop supplies the precomputed `ctrl_expression` and `dict_filter` from constructor state, so the loss function requires no data access beyond the batch. The L1 term iterates `model.parameters()` via a generator passed by the loop — under DataParallel this traverses the replicated wrapper, which is acceptable since replicas share parameter storage with the primary module.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L597-L633), [utils.py](/models/utils.py#L343-L421), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L62-L77)

## Batch Preparation: Single GPU vs Multi-GPU

The loop-level branching for batch handling is concentrated in one helper, `_prepare_train_batch`, keeping the epoch loop itself agnostic to parallelism. The two paths differ in both *data format* and *device strategy*, summarized below:

| Aspect | Single GPU Path | Multi-GPU Path (PyG DataParallel) |
|---|---|---|
| Loader type | PyG `DataLoader` (scatters into `Batch`) | `DataListLoader` (`use_data_list_loader=True`) |
| Batch object | `torch_geometric.data.Batch` | `list[Data]`, one per replica |
| Device transfer | `pyg_batch.to(device)` after `Batch.from_data_list` | Labels only (`torch.cat([data.y ...]).to(device)`); PyG DataParallel scatters graphs internally |
| Forward input | Batch | Raw list — wrapper distributes |
| Same helper used by `evaluate` | Yes (`_prepare_batch` in inference.py) | Yes |

The asymmetry in device transfer is the subtle part: on the multi-GPU path, graph data is *never* manually moved — PyG's DataParallel handles scattering to each replica — while targets `y` are concatenated and moved to the primary device once, so the loss can be computed on gathered outputs. Perturbation labels ride along as plain Python strings (one per `Data`), avoiding tensor scatter entirely. This is why the model output path `_split_model_output` and the loss path can both assume device-consistent tensors regardless of replica count.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L45-L55), [inference.py](/models/inference.py#L22-L41), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L561-L571)

## Mid-Epoch Logging and MoE Telemetry

Every 50 steps, the loop prints total loss and — when a balance term is active — the decomposition into task loss and the weighted balance contribution. Immediately after, `_format_moe_stats` converts the raw `moe_aux` dictionary into a one-line telemetry string. This is the training loop's principal observability surface: it reports the active ablation mode (decoded from a tensor-safe integer lookup), the router mode (`dynamic` vs `fixed_uniform`), the active expert mask, per-expert **applied vs raw** router weight averages, min/max weight ranges, and the router weight entropy. All tensor values are explicitly detached and moved to CPU inside the formatter, so logging never retains graph references across steps — a quiet but deliberate memory-hygiene choice in a loop that runs thousands of iterations. When `--no-moe-router-stats` is passed, `moe_aux` arrives as `None` and both the balance-loss branch and telemetry branch are skipped, reducing the loop to a conventional PyTorch step.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L615-L631), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L112-L159), [train.py](/scripts/train.py#L52-L53)

## Epoch End: Evaluation and Best-Model Selection

After the final `optimizer.step()` of an epoch, the scheduler steps once, and both train and validation loaders are passed through `evaluate` — a `torch.no_grad` inference sweep that collects predictions, ground truth, and per-sample DE-gene slices, then delegates to `compute_metrics` for per-perturbation MSE and Pearson correlation. The loop prints four headline numbers (overall and Top-20-DE MSE for both splits) and optionally logs MSE and Pearson (all-gene and DE variants) to W&B when tracking is enabled. The checkpoint rule is a strict improvement test on a single metric: **validation Top-20 DE MSE** (`val_metrics['mse_de']`). When it beats the running minimum, the *unwrapped* model is deep-copied to CPU, replacing the previous best snapshot. There is no early stopping — the loop always runs the full `--epochs` budget — so the best-model mechanism, not the loop terminator, is what protects against late-epoch overfitting.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> TrainingStep
    TrainingStep --> TrainingStep: steps within epoch
    TrainingStep --> SchedulerStep: epoch exhausted
    SchedulerStep --> EvalTrain: evaluate(train_loader)
    EvalTrain --> EvalVal: evaluate(val_loader)
    EvalVal --> CheckpointDecision: compute_metrics
    CheckpointDecision --> SnapshotCPU: mse_de < min_val
    CheckpointDecision --> KeepBest: otherwise
    SnapshotCPU --> TrainingStep: next epoch
    KeepBest --> TrainingStep: next epoch
    TrainingStep --> TestPhase: all epochs done
```

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L633-L663), [inference.py](/models/inference.py#L42-L87), [inference.py](/models/inference.py#L89-L120)

## Post-Training: Testing, Analysis, and Checkpointing

Once the epoch budget is exhausted, `self.best_model` is promoted from the snapshot and the test phase begins — *only if* a `test_loader` exists; otherwise the method returns early with an explicit notice. The test path re-applies the parallel pattern: the best (unwrapped, CPU-resident) model is moved to device and, when training ran parallel, re-wrapped in a fresh PyG DataParallel for the inference sweep. After `evaluate` and `compute_metrics`, the code runs two deeper passes — `deeper_analysis` and `non_dropout_analysis` — and, when `self.split == 'simulation'`, performs per-subgroup aggregation over the test subgroups defined by the split, logging each subgroup metric to W&B and stdout. Control finally returns to the CLI, where `save_model` writes `config.pkl` and `model.pt`; the state dict is taken from `_unwrap_parallel_model(self.best_model)`, so checkpoint files are always loadable by `load_pretrained` without prefix surgery (though `load_pretrained` retains a defensive `module.` strip for legacy checkpoints).

> [!TIP]
> The best-model snapshot lives on CPU for the entire training run — every improvement triggers a deepcopy off-device. This costs memory but buys two guarantees: checkpoint saving never interferes with the training device, and the test phase starts from a known-clean, prefix-free state rather than a live replica of a parallel wrapper.

Sources: [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L665-L744), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L399-L422), [scpert.py](/models/scpert.py#L357-L397)

## Where to Go Next

The orchestration described here is the skeleton; the pages below fill in the organs. For the exact CLI invocations that trigger this loop, see [Training and Prediction Commands](4-training-and-prediction-commands). To understand what `moe_aux` carries and why balance loss exists, read [Soft Router and Balance Loss](8-soft-router-and-balance-loss) and [Ablation Modes Framework](9-ablation-modes-framework); the composition of `loss_fct`'s four terms is detailed in [Prediction Decoder and Loss](11-prediction-decoder-and-loss). The `evaluate`/`compute_metrics` contract and subgroup analysis reporting are expanded in [Metrics and DE Gene Analysis](18-metrics-and-de-gene-analysis), the DataListLoader mechanics in [Multi-GPU Parallel Training](16-multi-gpu-parallel-training), and how the `simulation` split populates `test_subgroup` in [Perturbation Splits and Simulation Split](14-perturbation-splits-and-simulation-split). For a consolidated table of every parameter mentioned above, consult [Configuration Reference](19-configuration-reference).

# Multi-GPU Parallel Training



This page explains how DyMoE-Pert scales training across multiple GPUs. The implementation is built on **PyTorch Geometric (PyG) DataParallel** combined with PyG's **DataListLoader**, using a single-process data-parallel strategy rather than Distributed Data Parallel (DDP). You will learn how the CLI flags activate parallel mode, how batches change shape as they move through the data, model, and loss layers, and how checkpointing stays consistent whether you train on one GPU or many. This page assumes familiarity with the training loop described in [Training Loop Orchestration](15-training-loop-orchestration).

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L13-L16), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L36-L37)

## Why PyG DataParallel, Not Plain DataParallel or DDP

Every training sample in DyMoE-Pert is a **variable-size cell graph** (a `torch_geometric.data.Data` object), not a fixed-shape tensor. Standard `torch.nn.DataParallel` cannot scatter lists of graphs, and DDP adds multi-process complexity (rank management, process-group initialization) that is unnecessary for the moderate graph sizes here. The codebase therefore imports `torch_geometric.nn.DataParallel` — with a graceful fallback if the import fails — because PyG's wrapper knows how to scatter a *list* of graphs across replicas and gather their outputs back.

```python
try:
    from torch_geometric.nn import DataParallel as PyGDataParallel
except ImportError:
    PyGDataParallel = None
```

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L13-L16)

## Enabling Multi-GPU: CLI Flags and Validation

Multi-GPU mode is off by default and activated with a single flag. The training entry point defines two related arguments: `--multi-gpu` (store-true, described as "Use PyG DataParallel with DataListLoader") and `--device-ids`, which defaults to `"0,1,2,3"` and accepts either a comma-separated list of GPU indices or the special values `auto`/`all` to select every visible CUDA device.

| Flag | Default | Behavior |
|------|---------|----------|
| `--multi-gpu` | off (flag) | Enables PyG DataParallel + DataListLoader |
| `--device-ids` | `"0,1,2,3"` | GPU ids, e.g. `0,1`; `auto`/`all` uses all visible GPUs |
| `--device` | `auto` | Must match the **first** entry of `--device-ids` |
| `--batch-size` | `64` | Full-batch size, split across GPUs by DataParallel |

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L36-L38), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L65-L68)

Before any GPU work starts, `main()` runs a strict validation gate. It verifies that CUDA is available, requires **at least two** device ids (a single id falls back to the normal single-GPU path), checks every id against `torch.cuda.device_count()`, and enforces that `--device` equals `cuda:{device_ids[0]}` — because the first id becomes the master/output device. On success, the process calls `torch.cuda.set_device` and `torch.cuda.empty_cache()`, and the file pre-sets `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` at import time to reduce fragmentation under multi-replica memory pressure.

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L79-L99), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L5)

## Architecture of the Parallel Stack

The parallel mechanism spans three layers that must stay mutually consistent: the **data layer** decides whether batches are merged `Batch` objects or raw lists; the **model layer** decides whether the model is a bare `scPert_Model` or a PyG-parallel wrapper; and the **checkpoint layer** always unwraps to the bare model before saving or deep-copying. Helper predicates (`_is_pyg_parallel`, `_is_parallel_model`, `_unwrap_parallel_model`) keep these decisions centralized.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph CLI["scripts/train.py"]
        A["--multi-gpu --device-ids 0,1"] --> B{"Validation gate<br/>CUDA? ≥2 ids? device match?"}
    end
    B -->|"use_data_list_loader=True"| C["PertData.get_dataloader<br/>DataListLoader → list of graphs"]
    B -->|"use_parallel=True, device_ids"| D["scPert.train<br/>PyGDataParallel(model, device_ids)"]
    C --> E["List batch (N graphs)"]
    E --> F["PyG DataParallel scatter"]
    F --> G["GPU 0: sub-batch<br/>replica forward"]
    F --> H["GPU 1: sub-batch<br/>replica forward"]
    F --> I["GPU k: sub-batch<br/>replica forward"]
    G & H & I --> J["Gather on output device<br/>(device_ids[0])"]
    J --> K["loss_fct + MoE balance loss<br/>on master device"]
    K --> L["backward → grad sync → optimizer.step"]
    L --> M["Checkpoint: _unwrap_parallel_model<br/>bare state_dict, no 'module.' prefix"]
    D --> M
```

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L32-L41), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L79-L126)

## Data Layer: DataListLoader vs DataLoader

The switch happens inside `PertData.get_dataloader` through one line: `Loader = DataListLoader if use_data_list_loader else DataLoader`. When `train.py` passes `use_data_list_loader=args.multi_gpu`, all three loaders (train/val/test) switch types together, so training and evaluation always see the same batch representation. The train loader additionally uses `shuffle=True, drop_last=True` — dropping the ragged final batch guarantees every step sees a full batch, which keeps per-replica sub-batch sizes balanced across the `len(device_ids)` splits.

| Aspect | Single GPU (`DataLoader`) | Multi-GPU (`DataListLoader`) |
|--------|---------------------------|------------------------------|
| Batch type | Merged `torch_geometric.data.Batch` | Python `list` of `Data` graphs |
| Graph merging | `Batch.from_data_list` (done manually) | Deferred to DataParallel's scatter |
| Train shuffling / drop_last | `True` / `True` | `True` / `True` (identical) |
| Per-GPU graphs per step | N/A | `batch_size / num_gpus` (approximately) |

Sources: [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L419-L438), [ProcePertdata.py](models/ProcePertdata.py#L473-L480)

## One Training Step Under Parallelism

Each step flows through `_prepare_train_batch`, which is the junction point between the two batch worlds. If the batch is a **list** (parallel mode) it concatenates labels `y` onto the master device, collects `perts`, and — when the model is PyG-parallel — hands the raw list directly to the model so DataParallel performs the scatter. If the model is *not* parallel but the batch is a list, it defensively merges into a `Batch` first, so a saved parallel pipeline still runs on one GPU. The sequence below traces the parallel path for one optimizer step.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as DataListLoader
    participant P as _prepare_train_batch
    participant M as PyGDataParallel (master GPU 0)
    participant R as Replicas (GPU 0..k)
    participant O as Optimizer (AdamW + OneCycleLR)

    L->>P: list of N cell graphs
    P->>P: y = cat(labels).to(cuda:0); perts = [data.pert]
    P->>M: pass list unmodified (is_pyg_parallel → True)
    M->>R: scatter graphs, replicate module
    R->>R: forward → (pred_i, moe_aux_i)
    R->>M: gather pred (concat on cuda:0), gather aux dict
    M->>O: pred, moe_aux returned to training loop
    O->>O: loss_fct(pred, y, perts) + balance_weight * balance_loss
    O->>O: loss.backward() → grads reduced to master module
    O->>O: clip_grad_value_(1.0); optimizer.step(); scheduler.step()
```

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L44-L56), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L597-L612)

> [!TIP]
> The `_prepare_train_batch` dual-path design means a checkpoint trained with `--multi-gpu` can be retrained or fine-tuned in single-GPU mode without any code change — the batch adapter detects the model type at runtime, not from saved configuration.

## Loss Computation and MoE Balance Loss Aggregation

Two loss terms are computed per step, both parallel-aware. The **task loss** (`loss_fct`) receives `pred` gathered on the master device plus the original `perts` list and full-batch labels `y`, and also receives `model_params` as a generator over `self.model.parameters()` — since DataParallel shares parameter objects with its replicas, this transparently covers the underlying model regardless of wrapping. The **MoE balance loss** is handled by `_moe_balance_loss`, which reads `moe_balance_weight` from the *unwrapped* model (weights are attributes of the bare module, not the wrapper) and calls `.mean()` on the gathered balance tensor — necessary because PyG's gather concatenates per-replica auxiliary values into one tensor spanning all replicas.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L64-L77), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L604-L609)

The MoE router statistics logging follows the same defensive pattern: `_format_moe_stats` reshapes gathered router weights with `reshape(-1, last_dim)` before averaging, so the logged `applied_alpha_*` / `raw_alpha_*` values are correct whether one or four replicas contributed to the batch. Note that when `--moe-router-mode fixed_uniform` or `--moe-ablation-mode base_only` is set, `main()` forces `moe_balance_weight = 0.0`, disabling the auxiliary loss entirely in both modes.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L112-L169), [train.py](scripts/train.py#L73-L75)

## Gradient Semantics and Effective Batch Size

Under PyG DataParallel, each optimizer step processes the **full** `--batch-size` worth of graphs: DataListLoader produces N-graph batches, the scatter divides them across `len(device_ids)` replicas, replica gradients are summed back onto the master module during `backward()`, and `AdamW` updates once. Consequently `steps_per_epoch=len(train_loader)` (used by `OneCycleLR`) is identical in single- and multi-GPU mode for the same batch size — the schedule does not shift when you add GPUs. Gradient clipping via `nn.utils.clip_grad_value_(trainable_parameters, 1.0)` is likewise applied to the unified master parameters after gradient reduction, so optimization dynamics match the single-GPU run modulo floating-point summation order.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L574-L578), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L610-L612)

> [!TIP]
> Because DataParallel replicates the module every forward pass, multi-GPU speedups diminish for small models (default `hidden_size=64`). The feature pays off most on large datasets like `replogle_k562_essential`, where per-step wall time is dominated by the graph-parallel GNN forward rather than replication overhead.

## Checkpointing and `module.` Prefix Hygiene

The most common source of bugs in data-parallel training is saving the *wrapper's* state dict, whose keys carry a `module.` prefix. DyMoE-Pert eliminates this at three points: **best-model tracking** deep-copies the unwrapped model to CPU (`deepcopy(_unwrap_parallel_model(self.model)).cpu()`) whenever validation `mse_de` improves; **`save_model`** serializes `_unwrap_parallel_model(self.best_model).state_dict()`; and **`load_pretrained`** additionally strips a legacy `module.` prefix from old checkpoints (`k[7:]` for keys starting with `'module.'`) for backward compatibility with earlier data-parallel runs. The result: every saved `model.pt` is directly loadable into a bare `scPert_Model`.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L660-L666), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L399-L422), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L385-L395)

## Evaluation and Test Phase Under Parallelism

Per-epoch evaluation reuses the wrapped parallel model as-is: `evaluate(train_loader, self.model, self.device)` is called with the PyG-parallel wrapper intact, and `inference.py` mirrors the training-side batch adapter in `_prepare_batch` — list batches are passed through when the model is PyG-parallel, otherwise merged into a `Batch` — with the extra responsibility of slicing per-cell `de_idx` differentially-expressed gene subsets from the gathered predictions. The `evaluate` function also skips a redundant `.to(device)` when it detects either `nn.DataParallel` or the PyG wrapper, avoiding accidental re-hosting of the distributed module.

Sources: [inference.py](models/inference.py#L18-L34), [inference.py](models/inference.py#L42-L51), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L635-L638)

After training completes, the best model is **re-wrapped** in a fresh `PyGDataParallel` for the final test evaluation, then immediately unwrapped before the results are returned (`self.best_model = _unwrap_parallel_model(test_model)`), so the object stored on `scPert` for downstream use by `predict()` and `GI_predict()` is always the bare model on `self.device`.

Sources: [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L671-L682)

## Configuration Summary and Troubleshooting

The table below consolidates every validation guard and runtime failure mode specific to multi-GPU training, with the exact error the code raises.

| Condition | Raised error / behavior | Fix |
|-----------|------------------------|-----|
| No CUDA devices | `RuntimeError: --multi-gpu was requested but torch.cuda.is_available() is False` | Use `--device cpu` (multi-GPU unsupported on CPU) |
| Fewer than 2 ids | `ValueError: --multi-gpu needs at least two GPU ids` | Pass ≥2 ids, or drop `--multi-gpu` |
| Out-of-range ids | `ValueError: Invalid GPU ids [...]` | Check `torch.cuda.device_count()` |
| `--device` ≠ first id | `ValueError: --device must match the first --device-ids entry` | Set `--device cuda:0` for ids `0,1` |
| PyG wrapper unavailable | `RuntimeError: torch_geometric.nn.DataParallel is unavailable` | Upgrade/repair `torch_geometric` install |
| `no trainable parameters` | `RuntimeError: No trainable parameters available for optimizer.` | Verify model init completed |

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L79-L93), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L563-L566), [scpert.py](models/scpert.py#L574-L576)

Two practical notes complete the operational picture. First, `--test-batch-size` defaults to `--batch-size`; since evaluation gathers predictions to one device, a very large test batch can pressure master-GPU memory even though compute is distributed. Second, the printed training config at startup always reports `multi_gpu=... device_ids=...`, so you can confirm the parallel configuration before the (potentially long) dataset load begins.

Sources: [train.py](scripts/train.py#L101-L117)

## Where to Go Next
